Reviews.120964:
TL;DR: The game is much better, but if you don't like Sandbox type find your own adventure games or space exploration games, this might not be for you. It's a much wider puddle than E:D is right now, but nonetheless still a puddle. The base building aspect of the game helps relief some of these problems, and building your own fleet is a treat. Game is still grindy.

Detailed review:
I purchased the game back when the first big update came out, and I spent a little bit of time in the game then. It was... simple. There wasn't much to do and the performance was still pretty bad.

Today, however, the game is so much more. It has expanded into a much fuller game and performance is much more acceptable. It is important to understand this game is still a find your own adventure kinda game, with a high degree of freedom. I'd say it's close to E:D in its autonomy given to the player, except there's a few missions that will really help you out in the long run in NMS.

Space flight and combat, though, is really horrible. Control is sluggish, flight model completely unrealistic, but it does get you from point A to point B. If you're looking for space combat, I'd suggest you look at E:D instead. First person combat is quite forgettable and not really too fun, so for that I'd say look for other shooter games or maybe SC instead.  

There are lots of planets (obviously), but you start to notice patterns really quickly. Star fish on rocks that only give you material to make metal parts, specific kind of organism that looks like a jumping sex toy, every planet has some kind of flying organism with wings, etc. So far it's not been annoying, but if seeing new species is going to be a core gameplay for you, then you may start seeing more recognizable patterns than you would like.  

Mining and base building is very underrated and very fun. Searching for places to put autominers, researching new parts for your base, upgrades for your ship, tools and exosuit have become my core gameplay loop and is really satisfying. The amazing thing about this game is that aesthetics are not tied to item tier, so if you come by a beautiful class C ship, you can upgrade it all the way to class S. Freighters are the exception, and I heard stories of people spending up to 16 hours of just freighter hunting to find the exact right one they want.

My biggest gripe so far (besides performance and the lack of depth of the game, although deeper than E:D) is UI design and inventory management. The UI language is somewhat consistent, but the controls are not. Sometimes, you can only right click to go back, but other times you must use esc. A lot of things are not immediately apparently how you are supposed to interact with, and the lack of a button to "buy all" or craft multiple (I know this exists but I still haven't figured out how yet, which really speaks to how ridiculous the UI is) items at the same time is really getting on my nerves. A large chuck of my play time belongs to holding down the E key for a long time - the fact that selecting things also use the E key and typically have a long hold-time to activate does not help this.  

That said, the game is very fun and is gorgeous in a lot of aspects. For those looking for space sim, E:D, F-Sim, Orbiter and KSP are what I will point you to. Planets orbit in impossible orbits, physics is questionable (but I mean I guess you do have a magical gun that can absorb an entire landmass for you) and it is definitely not a space sim. However, it's more akin to Minecraft in space with much more upgrades you can get, but also much more creative restriction.

Watch the trailer, watch the gameplay. If you think you'll enjoy the gameplay loops, then I do recommend this game. For 20ish $ depending on region, it's quite value. The years of free updates really really helped improve the game and make it unique.

Reviews.120976:
Despite what was indisputably a rocky launch for this game, Hello Games has been continually working to improve and add to this game and their efforts really show.  This is a really fun, immersive space exploration game that has more depth to it than I initially expected of it.  Normally I'm not a big fan of survival games, but NMS is on par with Subnautica for me in terms of finding the right balance between survival, building, exploration, and story.  There are stories there for you to follow, but you are free to do as you wish and find your own way within the galaxy and pursue what appeals most to you.  Ordinarily that kind of freedom can be daunting, but NMS's quests, storyline, and lore provide enough guidance and direction for you to get your bearings and find what you want.

While there is combat in the game, it is nothing exceptional and any FPS or space sim veteran will not find much challenge to it, especially once acquiring some decent upgrades.  But the combat isn't the point in NMS, it's about the exploration and discovery.  For me, this is something that is lacking in a lot of games in this particular genre.  NMS delivers enough variety and spectacle that always has me wanting to jump to just one more system, explore one more planet just to see what new things it might show me, land at just one more space station in the hopes of seeing a new ship that I really want.  Being able to name the things you discover, from your bases and ships to the plants, animals, and minerals you scan is also quite refreshing and lets you feel like you are truly putting your own mark within the game.

The multiplayer is also completely optional for the most part and you can partake of it as much or as little as you wish.  Once you reach the place in the game where you can freely interact with other players outside of friends joining, you generally will have enough feel for how you want to go with it.  You can set your game to allow friends to join you freely or not, and the in-game voice com is surprisingly decent and not a pain to utilize.  Playing and exploring together can be a lot of fun, and friends jumping in and out is relatively seamless even if one of them was the "host" that you joined.  Visiting their bases and yours is also relatively painless, though some bugs still exist in terms of base placement when combined with terrain modification.

If you are into space exploration games then I would highly recommend No Man's Sky.  The graphics and audio in this game will appeal to any sci-fi grognard while the procedural generation of systems, ships, and worlds will create quite a wide array of variety for some time to come.  While you will come across similar things over time, there is enough difference between most where it will not always feel like the same thing over and over every time.  More than once I have stopped and looked around at the beauty of an alien world that I was on, all my other goals and drives simply put on hold for a moment as I took in my surroundings and just enjoyed them for being there.  Multiplayer is optional but can be fun with friends, and you can explore, build, and fight as much or as little as you wish.  I am impressed with how far this game has come since its initial release which I avoided but heard and saw plenty about.  Hello Games continues to put out new and compelling content for this game, and all of it without having to pay a single extra cent to access and enjoy.  No DLCs, no paywalls, just the game that you paid for.  In its current form this is a game that I am thoroughly enjoying and can see myself playing for some time to come, and I look forward to seeing what else is in store for it.

An awful, garbage PC port of an all right game. Is the game worth 55 eur? In my opinion, no. Wait for a discount. I'd never spend this big amount of money for a clearly unoptimised port of a console game. What makes it a bad PC port? Well, the controls for keyboard and mouse are pathetic. Why do I have to hold a button down like a peasant to confirm every single action? Why is the menu for base building a complete disaster? Who thought that a menu with horizontal scrolling would be perfect for a PC user? Why do I have to scroll through so many blueprints just to find the one? Why isn't there a search function, considering there are so many of these bps? Why couldn't you have implemented a base building menu as simple as something Subnautica has, where it opens up a window of the bps and you can just point and click the part you want, instead of scrolling like some caveman. 

Better yet, why are there no hotkeys? What the hell. Tell me WHY I have to press G to switch between weapons/tools. Why the fuck I can't just press 1, 2, 3 etc to switch between them. Or scroll my mouse wheel, quickly changing between each tools. WHO in their right mind decided controls like these would be appropriate for a PC game? Not having hotkeys is a completely immature design decision. Even flight controls are complete ass. I can't rebind pitch/yaw for some odd reason. It's no excuse, because Elite: Dangerous has amazing K + M controls for spaceships that make combat and exploration satisfying. But in NMS, the spaceship controls like a snail on crack in a whorehouse. 

I'll just say that the UI and controls need a major overhaul, as of right now navigating through it isn't good. A lot of QoL updates are needed. Or good mods that would fix the menu garbage. There are some mods like Instant Actions that make the game a bit better, but basic things like keybinds are still missing.

The game is great if you enjoy mining and grinding, mining and grinding, mining and grinding, 'cause this game is all it is at this core. Collecting resources, replenishing your tools and gear with said resources, grinding for credits, grinding for blueprints, grinding for gear/ship/tools upgrades. It's all about that grind, baby! Basically, it's a chore keeping everything maintained. Oh, my omnitool needs replenishing? Better grind some carbon... Oh wait, now my suit is low on life-support, better collect some oxygen. Thankfully, most of the resource grinds can be mitigated by playing in creative mode, which I highly recommend. What this game lacks, is something to do in the game. Sure it's a sandbox game, so you have to pretty much think up your own goals. But when you think about it, once you remove the resource grind from the game, what's there to do? Maxing out your ship, maxing out your suit upgrades, maxing out your omnitool, building a base, exploring different systems and planets. But once you do that, what's there to do? Like, actual gameplay. Exploration? I love exploring, but it gets stale pretty fast seeing planets in different colours, with a different hazard each time and the fauna AI being the same between different species.

The good thing about this game is that it often goes on sale and it's fun to play with friends, just messing around. The graphics are beautiful and the sound work is fantastic. There's some great roleplay aspects that this game does good than others, such as player customisation from various races and alien language learning, which imo is an interesting feature. The game offers deep base building, which allows you to build on land and underwater. The stations are filled with lively aliens and ships coming aboard, which you can buy (but sadly, you can't customise your ship). They also offer traders, other type of merchants and a mission board that sends you on a quest on a local planet. There's also a player hub where you can do community missions. All those things make the game a bit more lively and not so lonely, as you're exploring the systems.

I'm thumbing this game down because I believe the price doesn't reflect what you get. For something like 20 eur, it's worth a buy. But for the full price that Steam offers isn't worth it in my opinion, as it feels like an updated version of Spore's space stage (except they botched the PC controls). As I mentioned before, if you're offering 55 eur, the price of a AAA game, I'm expecting to receive an optimised PC port with good, satisfying controls that flow and not something that an intern cooked up in his I.T. supply closet in five minutes. For a game that features exploration as one of its main features, it doesn't offer much in terms of it. Instead of fixing core mechanics and QoL issues, the devs keep adding frivolous fluff like taming/riding animals. Pointless little things that make you ooh and awe at first sight, but add nothing to gameplay. The game has a lot of potential, the devs just need to stop pleasing the community and actually fix their game.

Forget the history of disappointment and broken promises, if you can.  This game isn't for everyone, but I love it and am closing in on 1000 hours of play time.

There isn't a story mode as such.  There is lore, historical content, some mystery and a backstory to unravel.  It's all disposable.  Think of it this way:  It gives the learning curve a fairly solid structure so that there will be answers to "so what do I do next?"  It provides a direction and over time teaches you the important in-game systems.   

When that aspect of it has run its course, and you still don't have an idea what to do next, then that's probably the end of the line for you.  There is no "endgame" other than to keep doing what you've been doing all along -- explore, gather, build, do missions to gain faction standing, do missions to gain units, nanites, quicksilver or other various in-game currencies.

Build a base and expand it.  Get all the portal glyphs and go looking for sites and locations you find on various websites.  See other peoples' bases.  Start over maybe.  Make a permadeath character.  Go to the "Anomaly", where you can see other players and do co-op missions (I haven't done this yet).

To make a vague comparison to Disgaea -- The "grind" *IS* the game.  If you have a low tolerance for unstructured repetitive gameplay, give NMS a pass.

I LOVE it, but I'm weird.

Fighting - not interested since enemies generally move better than me anyways.

Space Exploration - not interested ever since I got the upgrade that adds 6,000+% to Units rewards for fauna and flora. I can just scan a whole planet and get 2M-3M units which kills the economy of the game for me. 
Now I don't really have to farm for Copper or basic resources since I can just go to a Space Station and  buy those from randomly generated Aliens (they usually have 1k-2k of that resource available to buy).

Planet Exploration - not interested anymore since I can farm Units easily and buy Drop Pod Coordinates. This makes upgrading my storage a chore now rather than an awesome rare upgrade.

Quests - not interested anymore. It seems like after 40 hours the devs gave up on making the main quests (or side quests for that matter) "engaging". I just have to go to the marker, go up a building, activate a terminal, wait for whoever shows up to finish talking, then go to the next place, or talk to the next alien. Side quests are basically "basic", I mean you have an almost infinite amount of planets, but most side quests are: kill this, scan that, get this, deliver this. I have not come across a side quest with an engaging storyline (or even a storyline actually). With the right "writers" the devs could technically create "lots and lots" of short stories with this game. But I guess that's just not a focus for them which is a shame since I think (maybe) that could be fun (for me anyways).

Mech - not interested since I have an almost infinite amount of fuel for my ship. I can just daily drive my ship to go to places. I have not tried underwater yet, but I think it would not be as interesting as "Subnautica" anyway.

Multiplayer - never interested. Not a fan of multiplayer anyway. I know it's "there" but I don't usually like playing with other people. I'm here for the Singleplayer aspect of NMS.

Tech Upgrade - not interested anymore since I don't really "need" or "want" to have "more stuff" in my base. Base Building was never really something I enjoyed, unless it's fast paced and upgrades changes the "way you play". After I got the Electromagnetic Generator, I don't really "have to" struggle for energy. I know there is "a lot" to upgrade, but I don't believe those upgrades will "add to" the game anymore than it already has.

Alien Standing - not interested anymore sinceI have maxed out the Korvax standing and I think that makes the Korvax scared of me or something. I can just buy Korvax casing (4 or 5 per aliens) and max it out pretty easily. I'm sure the other races might have a different way of maxing them out, but after founding out about that Korvax Casing thing, I generally lost interest in even learning their language, since I can just gift them and they are happy.


Maybe you can get more from this game than I have (to each their own) but as far as I know, I feel like I've done everything after 40 hours, I still recommend to play it though.

I will not start out by saying this is a great game and to buy it.  The fact is you HAVE to do the story line to get everything in the game and thers a good chance that after 60's like mine it manages to skip a key portion of the ATLAS mission so that now I'm stuck with a quest I can't complete because I don't have the recipe for nor can I acquire it.  
  
The game is a simple rinse and repeat SIM.  You fly to planets, find the same buried modules, same ships, sames bases, collect the same overly underwhelming credits and nanobots.  You continuously have to manually refresh every system to keep it active.  Nothing is automated even when you have resources.  Landing is a real piece of work and because the ship never stops this is going to really annoy you.  Also flying or walking around a storming planet is probably the most irritating aspect of the game.

Space like much of the game is just a waste of time, asteroids move in then out of view, you HAVE to farm them for minerals to keep fuel reserves up.  The scanner on your ship is a joke with an absurdly excessive cooldown when there doesn't need to be one.  And you have to align just perfectly to a planet and have it show that its scannable or the scan means nothing and will miss.    The constant random pirate attacks of ships and anomalies that don't exist.  They just pop into existence based on a time or proximity.  You can't outrun ships scanning you even if you are already at warp.  Which is fake.  

You run around collecting 100's of monolith stones that give you a single word which is of no reward because even after 600 collections you still can't understand anything anyone says.  And theres no real reward for putting in the effort.  The biggest waste of time is the atlas stations when there is like 50 of them you have to run around to on this stupid long running cooldown which you are forced to do over and over.  

The most fun of this game is baiting the saves into giving you S class ships so you can sell them for stupid amounts of money and sell their modules for nanobots.  That really is the only reward in this game.   It will take you weeks to accumulate enough of the burried tech to get enough modules for building your own base.  It will be tedious.   

One thing they don't tell you that the game leaves out is that you NEED to pin a HOME/SAVE beacon at your atlas quest portal so that you can come back and use it later on.  This is massive miss on the quest line guidance, especially if you try to find a living ship.  There are so many broken links in the quest chains and no direction.  And that's a nother thing, you can't focus question, you can't turn them off, you can't turn anything off, notifications, everything is a click hold, the ui is clunky AT BEST and is nothing more then a controller game.  It was designed with consoles in mind.  

At the end of the day, I've finished lots of the quests, the stories lines, made money, submitted useless planetary data and flown to station after system after station.  And there is nothing new anymore.  Aside from a possible new random animal mutation, everything is the same, same looks, same tree's, same rocks, same minerals.   For being a simulation, what a waste of time.  I'd say the creator of this giant matrix abandoned it in the 'story' of it all because it lacked depth.  NO MANS SKY.  You are right, because no many would create one so damn boring.

I tried to like this game, I really did.  But at a little over 100 hours into the game it's just one buggy grind for materials with little other substance.  The main storyline, if you can call it that, is hard to follow and frankly I don't see any reason to actually complete it. 

Want to build a badass base? Better build it on stilts. Using the terrain manipulator to flatten an area will work for a while, until you come back and it regenerated. I built an awesome base in the base of a cliff, only to come back to everything completely buried in rock. That sure was fun digging it out in the middle of a storm. 

This is assuming you don't get frustrated at the base building mechanics and quit. Parts don't line up right,  the foundation legs magically grow shorter leaving your base floating in midair, and you are randomly unable to place items. 

Want to explore the universe, finding new and exotic things? Nope. It's the same stuff, everywhere you go. Oh, and have fun glitching through terrain. Decide to use the terrain manipulator to tunnel from one place to another to avoid a storm? You'll randomly glitch above ground. Want to land somewhere? Have fun getting randomly transported miles away and glitch into the ground. Then you have no choice but to sit there and wait for your ship to be destroyed. Oh, and you'll have to fix "broken" parts on your ship afterwards too. 

Tired of the glitches, tired of getting shot through walls by sentinels that can't even see me, tired of the grind. There is no end to this game. Literally, the entire point of the game is to reach the center of the galaxy just to get sent to another one and start all over again. Don't waste your money, even if it's on sale.

I bought this game not long after it launched on PS4, had a bit of fun with it, then traded it in. I later regretted that decision, but didn’t lose much sleep over it.

Imagine my disappointment when I returned to the game on PC, only to discover that the developers have turned it into [i]Fortnite[/i].

Say what you will about the developers’ boldfaced and manipulative misrepresentation of their product prior to launch, but at least the early builds of this game were distinctive. This game used to be a lonely and unique experience with minimalist storytelling that practically begged the player to come up with his own headcanon, to theorise about the origins and purpose of Atlas, the true nature of this strange universe, et cetera. The game used to be a meditation on foreignness, with the player shifting constantly from place to place, never at ease, never home.

Now they want you to plop down a base and set up shop on one planet, in one location, on at least a semi-permanent basis. Instead of, oh, I don’t know, [i]teaching me how to make warp fuel so I can go and explore the galaxy[/i], the tutorial wants me to learn a whole new crafting system so I can sit in a dour little wooden room waiting out atmospheric storms and refining ferrite till I weep. In the main menu, the game’s regular mode is called an ‘infinite journey’. Go figure! I’ve got enough worries about acquiring land in real life, let alone in an overblown intergalactic [i]Minecraft[/i] clone.

The real tragedy of this game—apart from the base-level dishonest dealing—is that the devs sacrificed a specific and unique (if controversial) concept for an anodyne one. It's the kind of design philosophy whose first and last goal is appeasing the ever unpleased Reddit horde. Don’t bother buying this game again. Your memories of wandering the galaxy will suffice.

I used to crap all over this game and the people who bought it when it first came out. At the time of release, it was a complete sh-t show and barely a shart of what was originally promised.

Now? Now it's great. It went from the poster child for why buying early access is a bad idea, to one of the greatest comebacks I've ever seen in video games.

Four years after the fact, and the devs have still been churning away and improving upon it. I haven't been this hooked to a game in years. I'm over 100 hours in within my first couple of weeks. I absolutely love randomly exploring places for absolutely no reason whatsoever. The exploration aspect is fantastic on it's own. 

While a number of the worlds start to feel similar over time, I still keep running into something new on a regular basis. (I kind of hope they keep adding new world types/genres to expand upon what's already there. There's plenty there, but I'll always want more.) The game kind of leaves the door open as to whether or not you want to make your game grindy or efficient. I'm all about grindy slow exploration, so for me that's *muah*, chef's finger kiss. If you hate that kind of thing, that's ok, because there's other avenues you can take that don't involve doing that.

Their hard work over the past four years shows. It's unfortunate that it got such a bad rap early on.

Now if someone would only just blend a game together that's a mashup between No Man's Sky, Elite Dangerous, and Kerbal Space Program...

I've had my eye on No Man's Sky for the longest time but just couldn't get myself to buy it before because of all the bad press. I finally decided to jump in when the Origins update was launched and let me just say WOW!! While all the criticism when the game first launched back 2016 was probably well deserved, the state of the game as it is right now makes it seem like a completely different game. 

Before you jump in as well though it's important to understand that the main focus of this game, at least in my opinion, is exploration. It's completely non-linear, you can play without ever touching the story quests and you'll get by just fine or you can decide to follow the story line to try to answer the questions regarding the creation of the universe. 

Among the many, many things you can do, you could focus on creating the base of your dreams, colonizing a planet or if your ambitions are big enough you could also make en entire solar system your home. Maybe you're someone who likes to have nice things and you'll go hunting for the coolest ship, the strongest weapons, a kickass freighter or pimp out all of your vehicles You could have battles in space with your starship, become a space pirate and loot other freighters. You could dedicate yourself to farming resources for construction or trade, or maybe you're more into wildlife and wanna discover the most exotic, bizarre creature in the universe... the possibilities really are endless with this game and weather you go out and explore on your own or with friends, only you are in control of your fate in the universe.

One of the things that surprised me most about this game is the sheer size of it. You start out on a single planet that forms part of a single solar system with multiple planets/moons. That solar system is just one of possibly millions of like systems that form up a single galaxy... and as you may have imagined, that galaxy is just one of many galaxies, each with it's own cluster of millions of solar systems and practically infinite planets to explore. Of course due to limitation of technology after a while you'll start to notice some similarities between planets, but the developers work very hard to make sure that each system is different and unique in some way, shape or form.

Visually this game is beautiful and the soundtrack, while not overly noticeable, sets a good mood for the game. The next-gen patch that was recently announced will only build up on that and we can expect to see another huge improvement to the aesthetics within each world. Some other things to look out for in the future are reworks to the cave systems and sub-aquatic worlds. While present in the game currently, they do leave a lot to be desired and I'm sure that the developers will expand on this in the near future. Hello Games may have had a rough start, but they're dedicated to make this game better and better, and I have high hopes that they will continue to build on this already great game.

Long story short, I absolutely recommend this game. I understand that it may not be for everyone, but if any of the things I mentioned before seem to interest you then this game is definitely for you. No Man's Sky is at a really good place right now and it will only keep getting better, it really has been the comeback of the century and I for one will be sticking around for the long run to see how far we can go from here.

Reviews.121353:
The good things. The graphics are excellent. The game concept is fantastic. The game would be a wonderful way to chill out if it weren't for:

The bad things. While the game concept is excellent the implementation of that concept is horrid. Many of the unique gimmicks the developers have created to try to differentiate this game from other games are clunky, immersion breaking, and are also inconsistent throughout the game. An example of this is the press "E" action. You watch the little circle sweep around for about 3 seconds to do a task that in any other game would be a simple click. When you earn an achievement you get a display covering announcement that can literally kill you if it happens at an inopportune time. You can hold "TAB" to clear it but once again it takes about 3 seconds for "TAB" to clear it. The story line of the game is thin and obvious. The developers continually release more content but that content is ALWAYS bug ridden and what little bug fixes are done usually have bugs in them too. There are still game altering bugs in the program from release and each update introduces more game altering bugs. The tutorial takes over 3 hours, and much of that is enforced waiting which drastically slows down the early game. There is also no way to skip the tutorial on subsequent game saves unless you use a mod or an editor to modify your save game file. If you play permadeath you can literally wind up doing nothing but the tutorial over and over again because you can get killed easily during the tutorial. Of course you can cheat a permadeath defeat by the simple method of backing up your permadeath game file before beginning your play session. So far 95% of my permadeath defeats have been due to the a fore mentioned game breaking bugs.

At release the game was single player and the now somewhat obsolete story line explained it. "Multiplayer" (dis)functionality has been added but the multiplayer features are essentially "play alone together." Multplayer functionality is not synced with the other players in your group. When one player experiences weather effects, such as storms, the other players may still see and experience bright sunshine. So while one player is frantically trying to take cover the other players are continuing their explorations.

At the time that I am writing this review I have almost 1,000 hours of play time in. I have to say that the bad things now outweigh the good things and I would not recommend this game until the bugs are patched out and the gimmicky attempts to differentiate this game are streamlined out.

I've played before on a pirated copy and sunk probably about a hundred hours into the game before I saved up for a legitimate purchase. I also played the game earlier in it's launch cycle, back when it wasn't that great. 

The patches and content updates have done wonders to improve the game. It went from a fairly repetitive, bland game that wasn't really worth playing, to one of my favourite titles and a must-have for space enthusiasts such as myself. While the wildlife and plants can still be somewhat repetitive, the game has definitely improved enough to make it seem like you are actually exploring a vast and unique universe. And with 255 galaxies containing hundreds of billions of star systems each, there will never be a shortage of space for players to explore, even in Euclid, the galaxy every player starts in. The addition of base building has vastly improved the replayability of the game.

Even better, it seems large content updates and new features are routine for this title. These content updates have so far all been completely free, as well. It seems there is usually a massive annual update that brings in new content and features to vastly improve the game, which is a refreshing change from other developers that tend to abandon titles the moment gamers turn on it. The makers of the game clearly love what they do, love this title, and it shines through in the quality of game they have made for us. 

This game is definitely a must-have if you are a gamer, if you love space, if you love exploration, or if you are big on crafting and base-building. As for things like combat, while there is some light combat in this game, it is not a big part of it. If you are more into first person shooters or action games, this might not be the title for you.

Reviews.121402:
I wish there was an option between recommend and not recommend.  This is a unique, open world game that is huge in scope and ambitious.  Maybe too ambitious.  It feels like a movie with no plot.  The Player wanders around the universe alone, with only the need to obtain (AKA GRIND) the next materials for the next upgrade to motivate them forward-- this leads to 2am rage outbursts of "Why can't I find any frakking COPPER-- WTF!"   
There is a whisper of a story-line, but it is badly written and without narration, feels awkwardly written.  It has all the depth of a high schooler's sci-fi short story.  There is simply no motivation for my character to run around the solar system looking for copper (or anything else).  There were some really detailed aspects that immersed you in the game like having to learn the language word by word from AI travelers in the game, and you can build bases, but I can do that in Fall Out.  There are no voice overs for the AI either. 
 There is virtually no tutorial.  Not too much of an issue for a long time gamer, but there were things I still had not figured out in 13 hours of gameplay.  Like why you cant store certain things in certain places in your inventory and why the slots were randomly placed -- DROVE MY INVENTORY OCD NUTS!  There are bonuses for placing certain tech items next to each other, but the randomness of locked slots in the inventory made that nearly impossible.  
 The mapping feature was also not great.  Revisiting places I wanted to return to was problematic.  You can place a custom marker although I could not find a way to label it a unique name.  It just remained "custom marker".  So when you find interesting things, place a marker and hope you can recall what system and planet it was in.  You can rename locations where there is a save marker/beacon.  I would HIGHLY recommend renaming these places something you can remember.   All in all I cannot recommend this game even though the developers have the frame for something really great here.  There are other games with a better story, that allow in-depth camp/fort building and have better interface with the AI.  I returned No Man's Sky for a refund.

Finally decided to buy NMS on my PC, after playing about 250h on my Xbox (that I haven't touched since I bought my new PC, oh well), had trouble re-adapting myself to a new set of commands, how to control my ship etc. but I managed. Still, before today's patch (31st of October), I thought that some textures were... off-putting. I don't know, maybe I just didn't too much stock on them on my Xbox, but hey, instead of having a screen 10 feet away, now I have one about 1 feet away, so yeah, must be it... anyway, managed to build a base on a lushful planet, temperate, with no extreme weather, relaxed sentinels, just in front of a spot of water, flora and fauna are plentiful, well plentiful according to what it was supposed to mean before today... twas a beautiful place, when I set it up. Oh, and yeah, planet is a chlorine paradise... (helps a lot) 

But then, textures suddenly became... ugly. Of course all the conditions I mentioned were THE reasons I built it there, but, the spot I chose, well, there was an aesthetic reason for that, and all of a sudden, it kinda vanished... I'm not vain to the point to stop playing because of that, but it just didn't help. (stopped because I got some other games, damn you Steam with your promotions !)

Now, today's different.

Knew there was a patch coming, so just waited til it got downloaded and installed, kinda forgot about it for an hour, then decided to see if what they mentioned was true, and to what extent. The revamped graphics, and all that...

Damn.

This game is now gorgeous.

Last save I did was on a star base, on a system that I just discovered at the time, so I decided to walk around, just took a look at my ship, and the difference was striking, texture details man... turned around, went to talk to a Vy'Keen captain near me, and again twas striking, the details in his face. Walked around the base, colors are more vibrant than they were, but, knew that to see the extent of those changes, I'd have to go on a planet.

So hopped in my ship and got out, just to see that the planet near me was different too, can't quite explain that one though. So, I target an unvisited planet, and boom I go. When I neared it, saw what I was wondering about, the surface, the clouds, they were moving, and they had depth ! Ok, went to a nuclear planet right into a rad storm, maybe not the best situation, but suddenly I saw peaks, but the surface was moving, didn't know where I was exactly, til I managed to understand I was still in the clouds... I dived to discover a vibrant nuclear world, with a lot of lifeforms, all, of course, with very detailed textures. The colors, damn the colors... 

Finally decided to go back to my base, that I thought was in an ugly spot... when I got there... it really was lushful, flora was everywhere, sand looked like sand (and not some puddle of pixelated oatmeal), and there was lifeforms everywhere ! Flying lifeforms, quadrupedal herbivores walking around peacefully, then a bipedal predator just chimed in... in the water, there were fishes everywhere !

Hello Games outdid themselves, yet again.

Cause I hope people realize that after their less than satisfactory start, they could simply have dropped the game and declared bankrupt... but they persisted. They totally redeemed their slow start, in fact, to me, they already did before today, but now, damn...

Suddenly, I just can't wait to discover new planets again.

Pretty much what I'm going to do, like right now...

No Man's Sky is an exploration game. There are base building, ground combat, and space combat portions; a dynamic economy; a multiplayer challenge hub; and dozens of free content updates in the past, with no sign of slowing down.

But No Man's Sky is an exploration game.

You'll just see things... you'll see a turtle with a mushroom on his back beneath a burning red sun, as a rainbow forms in the oily haze in the distance, while pterodactyls with tentacles wheel above. You'll get into fights with enormous 'mechs that pursue you until you either die or run.

In the start, you'l feel powerless. Overawed by the scale and beauty. Lost, small. And that's something that never, ever really goes away. You're just a fleck here. You'll never be more. But you can be a fleck that burns across the stars, leaving a trail of incredible sights in your wake, memories of storms weathered in creaking bases while tornadoes whipped against your walls. You'll get security, safety, a home, but you'll always feel small.

And you'll always discover something new. I'm almost 400 hours in. Today I found a beautiful pink butterfly on a world of blue grass and silver seas, with golden palm trees stretching impossibly into the sky, and flying little fluffy rhinos brushing along the grass. I don't know how this world exists, but I called it Pretendland. It fit.

I flew on to another solar system. There's a lot to see out there. I'm still exploring. And I think I will be for a long time.

This is a game that sounds good on paper and even better in theory, in practice however, it fails to meet the marketing pitch.

I purchased this game some time ago as the procedural generation mechanic caught the attention of my exploration bug. However, after the first couple of hours it became clear that while, yes, this game produces an infinite amount of procedurally generated worlds and environments, the definition of "procedurally generated" in this instance is a single word limited to one syllable, "bland". 

Restricted to geography mapping, and randomization of the same stored assets, every generated environment begins to nonetheless feel the same after the first 5 or 6 locations. I often found myself leaving each location after only a cursory dive into what was in front of me. Most locations don't have a plethora of characters, enemies, or fauna either making the worlds feel fairly empty and lifeless for their scale and leaving you without much to explore beyond what you first encounter. 

There is not much of a story to speak of either as it mainly consists of cookie cutter quests that have you repetitively accomplishing the same, or similar, tasks over and over. The characters you meet don't feel varied enough to add any sense of immersion either and after a while I felt like I wasn't even doing anything productive to actually drive the quest lines towards a notable conclusion. 

The only real solid mark this game hits is with the visuals. Even with a lack of depth to the worlds and environments, every asset is visually pleasing and does bring about a sense of appreciation for what has been made and it can occupy your short time just to take it all in. 

With a severe lack of depth to both game mechanics and no real story driven arc to speak of, this game generates a lack of entertainment in about as much time as it takes to generate the "random" worlds you visit. In short, I would not recommend this game at it's current asking price of $60. I would even consider $20 a bit steep at a discount if only other than the fact it is still being actively attended to. It may be best to wait a while and see where this game ends up down the road, but at almost 5 years running, it may not end up anywhere other than another "procedurally generated" video game.

This was a real piece of work. The hype train that was driven over this game by developers before launch only equated to a sub-par game to players at the very day of it's release. Unless your PC was built by jesus or sth, this game struggled to push beyond 30 fps and really had your divided attention between focusing on story and unreasonable amount of grinding for resources as a pre-requisite to fix broken machinery(s) or to progress further in the game.

Four years and extreme amount of dedication later, this game reincarnated from it's former shell to a game full of life, color; planets with lush, atmospheric terrains, weathers and vivid landscapes. Diverse breed of algorithmically generated species and plants that differ in every planets which, in terms of user experience, may become repetitive at some point but at times the game will surprise you with what else you can come across. 

The developer said during the GDC 2019 conference talk, "For me transcendental joy beats average happiness." And I firmly believe that philosophy was the basis on how he wanted to deliver this game and he certainly managed to do so without a doubt.

P.S. Bethesda, please learn something.

No Man's Sky was a rough release originally. There were a lot of mistakes made, but the biggest mistake of them all was not hiring a dedicated PR guy (to understand why, watch the Internet Historian's video on the Engoodening of No Man's Sky). To call it rough is honestly an understatement. Underdelivering by a huge margin was just the beginning of the hell that was caused by this game's release.

That release is now more than four years ago. Nearly every hour I put into this game... Was at release. I enjoyed it even then. Dumped plenty of time into it.

After release, the blunders stacked up even more until they finally did the smart thing and went silent... Before releasing a massive update, fixing a few of the missing features and adding more to the game.
Then, they stayed mostly quiet and made a second major update, adding in more missing features and more new content.
Then again.
And again.
And again.

Since 2016, the devs have been single-mindedly fixing every single thing they possibly could. They refused to just give up on this game.
Make no mistake, if a AAA company had been panned as hard as NMS did, they'd have reduced updates, reduced efforts, and let the game fade into obscurity. Hell, we've got regularly appearing proof of this. There's an endless supply of proof that a company that only gave a crap about the money would have dropped this thing in Q1 2017.
These guys didn't.
They updated. They improved. They added.
And now, the game is almost more than what they claimed it would be. Some details may still be missing (certain functions were playtested and proven to only be problems for the players, too), but a hundred things they never promised have been added since, and these days, there's no doubt in my mind that the game is worth what they say it is.
And all through this, they're STILL updating it. It's been MORE THAN FOUR YEARS. Another update is planned to go live in mid-november. About two weeks from now.

No one who has already paid for the game needs to lift a finger. They're getting that content. It's free. Just like every single other update has been.

The release of NMS was a seriously damaging event. It is rare that I would suggest anyone forget such a thing. But in this case... Well, maybe not forget it, but at least look past it and see what the game has become, and how hard the devs have worked to bring it to you.

I have by no means poured as much time into this game (yet) as others but: I was among the people that bought No Man's Sky when it initially released. I went through the whole process with this game - the insane hype pre-release, the disappointment, the letting it sit unplayed on my steam library for months at a time... and then, the redemption. And My GOD has it been a redemption. This game is no longer what it was when it first released. It is so much more now than what was promised, and there is still more coming. The game is, to me, the ultimate sandbox. It drops you in a massive, procedurally generated universe, and after a little bit of initial hand-holding for you to learn the mechanics, what you do with it is entirely up to you. There are various factions to gain reputation with - do you want to be an explorer, travelling the galaxy in search for the strange and wonderous things? Do you want to be a mercenary, fulfilling contracts all over the galaxy? Do you want to be a bounty hunter? A pirate? Do you want to settle as many worlds as possible, building bases on the strangest planets you can encounter, braving the elements and the dangers? Do you want to team up with strangers or friends or do you want to go about it on your own, a lone wanderer among the stars? Whatever you want to do here, you can. Is this to everyone's liking? Probably not. But at this point in its growth, you can' really say 'No Man's Sky isn't what I want it to be' anymore, because at this point, No Man's Sky is what YOU make of it, it's up to you to find your adventure in this game. 

No Man's Sky is vibrant now, it's colourful, it's unexpected. There is almost nothing left of the painful initial release of this game, and Hello Games has delivered on pretty much every promise they made - and then some - and while too many game studios now rely on microtransactions and forcing dedicated players to buy DLC in order to actually play a complete game, every update that has come out for No Man's Sky has been completely free and has basically transformed this game from the ground up. And there seems to still be more to come. I for one am incredibly excited to see where this journey goes in the future. If you are on the fence about buying this game - or getting back into it after having cast it aside in disappointment four years ago - take this as your sign.

I've bought this game several times over, for both Xbox and PS4 and just recently for my new PC. I've gotta say the game is fun. I mean its got some great replay value and starting over is a blast every year or so. Everyone is pretty familiar with Internet Historians coverage of this games past, and the stigma with the release. The game really has gotten better. 

However, there are a number of weaknesses and strengths with the game. End game gets insanely boring. The cycle is repetitious, and nothing new forms after a certain point. So when you hop between procedurally generated this and that you start to see the sameness in the core of the code.

However the journey up is interesting to say the least but not much more so than say playing Minecraft on creative. This game would be better off with some significant challenges to push your accumulated resources to the test. Thats where a significant portion of the player base falls off. There is nothing keeping you there unless you find endless exploration of the minutiae of the procedural generation fun. "Oh look slightly different tree, oh look that coral that resembles another plant I saw on a samey planet".

There's one thing a select group of individuals that play this kind of game is looking for. Its epic space battles. Not a smidgeon of pirates coming at you in an asteroid field. What's the point of all the space in between planets and moons and stars if you can't fill it with lasers, and missiles and bits of destroyed ships flying all over the place? Or maybe some epic scale death star-esque fight? There is so little to lose in this game that you don't feel like you're accomplishing anything and the ways you can lose stuff in this game don't feel fun.

Playing on hard-core with the difficulty cranked up is just doing things at a snails pace. Collecting resources slower, walking from thing to thing slower, filling up your ships fuel slower because resources are more scarce isn't fun. Its boring filler. 

Still going to give this game a thumbs up. Its fun to play when you're looking for something that has almost no stress value added to it and the diversity of the planets and randomness has grown over time and multi-player features have become much much stronger. Just wanna see more interesting story, combat or lore added really. Which I gotta say is a small complaint but a reasonable thing to ask for.

3) There is an integrated language system which makes talking to each NPCs more of a fun conversation rather than dialog you skip just to get to the next quest. So far, learning the languages for the Gek, Vykeen, Korvax, and, of course, the mysterious Atlas. Hopefully more races are added some day to expand this universe further.
4) The game takes place inside an entire galaxy. No planet off-limits. No system unreachable with the right technology. One could even travel to the core of the galaxy if they are so inclined. A near endless adventure.
5) There are challenges around every bend. The sentinel robots that keep you on your toes. The space pirates, whom seek to take all your valuables. And if you aren't careful, any of the factions could become your foe

There is much more, but really its better to experience it for yourself.

Unfortunately, there are some down sides...

Cons:
1) The game attempts to create unique planets in each system by piecing together different options from its procedural Generator. This would be great, but currently there is a limited amount of options. After a while, you start noticing that a lot of fauna and flora have the exact same models as the previous 5 planets you visited. All ruins are the exact same thing, no real variation. This will probably get better as more content is added into the generator, so don't fret too much.
2) Now the game is way too big to save exact objects and structures on the planets you visit. The game does try to approximate where they were though. For example, If you dig out an entire ruins on a planet, then save and reload, the ruins may have moved, making all that work just an empty hole in the ground. Or if you are one of the lucky people to find the "yoda hut" on one of the swamp planets and set up a base there, the hut may vanish when you reload your game or be off set to your base design.
3) The part that saddens me the most right now is that the game can sometimes wipe your current save. You either lose everything or it shoots back to a save so far in the past that all you worked for is gone. This particular bug has affected me 3 times. There are a couple work-a-rounds, but currently there is no official fix to the issue. I suggest making a copy of your save file until this bug is fixed.

Overall, I do still recommend this game. The potential is there and I want to see what it becomes.

The game has been updated from its disastrous launch to a completely "meh" experience. 

It still has not really met the impossible expectations it set for itself at the start, but at least its a completed indie game now. 

The reason for the negative review is because the game feels very empty and boring, the pop in (draw distance) is atrocious and extremely un-immersive even on max settings, and there are constant frame drops and stutterings for no reason even on powerful machines. If they fixed both of those things then this would be a positive review, like I said the game is "meh" and not that far away from being just "okay". 

The reason I have stopped playing is that the game advertises itself still to this day as a game about exploration and immersion, which is true for your first 10 hours of the game but then quickly becomes a lie, a thin vernier that pretends to coat everything but is really just window dressing that poorly hides the actual fairly grindy mechanics of the game. And the supposed exploration was the only real draw this game held for me as other games do everything else (survival-crafting, base building, space combat, shooter combat, trading, immersion, etc) much better.

If you're like me, you probably followed the news surrounding this game when it first came out, were aware of the controversy, and then haven't really checked it out since then. I can't think of many other games where one of my favorite activities is just to fly from planet to planet learning words.

The inventory management is a little clunky, and doesn't feel very intuitive (I have no idea what the misc. numbers displayed when you're working on crashed/damaged tech actually mean). The save system could also be improved. It's not as simple as just going to the menu and saving the game or quitting and saving at the same time. You can build these save towers or simply just hop in and out of your ship. But either way, seems like it would be simpler and more straight forward to just allow the player to save manually or by quitting to desktop/menu.

There doesn't feel like there's much an existential crisis or any kind of creeping doom that raises the stakes, so if you're looking for that you might be disappointed. I'm playing it currently on normal mode, but there are small bands of raiders or things called Sentinels that will attack you for various reasons in various locations.

I picked up the game on a half-off sale, and I'm pretty pleased. After the initial hurdles of getting a grasp of the controls, I've quite a lot of fun blasting rocks and learning alien languages. TL;DR - Okay, but not really a strong game. Have played it a lot and I enjoyed it a for a while but it has some major issues.

- Flat gameplay development. The progression of materials/ships/upgrades just doesn't have a lot of depth. As you move towards the core and advance through quests you'll find that the more exotic planets have little benefit over those you encounter in your first few systems.

- Weak enemies. The npc enemies pose little to no challenge and serve as little more than an inconvenience.

- No ship customization. Meh

- Buggy as sin. The game still plays like an early access title. In my last hour of play I had one npc interaction menu bug out, requiring a restart, and then had my ship glitch through the ground into a cave, again, requiring a hard restart else I destroy my ship and have to repair all of its systems.

- Main story is pretty weak overall, but I guess it kind of has one which at least gives you more direction than if there weren't any at all.

- Navigation and waypoint system suck ass. You cant view the galaxy map unless you're in your ship and in space (not landed on a planet or station). There's no map of your local system or planet that you're on. Way points go away after you leave the area. An example of why this is problematic: quest to repair sub requires you to build a fuel cell for the sub, no ingredients in immediate vicinity, go back to base to get some, waypoint no longer exists to go back and finish mission!
Reviews.121868:
Its a great game now that it has had some major updates but I find there isn't enough new things like more varieties of plants and minerals etc there are so many planets and galaxies and yet it gets repetitive finding the same things you already have.

The tutorial and slow build up into the game is done extremely well. One of the few games I look at and needed the tutorial because of its complexity but now is simple because of the effectiveness of it.

The story of the game honestly I have no idea and cant remember it at all, but the game isn't there to tell a story its mainly just thrown in there to give an indirect goal as to what you can strive to reach if that is what you want to do, if it isn't then you aren't missing out that much from the game, you can explore for hours or build bases everywhere, or spend ages upgrading yourself or learning languages, little almost insignificant things even that can take hours to do and yet its extremely enjoyable.

The sound design is amazing, I really love the eerie sounds and effects when you enter the Atlas Structures, its so bizarre and yet outstanding and although graphical it isn't the best game ever the galaxies and systems look gorgeous.

The building and base creation is amazing in some parts and poor in others, just falls flat with some parts that wont attach or snap that could and the deco and foundations get dry and repetitive after constant use. It is poorly optimised for large projects and my game has crashed numerous times because of this. On one occasion I have lost a full sessions worth of progress on a base because of the poor autosaving mechanic which is ultimately why I’m not going to play the game again.

The space exploration and planet exploration is extremely fun at first then begins to die off as the planets are all similar. The extreme weather planets are the most fun places to be because of their unpredictability and even an experienced player can meet their demise if unprepared. The missions get extremely repetitive after a while and I find the most fun comes from aimlessly wandering space. The creation aspect of the game is what intrigues me the most and if it was really fleshed out into more of a sandbox style would be amazing, there could be new ores and plants giving you a reason to go out and get more things which could then unlock more things to build with to keep things diverse.

The terraforming is strange, the flattening and restore are very useful but the mining tool is very bad for trying to shape your base. I often found the ground making odd shapes or layering wrong.

I love the freighters and the customisation of them, although limited it gives another area or versatility other than just having a base on a planet, a mobile one. It would be even better if you could customise freighter parts and ship parts to make them have more variety and look as you choose, you could use scrapped parts from destroyed ships etc as part of the building of them rather than selling them off. It sucks finding a good ship that looks awful or spending ages waiting to find a good looking one when you prefer aesthetic over practicality. The ships should have more highlighted strengths and weaknesses for example my fighter has 48 slots and yet a hauler also has 48. I may be wrong in this but I thought they were supposed to be specialised and yet my fully upgraded start ship trumps every other one I've seen.

I love the grade system. going C - B - A - S. The ranges give a little luck for having that extra edge without it being so meaningful the average player would have to grind forever to find the best. You can do that but its not mandatory by any means, I do think the slot mechanic for the upgrades is poor in that to have good upgrades on things you lose on variety, however the amount of ships you can have helps this so you can pick multiple ships having 2 each for example. It just drops short with your multitool where I have good upgrades on but I've never once really even considered using some of the other technology throughout the entire game as id have to destroy my upgrades. The illegal parts I really love, they give an opportunity for the avid player looking to squeeze everything they can out of the game grind for the slightest edge over someone with complete S class gear, again without it being so necessary it negatively impacts the game.

The multiplayer for the game is extremely fun and helps the often repetitive nature of the game feel more fresh and fun, you can often get off track from what you are doing just playing and enjoying the experience with some friends, you haven't accomplished much but you've had a lot of fun and the variety of the game keeps you being side-tracked but you enjoy that fact and revel in it.

It's a really solid game overall and has come really far from what it started as. I can see how people would put in 1,000+ hours into it I really can but it has so much potential that can be built on to become even more of a really amazing yet underrated game.

Reviews.121892:
Deep as the ocean, shallow as buket.

No man sky is not a bad game. And people will tell You how amazing it is. Endless space exploring, with all sorts of different starships. Space stations and outposts inhabited by aliens from 3 races. Quests and missions to part take, space battles and so on…

It offers much, however most of its offerings feels half-baked. You may have omg this so cool and few minutes later see that same thing. Almost everything what you will see in NMS will repeat itself over and over again. And most things won't matter, they will look different, but will be samish...

 There are “endless’’ supply of planets, but most of them feels and looks same. Whenever I find an awesome looking planet, I will find the next one of its kind later. And on these planets will live mostly weird animals, which are mashed together from different parts, something like the worst aspects out of the SPORE creature assembly line.  And that goes for everything in this game, you found it once and now you will see it again over and over. All of the space stations inside are the same, all the aliens feel the same and after wasting my time learning their language I can finally see all those same copy/paste dialogs. 

There are plenty of starships with different classes and ranks but they don't matter. All the differences are in some stat bonuses, like explorer will have better hyperdrive and fighter better damage but none of this matter, only if for people who min/max. In my survival game I bought A class Explorer and didnt have a need for any other ship. It melted any hostile ships as good as my S class fighter in a normal game and upgraded it had almost the same storage space as the S class hauler.

And this applies for multitools, there are no meaningful differences. In both permadeath and survival I melted my enemies with basic weapon technologies( upgraded with s modules, which are not hard to find) Only thinh what matters are slots and even A class pistol multitool will have enough slots/damage to serve you well. And to be fair, comat feels just to be there… the highest challenge what i got was when get in a fight while in the start of my permadeath run while in the starter ship without any upgrades.

As for the gameplay loop, that's where you hate it or love it. You will be grinding the same resources no matter how advanced your tools/ship/base.. Yes, you may find your way of earning money so you can buy whatever you need, but at best you gonna sit through lengthy loading screens while hoping through portals to your mining sites.

Yes I said loading screens. No matter what people say to you this game has plenty of them and they are more than a few sec long(i would say around 15-20 sec). Each time you warp, each time you go through the portal you will be greeted with one. 

As for the story, I can't really say. Sometimes its get interesting, but then again i had seen most of things ahead of it. And in Survival, where I finally decided to play, I got locked out of the story by bug. So be warned, there is at least one game breaking bug for which I could not find a solution.

Overall, if you like base building, one of the best parts of this game(although can still frustrate you), and resource gathering and making profit out of selling high value goods, while searching for the best deal, this game may be for you. However if you look for imersiver exploring, punishing survival or good starfighter game with nice story, you better look elsewhere.

It's all been said before but here are my plus and minus points...

- The interface feels like it belongs on console rather than PC although most of it can be adequately configured.
+ The freedom and variety are great.
- The inventory system sucks at the beginning, necessitating tedious toing and froing.
+ Some of the vistas are epic.
- Space battles are arcade style rather than requiring any thought.
+ There's lots to discover.
- Much of the game mechanics (not just the story itself!) are unexplained and confusing.
- it's hard to keep track of messages - I regularly find things in my inventory without knowing where they came from!
+ Fixing up a crashed spaceship and fitting it out is satisfying.
- The galaxy map controls are awful and you can't study the map unless you're in space - which is silly.
- The base building controls are pretty poor and could learn a lot from Satisfactory and Subnautica. Again probably feels different on console.
- I find the target direction indicators in space combat a complete nightmare. They're read triangles which can be anywhere on screen and often on top of the cockpit graphics which glow red during combat! Silly.
- When you sell something the computerised voice sounds like it's saying "Eunuchs received" instead of "Units received" which is quite funny... the first 10 times you hear it.
- 'Summoning' your ship or freighter is instantaneous which rather breaks immersion - either you should be teleporting it in some way (so pretty much instant) or it should take longer depending upon how far away it is.
+ Finding derelict freighters and weird anomalies is great
- There's no explanation as to why picking up certain things causes 'sentinels' to attack, you have to learn the hard way.
- I've got stuck in the environment and found a broken collision map in my freighter, necessitating a reload.
- A 'community planet' inexplicably appeared in my list of stations. When I went there I got stuck in the terrain trying to rescue a freighter which also seemed to be buried! Apparently a long-standing and well known bug.

Well that's a lot of negatives but the game has enough personality and uniqueness to shrug them off. Add to this i'm playing on Linux without any real issues and it's a big thumbs up from me:

9/10 would receive eunuchs again.

I went into this game blind. I remember hearing about the game up until its release in 2016, but I never kept track of it after that. Now, 4 years post-launch, the game is what I believe everyone hoped it would be. This is a visually gorgeous and beautifully intricate game that I continue to play as a source of comfort as well as waiting for my next big wow. Every time I think I've seen it all, the game throws in another surprise. 

To clarify, there is a daunting learning curve to get into the game. The first five hours I spent stumbling around a hazardous planet, trying to figure out what to do. I nearly quit. Luckily, I had a friend to play with and we stuck it out together. Boy, am I glad I kept playing. Now, after 100+ hours, I find just as much joy exploring the cosmos as I did when I flew into space for the first time. That being said, I have spent a good amount of time doing research and figuring out bits and pieces that the game does not directly address. This was all possible due to the wonderful NMS community and the NMS wiki page that countless members have put time into crafting. 

I now frequently spend my evenings streaming this game for my friends, who seem to get as much enjoyment out of watching as I do playing and talking about the content. Kudos to Hello Games for putting an immense amount of love into a project of this magnitude. Their effort truly shows. 

To conclude, I would highly recommend this game. No Man's Sky is an absolutely stunning game that successfully recovered from a dodgy release. The learning curve may seem daunting, but is more than worth the time and effort. Consistent FREE updates from Hello Games gives returning players a reason to boot it up again and provides new players with seemingly endless content to dig into. 10/10.

Reviews.122166:
“Each Man’s Sky”

A review of ‘No man’s Sky’ from Hello Games

Famed movie critic Roger Ebert was skeptical that video games could ever
achieve the status of art (2010). His argument was that games had rules and winning
conditions while art is something that is experienced. If a ‘video game’ was centered on
experience, it was no longer really a game. In August, Hello Games released No Man’s
Sky onto Playstation 4 and Windows PC after three years of development. It is one in a
long tradition of space exploration games like Freelancer and Elite, with a startling 18
quintillion planets to explore. But with its beautiful vistas and gaping moments, it is also
an artistic statement by the developers. No Man’s Sky bridges the gap between a video
game and pure art.

The game begins when you wake up on an alien world near your broken
spaceship. As you take your first steps, you are greeted with a gorgeous vista of an alien
world created just for you. The game’s elements, such as geology and star formation, are
procedurally generated from a string of numbers. This clever programming method
creates near-infinite variety while avoiding near-infinite memory use. The world is rich
and vivid in colors, hues, and shapes. These visuals imitate nature and yet go beyond it -
each frame resembles a painting or drawing. On their web page, Hello Games states that
they intended the game to look like a science fiction book cover come to life (2016). You 
are soon given a choice: you can wonder around freely on your own, or you can accept
the guidance of a being called Atlas. If you choose to follow Atlas, you will be sent on a
journey to the center of the universe. It is no accident that this plotline is reminiscent of
classic science fiction. Hello Games intended their games to reflect the realism, the
optimism, and the cosmological significance of books like Arthur C. Clarke’s 2001: A
Space Odyssey and Frank Herbert’s Dune (Hello Games, 2014). You will encounter
direct homage to the latter work when you meet your first sandworm. Imitating nature,
as well as being inspired by or directly referencing prior art, are both criterion that No
Man’s Sky can claim towards the case of its own status as a work of art.

No Man’s Sky has all of the usual game play hallmarks of its genre.  You can
upgrade your starship, your space suit, and your multi-tool (a gadget that functions as a
weapon, a scanner, binoculars, and a mining ‘drill’) with resources and technology
gathered on worlds (or in space) and through trading. You can accumulate currency to
buy a stronger starship. You can fight in combat with hostile planetary life forms or
pirates in space who want your cargo. You can learn alien languages to better
communicate with the other major races inhabiting the universe by encountering
monoliths (homage to Space Odyssey). You can also discover and name locations on
planets, new planets and star systems, and alien biology. Players who upload their
discoveries to the Atlas can earn additional money, as well as credit for being a space
Christopher Columbus or a space Charles Darwin. While the mining, trading, combat,
and exploration mechanics are all visually stunning and artistically directed, they are
otherwise par for the course and not particularly groundbreaking or rewarding. They can even be strange and burdensome – for example, the grid inventory system is not intuitive
and adding new slots is of too great importance.

However, No Man’s Sky is, fundamentally, a beautiful aesthetic experience. It is
less concerned with mechanics and more concerned with creating a rewarding journey of
space exploration for the player. The game play is there to serve the experience, rather
than the other way around. It’s up to you if you will let your enjoyment be constrained
by the mechanics or if you will forgive them as necessary and embrace the journey. You
can climb to the top of the highest mountain on your current planet and call it your own
accomplishment. You can watch the sun set and see the stars come out – each star in the
sky is a place to visit. Instead of rushing to new planets, you can explore your home
planet for a very long time. There is no one correct destination or goal. Even accepting
and completing the optional Atlas plotline does not bring the game to an end. The game
offers total freedom to the player, and yet, it doesn’t add up to a lack of structure.
Instead, it gives the player the license to experience the journey at whatever pace and in
whatever way he or she chooses, while adding to the sense of grand scope and scale, like
touring an enormous museum with the whole day off.

From waking up near your ship to reaching the center of the universe (or
wherever), No Man’s Sky is a game defined by a series of captivating moments. Each
one is meticulously crafted with intention by the developers to give you an experience of
your own science fiction novel all the way down to the little details, like the prolonged
time spent in a colorful warp tunnel when you jump from one star system to another,
giving the player the impression of traveling a vast distance. When you fix your broken
starship and leave your ‘home’ planet, the atmospheric transformation of ascending into space is breathtaking. It begins by simply tilting your spacecraft upwards and starting
your ascent – all transitions in the game are seamless. Your maximum speed gradually
increases and the thick atmosphere blocks much of your view for some moments. Then,
suddenly, the atmosphere melts away and your front-view windows are full of stars,
nebulae, planets, moons, and other stellar features. If you take a moment to turn
sideways or backwards, you will see the massive presence of the planet you just left
behind, with its thin atmosphere and rough geology spread out across the horizon – the
sense of scale is rich and convincing. In an interview with the New Yorker during the
development phase, Hello Games stated that they made a conscious choice to break with
realism in order to have the atmosphere seem thicker as you exit it, so the transition to
space is more sudden. They also modified gravity so that large worlds could exist near to
one another without colliding so that the player can see nearby alien worlds when they
gaze into the sky, a picturesque sci-fi art trope (Katchadourian, 2015). This ‘fixing’ of
nature in the game for a specific experiential and artistic purpose is arguably the strongest
criterion for claiming that No Man’s Sky is more art than game.

It’s true that No Man’s Sky could have been a better game. But as an experience,
there is nothing like it in the history of the genre. It’s true that the player will notice the
procedurally generated elements forming recognizable patterns and, slowly, the
experiences will lose their novelty and eventually their interest. But they never lose their
beauty. The ‘game’ is best seen as a universe-sized digital sculpture. It is meant to be
experienced, meditated on, and left behind with a greater understanding of who we are
and our relationship to the vastness of our own cosmos.

< www.no-mans-sky.com/2014/10/your-favourite-classic-sci-fi-books/>

This game is virtually everything I would want in a idealized, Platonic Form of a space exploration game. The procedurally-generated worlds are awe inspiring and, especially on ringed worlds, breathtaking. I feel like I'm taking screenshots and saying "WTF?" at whatever the game has cooked up. That being said, there are a few specific types of flora that are somewhat repetitive, but after seeing the diversity of the planets I realized it was solely for easier recognition. 
      The storyline is very intriguing and I'm curious to see where it goes. i hope future quest lines will be implemented down the road. I've only done a couple, but being able to do multiplayer quests is pretty enjoyable. 
      Spaceship hunting is a ton of fun, and while I understand not being able to customize parts, it would be nice to be able to customize the color. 
      I have encountered some minor bugs, most notably one where my camera seems to get dislodged from my character (you can see them still walking around if you hit WASD), then abruptly the camera will start spinning rapidly like I'm in a flipping car crash at 50x speed. Other times, NPCs and ambient foligage will clip into walls and floors. In 60 hrs of play though, I've only seen it twice. 
      Crafting and base decoration is fairly in depth, and I'm excited to build out my freighter base. A couple of QoL features would be nice. For example, the having the crafting feature recognize when you have ingredients across your backpack and spaceship inventories, and you're within bounds of your craft, not having to manually transfer the items to your inventory first. The other thing is the Quick Store feature seems to not recognize when I have a particular item in storage and just randomly places the stack in another slot, instead of merging the items together. Really, though I'm being nitpicky.
       Overall, the game is extraordinarily fun, and props to Hello Games for releasing free updates.
