Since I was a young child, I've wanted to visit alien worlds in my own, personal starship and just roam.

I could tell from the title of this very well-named game that it was going to be almost exactly what it turned out to be.  I fly to vast expanses of unclaimed land and explore, even claim a bit here and there for myself.

Don't expect this game to be everything that all other RPG's are.  It has a certain amount of repetitiveness, sparseness, and other experiential limitations.  For instance, every solar system has a space station, and, really, they're all clones of of another, with only the slighest of variations.  Nonetheless, at least for me, this game's richness, variety, and xenobeauty has me HOOKED.  Minecraft can engage a person in spite of being made entirely of cubes, and NMS can still suck a person into its gravity well in spite of its limitations.  Computers aren't God, so don't ever expect any game to be infinite and perfect in all respects, you little whining , entitled panzy.  Hello has created a nice piece of work here, and I appreciate it deeply.  In NMS, the mix of space flight, pedestrian exploration on planetary surfaces, resource gathering, and base-building have kept me and will keep me endlessly busy for quite some time.  The very ALIEN critters, plants, and mineral deposits submerge you in a feeling of being somewhere very strange no matter where you go.  Combat, be it against pirate starships in space or against critters or robots on planetary surfaces, doesn't feel as developed, fierce, and engulfing as in most RPG's, but NMS gets away with it anyway.  There are hazards.  You want trouble?  You can stir some up, especially in certain locations, but although this game certainly doesn't lack for laser pistols, that doesn't seem to be its main emphasis.  In most RPG's, it seems like everything you do is ultimately just a long means to the end of increasing your combat stats, but you don't get that feeling in NMS.  

I am especially pleased that I, on my PC, through Steam, can play this game with a friend of mine, who's playing it on an xbox via Gamepass.  In NMS, I had an easier time getting my headset to connect with his than I did on Fallout 76 (which I also ended up loving), and FO76 isn't even cross-platform.  (We've done FO76 both pc to pc and xobx to xbox.)  After all, NMS involves aliens from different worlds reaching out and learning to communicate and trade and cooperate with each other, so it seems very much true to that spirit that cross-platform mutli-player interactions should be possible and, I say cautiously, relatively easy.

I really, really want to love this game. And judging by the 100 hours I've put into it, maybe I do.

No Man's Sky feels incomplete. Not for the features HG promised and didn't provide, but for the stuff they apparently never thought to include.

I was hoping to find myself a space simulator- something like Space Engine, only with pew-pew lazerguns and big booms and aliens. But space as depicted in NMS is weird and inconsistent with everything we know about space, and it's missing some key features.

You can't visit stars in No Man's Sky. Like, straight up you can't do it. Stars are just images in the skybox of No Man's Land- you can head in their direction for an hour and not ever arrive any closer. That seems like a critical oversight for a galaxy exploration game no?

No Man's Sky has only rocky planets with routine day/night cycles. Where are the gas giants? Where are the tidally-locked planets that have a day-side and a night-side? How come a given system will have like, 3-5 planets and only 1 moon, when we know moons are more common than planets? How come moons aren't tidally locked to planets, even though Luna is tidally locked to Earth and is why we understand what being "tidally locked" means so well?

"Red" stars? "Blue" stars? Are you talking about red giants and supernovae? Why are you making up science fantasy star types when this stuff already exists in laypeoples' speech? What the hell is a "Green" star?

It's like you took a child's understanding of space and made a whole-ass universe out of it when reading a couple short books intended for that same child could have given you a clearer, deeper understanding of how to generate a complex, interesting, dynamic universe.

There are so many annoying bugs, multiplayer barely works, and the animations are really stilted and weird. No Man's Sky had/has such promise, and as Hello Games continues to update it, I hope we will see big improvements. For now though, I recommend staying away from this title.

No Man's Sky's launch was a spectacle of disappointment.  A lot of the game felt half-assed, from the creatures and planets to flight controls.  It was extremely underwhelming and YES YOU DID SAY THERE WOULD BE MULTIPLAYER, YOU FUCK.

Ahem...anyway, I'd easily recommend No Man's Sky as it is now.  It finally feels like the game it was supposed to be.  Planets look better, creatures look better, controls feel better, there's a lot more to do, and there is actual multiplayer.  There have also been a lot of quality of life improvements over the years, so starting from a new game doesn't feel nearly as uncomfortable as it once did.  Right now I'd give the game an 8/10 overall.

For what it's worth, I'd value NMS as a $40 game.  Given the debacle of a launch and how long it took to get from point A to point B it's really hard from the consumer perspective to justify the $60 price tag for a game that still lives in infamy.  That's coming from someone that bought it at launch.  If you still aren't sure about the game, add it to your wish list and wait for a sale.

One of the best video game comebacks of all time. What started out as one of the biggest video game controversies of all time transformed into one of the best examples of game development in the industry. Credit to Sean Murray and Hello Games for not taking the money and running but instead being quiet and developing the game you promised. 

No Man's Sky has some issues for me, but overall it's a very good experience if you enjoy survival games and a chill experience. 

Over time, No Man's Sky has continued to add amazing things I like that include: an interesting main story, very friendly and fun multiplayer between friends, interesting world generation and resource management, base building and vehicles, wack creature generation (there have been times where I have been amazed and horrified), random world events (freighters and anomalies), and much more including a vast array of ways to make money and more events I am sure I have yet to discover. 

While there are many things I enjoy about NMS, the gameplay cycle can get annoying sometimes and the mission design is very bland. Most quests often come down to fetch quests and exploring the same things over and over again. A lot of the features of the game are locked into doing the main quest as well. Often times I would be confused on where to get something and give up on ever getting it until I did the main story. The game also has the design of "figure it out yourself" instead of explaining everything to you which I appreciate but I have had to do a lot of outside research when I would appreciate if that was somewhere in the game. This game can also get boring with the gameplay loop because constantly exploring and finding the same general things over and over again can get daunting. The recent planet generation update has been very helpful with this problem though.

No Man's Sky is a cautionary tale and a redemption story. What started out as a worldwide failure, quickly changed into a very enjoyable game with some awesome elements. If you put this game off since release, I highly advise giving it another try because the game is completely different now. I look forward to even more updates from Sean Murray and Hello Games into No Man's Sky and appreciate everything he's done for this community.

No Man's Sky is a marvel of technical and gameplay achievements. While the launch was disastrous I feel it both showed the horde mentality of people and the desire to address and support the game in that matter. Whether before or after this game was released there have been games that failed to deliver on promises at a much higher calibre but they still are seen better in the public eye than NMS.

The game isn't perfect but its bloody brilliant in multiple ways. The has never heavily tanked my fps which is surprising due to the scope and seamless world. You will likely never experience loading in-game (other than loading saves and such) which makes the game extremely immersive. This immersive nature is helped by the beauty of game and how it doesn't try to mimic life with its designs.

From a gameplay standpoint there is much to do as of Origins including: the main story, reaching the galactic centre, bounty hunting, exploring derelict freighters, finding abandoned buildings, finding crashed ships or freighters, radiant missions from the anomaly and quest givers, learning the language of alien races and so much more each rewarding the player with items from materials to extremely useful upgrades.

What could be improved is material gathering and processing. The game has a crafting system but its only really used (in my experience) for vital objects or upgrading parts. A way of auto crafting and gathering would be much appreciated as well as a better way of sorting and storing items in bases and freighters.

Reviews.122380:
Yes. You want this.

Some key takeaways:

+ Hello Games is the undisputed master of procedural world generation. The scale, diversity and design of the No Man's Sky's universe is really impressive. Even if you disregard the gameplay entirely and buy the gameplay only for the sake of exploring the scenery and taking pictures, you'll get your money's worth out of it.

+ Hello Games is also the undisputed master of redemption. After failing the meet the inflated expectations of their game at launch, they were drowned in negative feedback. Any other developer would have given up and walked away, but they didn't. Instead, they ceaselessly worked to make good on their promises by delivery a major content update each year for free. And by now, NMS really is a great game that'll give you dozens, if not hundreds hours of fun if you're into this kind of gameplay. Much respect for this developer!

+ The multiplayer experience. It isn't flawless and takes some getting used to if you're used to server-based multipay. But once you get the hang of it, it's a pretty solid experience that fits the game and offers a lot of flexibility.

+/- The writing. It stands out, but not just for the right reasons. On the one hand, it's a well-crafted storyline with a decent amount of lore that explains the universe as it is nicely. On the other hand, it's all cliches and vagueness. None of the NPC's you meet - story-driven or procedurally generated - is able to strike up an even remotely sensible conversation. They either stick to standard tropes about their race/occupation or blather incoherently about the Great Secret that is the main storyline. Which gets stale pretty quickly, but unfortunately never stops.

- No Man's Sky sorely lacks challenge and endgame content. The game starts out very promising, with lots of stuff to explore, achieve and unlock. However, about halfway through you'll realize that beating the game, even on surival, requires at most mediocre equipment and no skill whatsoever. For instance, you can easily win pretty much any space battle with just a few upgrades to your starter ship. This makes playing dozens of hours to gain the best combat ship possible feel rather pointless.

Even more perplexing for a space exploration game, No Man's Sky's gameplay doesn't give you a convincing reason to explore. You can finish 95% of what the game has to offer - quests, skills, base building - without ever leaving the vicinity of your starting planet. 

This is mostly because almost anything that makes a planet unique - landscape, flora, fauna, inhabitants - is purely cosmectic: you can't do anything with it, other than make screenshots. You'd expect, for example,  that you could bring unique(ish) flora/fauna, artifacts or building materials home with you to showcase or use it for base building. But that kind of stuff is - with the notable exception of spaceships - unfortunately not possible (yet?)

Still, you want this.

After years of updates, refinement, bug fixes, patches, optimization and continued support of their community, Sean Murray and his team at Hello Games have done what many, much larger in terms staff, funding, and player number studios have failed to do. This game has been wholly revived and redeemed to become one of my favorite games I've ever played, specifically in the survival genre.

TL;DR: This game has a scale I’ve personally never played before, it’s truly fantastic. The exploration is awesome, there’s a substantial grind that is there if you want, it runs well, and multiplayer is a pretty awesome experience, both with friends and random interlopers alike. The overall experience is hindered slightly by small bugs. Overall, this game is a solid 9/10 and I’m thoroughly enjoying my time in the No Man’s Sky universe. 

The Good: 
- The game is truly engrossing, especially in terms of scale. From the amount of planets, their variety, flora and fauna, it’s truly awe inspiring. Nothing quite comes close to the feel of flying off a planet's surface, into space, flying to another planet that no one has ever been to, landing on it, all with no loading.
- The art style is great, a good blend of realistic enough, but also nails the aesthetic of the 1960s space race vibe of what we’d hope space travel and exploration would be like in the 2000s. 
- The goal of mixed single player with elements of multiplayer is an awesome concept. (There’s still some minor bugs, but it’s overall cool how it can be enjoyed alone and with friends)
- The storyline is massively improved, even from a year ago. It’s long enough that it’s something you get invested into, exploring concepts such as what it means to be alive, a friend, relativity of time, and how to leave an impact.
- The last big point is the “feel” of it all. Lasering rocks and sentinels with your multitool feels cool, flying is easy to understand but takes time to really master, the grind is there if you want, but can be ignored if you’re not into that, and the balance of being able to have a base, go explore, never lose your base, but also not be tied to it is great. 

The Bad:
- The biggest issue for me is all the annoying little bugs that I and my friends have run into. Thankfully all of these minor issues can be solved by simply saving and reloading the game, but it is a bit tedious and frustrating. Sometimes your ship just won’t take off, from both a planet’s surface or from an anomaly, space station or freighter. Sometimes, especially in multiplayer, when trying to wait for just the right ship to show up to buy, sometimes they just stop spawning and landing or the ones you buy and scrap just don’t disappear from their landing pad. Other times you’ll be searching for a buried technology module, and for whatever reason, they just don’t spawn, making researching base blueprints very time consuming. 

Miscellaneous: This is a slight criticism, albeit one I assume will be fixed soon. Often times when using your pulse engine between planets, you’ll get a notification there’s something interesting to see. You’ll stop, and it’s some cool object (I won’t spoil these as they’re really awesome), but so far, it seems as if you cannot really interact with any of these objects. I’m hoping they’ll be a bit more meaningful with a future update.

First of all, I want to say that I'm a huge fan of this game. I originally purchased No Man's Sky for PS4 on launch day and was ecstatic about the idea despite being disappointed by the unfinished product. When it was announced that Hello Games would continue working on the title, I decided to shelve it and with each big update I returned to NMS and spent more time in the game with each return. This is the perfect game for a person who likes to explore without too many restrictions, NMS has plenty to offer in 2020 for any player ready to sink some hours into discovering a seemingly infinite variety of planets with different conditions and creatures. Collecting blueprints to upgrade ships, bases, weapons and tools. Taking part in online missions either alone or with other players, just to name a few things.

I repurchased recently on Steam to get the better experience and I find myself becoming committed to this game. I really like the multiplayer support even though I enjoy playing alone. I love all the recent updates including Origins which is a great sign that Hello Games still has a lot of surprises for No Man's Sky. With this update, I really enjoy exploration on planets far more than I ever did, and it has left me a bit thirsty for some more space exploration to make more use of the exotic ships I have in my collection.

Here's a list of some things I would like to see with future updates:
- Space exploration expansion with freighter mission board for more space fights, enemy freighters, freighter escort, etc.
- Ability to hire more freighter crew to repair ships and aid in space combat.
- Having potential enemies attack player-owned freighters and getting blueprints for freighter defence systems.
- Dangerous rare space creatures.
- An interactive 3D map of current system showing planet distance and locations of interest (similar to the galaxy map).
- Ability to hire drone companion which follows and attacks enemies.
- Addition of roaming bandits on-planet with bases which can be infiltrated and claimed.
- Base defence blueprints to defend against attacking bandits and creatures and/or hired security drones.
- Ability to hire land crew for planet expeditions.
- Ability to change flagship home base.
- Mega-structure blueprints for base.
- Ability to restart a quest line. (I have some missions that I cannot complete without restarting the game unfortunately)

I can't wait to see what comes next for No Man's Sky!

This game could be a masterpiece but it has so many bugs. 

For example, there's no point building impressive or elaborate bases because if you leave for a while, you'll find all your doors have disappeared and half of your solar panels and batteries are gone. Not to mention all your wiring will be torn apart. 

And don't bother using foundation struts, either. They will deploy to the ground when you first install them. But once you leave the base and return, they will remain fully retracted forever. 

So this is yet another exploration/crafting/survival game that could be brilliant but is unfortunately defective. There is really no excuse for these fundamental bugs to exist since this game was released so many years ago.

Edit: God this game is hot trash. It's really super cool that you can build a mobile base inside your freighter. But it is glitchy af. Plants will randomly disappear from their hydroponics trays and sometimes reappear later. And there seems to be specific places where they won't receive any power—but no indication of why they won't. The trays immediately adjacent on either side have power. Why doesn't the one in the middle?

I also like to keep a save game device on my freighter for saving game purposes. Well, about half the time when I go to save, it's just... gone. Where did it go? Sometimes it reappears. But it would be nice if it would just continue to exist. 

And speaking of freighter... whoever came up with the ridiculous conditions that must occur in order to trigger a freighter battle is an idiot. You would think a game with so many randomly generated elements would not have such a rigid structure for spawning freighter battles. None of this silly three hours of playtime and five system jumps is necessary. There should just be a chance of a freight event happening each jump. And actually, why does it have to be jump related? Why can't it just happen any time?

And there are other ways this game could be so much more interesting. Like why is the pirate I'm supposed to kill after accepting a mercenary contract always just waiting right outside the space station? Are pirates not other places sometimes? I feel like pirates should be in all kinds of different places. It would certain make hunting them more interesting if we had to track them down. 

It's sad they created this amazing (if you ignore the bugs) sandbox platform but completely fail to utilize it in any interesting way. If they put the same effort into dynamically generating missions as they did for generating planets, this game might actually be amazing.

This game is so thoroughly disappointing.  I've had it since it released and they've added stuff to it, yes, but none of it improves the game.  The gameplay loop is essentially: gather stuff so you can upgrade your suit so you can gather more stuff.  And thats about it.  It has a very basic base building system.  It has a multiplayer option, but there still isn't anything to do.  

This game really hyped itself up.  Quadrillions of planets!  An infinite randomly generated galaxy!  But what they forgot to tell you, is that all these planets are empty and there is nothing fun to do on them.  So the game drops you onto a planet to start.  You are equipped with your mining lazer.  You use this to shoot random rocks and plants which give you materials like carbon, oxygen, and salt, which are used to power your various tools.  Your suit also has a life support system and a hazardous environment system which are both constantly draining at all times.  These need to be charged with the materials you gather.  As does your ship's engines.  And your mining lazer.  So you are walking around shooting stuff gathering materials so you can keep doing exactly that.  And yeah, you can take off from one planet and fly to another, but why?  You just do the same thing there.  All of the planets are basically the same except for what colors the plants and stuff are.  There are sometimes bases with 1 alien you can talk to but not understand cuz the game has a language system where you learn one word at a time, which ends up being hilariously useless.  I learned over 100 words for a language and still could only read like 2 words per conversation.  You can get new suits and ships, but all they do is give you more space to hold more materials so you can keep on gathering.  This game promises so much and delivers on nothing.  Its as wide as the ocean, but as deep as a puddle.  Its aimless game play never becomes fun.  It has a very vague story, and you can finish the game rather quickly if you choose.  The goal is to reach the center of the universe.  I wont spoil the ending, if you can call it that, but I promise you will be left with a feeling like, "Thats it?  Thats what they came up with and thought people would like?  WTF..."

If you want a really good open world survival game, just get Subnautica.  It does everything No Man's Sky tries to do but actually succeeds at it.  Subnautica does base building and exploration and survival so much better, while always being fun!  

No Man's Sky might be worth it if it was $15.  But at full price, you're just getting ripped off.  I know not many people like Angry Joe, but if you're on the fence about buying this game... Watch the first few minutes of his review.  It perfectly sums up the entire game.

Reviews.122572:
Let's start with the graphics.

The visuals (in my opinion) are upper-level indi style. Not by any means photo realistic but definitely still nice to look at. Decent textures and decent shadows and lighting for a non Triple A title. Space looks downright stunning at times and if you can line up the shot, you can get some pretty good looking screenshots planet-side as well.

Audio

The audio here is just good. Not crappy but nothing to write home about either. The sounds do match the game for what it is if that makes sense. I personally love the spaceship and exocraft sounds.

The gameplay 

This game has a lot to do plain and simple. Find spacecraft and upgrade them, build a base and create a hub for yourself while you explore the universe. Discover abandoned structures and loot their treasures. Document the various creatures and plant life which by the way are also all procedurally generated meaning good luck discovering every species. Because you won't. Also prepare to find some pretty crazy looking creatures outside during your expeditions. Acquire a freighter and a fleet of frigates and send them on expeditions to acquire money and materials for you. And much much much more.. So if you watched any of the trailers you would already know that this game offers a near infinite universe. You couldn't explore every planet in the first galaxy alone within your lifetime. It's simply not possible. So in an infinite universe, exploration and loneliness go hand-in-hand. So it would be a good idea to find a friend or two or even three to tag along with during your adventures. You'll quickly learn that bringing a few friends during some of the many missions you'll go on is a good idea. 

The Story

The story in this game is completely optional to follow. If you don't care to follow it then you don't have to. BUT, it does open up some doors gameplay wise if you decide to play it. The story is.... interesting.  Without spoiling it for you, It makes you think about your existence and your place in the universe. Your purpose in all of it. But then again, if you want to say "screw it" and just continue doing everything listed above then you can do that too! It really doesn't matter. But like I said it does open some doors later on gameplay wise. 

Price

Just buy it. If you like games like this one then don't just wait for it to go on sale. It's worth the price tag. Honestly it's pretty cheap for an infinite universe.

Conclusion 

This game definitely had a rocky start after launch. It was cold and dead. But not anymore. The developers have brought new life to this game through many updates and tweaks throughout the years. They have thoroughly proven that they truly do care about their game and have every intention to continue enhancing it and bringing more and more to the table with every update and have shown no signs of stopping any time soon. I wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone and everyone who yearns for exploration, danger, and a whole lot of fun and excitement. And it's only going to get better.

I'm absolutely hooked. There's a ton of stuff to do and the multiplayer adds a nice touch of spice to the game. It's mostly a single-player game but you can connect with friends and meet new people in a certain area where you can do missions together. It's one of those classic "collect resources to upgrade/build things so that you can collect more things but also survival" games, but there's also a lot more to it.

The whole concept is grand. Basically infinite star systems and planets to explore but also a lot going on in space. The whole go from planet-to space-to another planet-and back into space seamlessly (no loading screens except when entering a new system) is a massive plus. Building bases, creating a fleet, having your own personal freighter, collecting starships, etc. is really cool. You can even travel to other galaxies but I'm not that far yet.

Exploration is a lot of fun. I was a little skeptical at first with everything being AI generated BUT it actually means you always see new things, and some of those things can get really bizarre. For example earlier today I found a "planet of flame" where a wall of flame storm came and half the planet caught on fire, I found a species of animal that looks like little teddy bears, and I found another planet that was entirely made out of mountains that went into the upper atmosphere with small valleys that are almost little dots from the top of the mountains. 

The only downside for some people is that the game isn't super mission driven. It is upgrade driven though, even at 73 hours I still don't have everything that I've been trying to get and I keep finding more ways to get more stuff to make exploration easier. Basically, you have to be okay with sandbox games. For example, I'm told that the main mission revolves around working your way to the center of the galaxy, but instead I've decided to go the opposite direction and try to find the edge of the galaxy. 

So anyways, I'm going to go continue my journey to the edge of the galaxy.

The game is fun for the first few dozen hours. Once you exhaust the non-procedurally-generated content, the rest is all the same. Like many other reviews have already pointed out, the "2^64 unique planets" claim is extremely misleading -- there are infinitely many ways to pour a bowl of cereal, but in the end they all look just like a bowl of cereal.

The plot is very unconvincing. It tries to create something grand out of the simple premise that everything is a simulation, and completely falls flat. There are no deep philosophical discussions, or compelling character plots; instead, you're just provided with a few passing remarks and then the narration makes the "you" character produce over-the-top emotional responses. It's just impossible to be engaged in this story (if you can even call it that).

And then there are the weird design choices, which are sometimes so bizarre that I seriously can't tell if they were intended or just bugs. For example, sometimes quests ask you to warp to a distant star system, and you have to warp repeatedly from one system to another until you reach your destination -- but saving and reloading sometimes immediately "teleports" you to the destination system.

The reviews are up and down for this game, and having just finished my "normal" campaign, going through the story missions, I thought I'd chime in.
I had no real expectations. I came from a KSP background really with another thousand hours in Factorio. This game has a learning curve. The tutorial is a do-this-then-do-that kinda thing which is fine for understanding which button to push, but doesn't really explain *why* you're pushing it. YouTube though is a life saver, and this is my third time persevering before finally getting hooked. The UI is clunky and mildly unintuitive, and there are some real MMO elements to it (no colouring of your ship - just keep hunting for the right one!) but it's still a great game.
And the reason for that is twofold. First - I really enjoyed the story. It's outside the box, and tries a different approach. First game to make me physically smile at the screen since Project Zomboid. Second - once I'd finished the story, the game most definitely wasn't over. Don't get me wrong, the story has its issues: It's just a shade too long on the go-here-do-this mentality for a start, but I felt like I'd been reborn afterwards (spoilers deleted).
I picked this up on sale and at £40 I'd still say it was worth it. At the sale price though, it's an absolute steal! Just be wary of YouTube videos advising you on tactics for making [money/nanites/currency] because the game has changed a lot since launch and older videos are very much out of date.
Finally, before giving up on it because of UI/control issues, check the subreddit, or Google. I made quite a few tweaks to the controls to make both flying the ships, and walking around, far more manageable. Well worth taking half an hour to get the controls so that they are comfortable.
I'm about 60 hours in and still haven't really touched base building, or proper character min/maxing. I just stuck what I thought would be good into whatever place I thought it should go and I managed fine. It's a forgiving game (once you get the hang of the UI!!) and that makes me want to have another go now on the Permadeath level. The XCOM in me won't let it go :)

Might update this review as I play more and remember to.

[b]Summary[/b]
Could use some polish and bug fixes but it's good fun with friends or solo too. I'd recommend making backups of your saves after each play session and saving often in game.

[b]Experience[/b]
The early game was kinda scary (we died a couple times because it was really hot starting planet) but after that things were pretty smooth. Inventory management is a concern but it's a lot better once you get storage (they act ender chests from Minecraft but you get up to 10 different chests) Also look for merchants that sell drop pod data that you can find and repair for inventory slot upgrades once they start getting too expensive. Getting a cheap ship upgrade was nice but most of them were really expensive so it would be a lot of work to get them. I collected these spiky green orbs from these dangerous purple fruit / eggs for money enough to get a decent second ship and multi tool eventually. My friend lucked out and found a crashed ship to repair and own, so be on the lookout for those! Found a merchant that sold drop pod data which is great for when the slot upgrades becomes too expensive.

Liked talking to the other sentient beings on the space station, trade stations and elsewhere was fun and just flying around in the ship is really fun too. Especially satisfying is when you travel from the planet's surface out to space or back again. It's also fun to look at the wild life and scan them. Think it would be nice if scanning was a little faster and there was a little more variety in the hazardous flora (I didn't notice more than about 3 types but maybe there's more I haven't seen yet, it does feel strange scanning what looks to be the same on multiple planets and being rewarded for it XD).

[b]Friction points and Bugs[/b] [i](bugs could be the recent update and probably fixed already)[/i]
Something that I wish was made more clear is that you'll want your own base even when playing multiplayer with friends since you'll need it for doing missions.
Leaving items in machines can result in them vanishing and later maybe reappearing. We're not sure what causes this to happen but it doesn't seem to happen as long as you don't leave the area (storage is okay though).
Using the pulse drive towards a freighter can get you stuck inside it if the pulse drive doesn't automatically stop when you get close. (It's okay though you do spawn a grave in space so you can collect your stuff).
Game did crash a few times but haven't been able to pin down what causes it to. The most recent was just when collecting some gravitino balls from these coral looking creatures. It didn't happen right away though.

[b]When did I get it?[/b]
Got No Man's Sky just after the Origin update. A friend showed me a video about the story behind what the developers of the game went through and it was so sad ;-; But they got through it in the end so yay~

[b]Was it worth it?[/b]
Got the game half off which I think is worth it for me with fun with my friend so far. The game does have a lot of custom code (they couldn't use some game engine to help achieve what they desire). Also I heard that the game got lots of updates that could have been DLC but were free so that's amazing too!

It's improved a lot from what I was told were the early days of the game. The devs initially were overly ambitious, but they showed they did care, and that really says something for the integrity of the devs that they continue to add new content despite its initial crash and burn. Nowadays, it's a hella fun and interesting romp through space, exploring different planets, collecting resources, chilling out. It's like a 3D Starbound, really. Plenty of different ways to play the game, whether it's trade running, farming, hunting, questing, exploring, whatever really. 

If I had to suggest features for a potential sequel: take some pages from Spore. Add the ability for players to make custom plants and animals and minerals and share them online for other people to discover. That would prevent biome-specific plants from starting to look repetitive, and further encourage exploring to see new, weird sights. Extra customization options for players along the lines of Skyrim would also let players really feel like their character is THEIR character. Adjustable proportion sliders and what-not would be very nice. No Man's Sky is a game that begs for a lot of assets, I think, even more than are already in the game, and I feel like having player-designed props would take the game that one step further. 

Also let people scrap multi-tools.

This is the epitome of the story of the ugly duckling that turned into a beautiful swan.

I didn't buy into the game when it launched. I really wanted to and it was on my wishlist, but when I read about it back then it put me off completely. Years later and Hello Games have worked hard to give this game its redemption. And sandworms!

The gameplay itself is a bit on the grindy side but it can be as laid back an experience you want it to be. You pilot your spaceship between star systems and planets. You can land on the planets and various points of interest in space and exit your ship. On the planets and in space you can mine for resources, you build stuff, rinse and repeat. You can also pick up freeform missions at various places. There are some stressors - mainly that you sometimes have to keep track of and recharge the various levels of technology that's keeping you alive on some planets. And sometimes there are more pressing matters to deal with too. There is a story to progress through, but you can veer off it at any point after you have gone through enough 'tutorial'-lessons to make it on your own. The general storyline is that you need to head towards the center of a galaxy of billions of star systems. To be fair I never got that far, something always came up or I got bored. In the end it is up to you what you want to do in the vast, but certainly not empty and sometimes very gorgeous playfield.

The trouble with these kind of sandbox games is that they end up feeling as they are miles wide but barely an inch deep once you come to grip with them, when you know all the mechanics of them in and out. And I suppose this is inevitable. [i]No Man's Sky[/i] suffer from this as well, but the updates Hello Games have kept churning out for it always come with new content and seem to give it the feeling of coming back to something fresh. Mind you these updates can't come forever, but for now there is enough of a game to keep you entertained for as long as you like.

I really, really, REALLY want to recommend this game to others.  I do still, kinda, but ONLY if you get it for at least half off.  First, the game is several years old so the fact that the price point is still sixty bucks is kinda lame.  Second, I have had to reload my game three times now due to game breaking bugs.  They have had three major content patches in the game, but those patches merely brought them to where they promised the game would be ON RELEASE.  

As to the game breaking bugs, when I searched for them TWO of them were reported in the bug forum in 2018.  TWO YEARS AGO.  Literally they have been so busy making up new content to fix the fact they lied through their teeth that they cannot fix GAME BREAKING BUGS.  One big part of this game I didn't realize is that it is NOT like a typical sandbox/mmo/etc.  You do NOT auto-save when you quit.  You cannot save anywhere you want (without building a special thing and wasting an inventory slot to lug it around) so if you ever find yourself clipped into the wall and literally unable to move, your only option is reload the most recent save, so hopefully that's less than an hour's worth of progress you're about to lose.  They *do* auto-save for some things like entering/exiting your ship, so at least you MIGHT have an auto-save that isn't TOO old.  

TL;DR - A for effort in making up for broken promises.  F for the fact that they still have 2 year old bugs that hard lock your game.  Overall grade?  D.  Fun when it works, but you will rage over the fact that you lose progress when their shit breaks.  If you are still interested, pick it up when they drop the price in half for a sale, do NOT pay full price for this bug-fest.

*edit*

Also - if you just wanna say 'you forgot to save' maybe you should pull your head up out of your mom's basement and look at total time played. 20 hours. Got this game on sale after the 'promises realized' patch and wasn't aware it was still buggy as hell and I needed to save every 5 minutes. This *will* result in many more angry newbies leaving bad reviews and wanting refunds. I'm not asking for a refund. I am asking for someone to realize that 2 year old bugs are a BAD sign and should have been eliminated by this point in a sixty dollar game.  Seriously, I had landed at some kinda trade hub, exited my ship (auto save) talked to 5 vendors and sold some stuff, hit the invis wall, figured out I could jet pack over it, got stuck in floor.  At what point between the auto-save and the bug should I have saved again?  Do I carry the portable save beacon with me and save after EVERY transaction with a shop keeper?  After EVERY time I mine something?  To suggest this is the product of my failure to save is fucking idiotic.

I'll save you fanbois the time - I am NOT here bashing this game to bash it.  I WANT it to be better.  I *want* to recommend it.  Despite those bugs I listed I *will* still probably sink MUCH time into it.  But if those bugs persist, and newbies hit them early in the game, they WILL rage quit and get a refund.  I am trying to save the devs money in the long run with this review in the hopes they'll patch the bugs.  If they do, then by all means I'll happily modify this review.

If you have done any amount of research into this game, it is most likely you've heard of the terrible controversy this game was flagged for at its launch. Well, after many years of continued development and free updates, it is safe to say that in many ways, it has surpassed what was previously promised at launch, and completely cleared its name in the community. 

This game is about exploration, freedom, discovery and the desire to get all of the things. There is many things to do. You can purchase, upgrade and sell aircrafts, you can own giant frigates and build a fleet to send on various missions, build and upgrade your own land vehicles, construct glorious (or more humble) bases on land and under the sea, fight against wildlife, fight against pirates, play with your friends, harvest resources, discover new flora, fauna and minerals, complete missions, follow the story, etcetera, you get the picture. 

While the game does get quite grindy at times, to me at least, that grind is often overshadowed by the shear wonder and scale of this game. With so many things to do and explore in a practically endless universe of literally trillions of systems, there is so much that you may just very well sink hundreds, if not thousands of hours into this game. I've also found that it is also a very relaxing game. Exploring the endless cosmos, looking at beautiful planets, flying around in space, listening to the calming soundtrack, it all emits a very comforting and welcoming aura. It is perfect when you're trying to relax and wind down after a rough day. 

That said, there are a few problems, like I said previously there can be a lot of grinding at times, which is never really a good thing. Furthermore, the performance can often dip at times, especially when rendering in a lot of assets. A major problem however is the many bugs that I've encountered. Some models will refuse to load, textures will sometimes flicker, particles will flicker as well, cave interiors will not load, the varying draw distance, etcetera. That said, all but one bug that I've encountered thus far has not been entirely game breaking. That one bug however occurs when you alt+tab out of the game and back in. The screen will freeze, and you'll have to alt+F4 or use task manager to close the game and reload. 

In the end however, there is many hours of wonder and fun to have in this game, and I look forward to many more. It has been a very positive experience for me and I intend to explore the universe further and collect all of the things!

I had yet to write a review on this game, purchased it in 2016. My year of space games. I was heavily invested in Star Citizen for instance. And I thought No Man's Sky is nothing but a bandwagon game, that tried to copycat the Kickstarter Space game formula to make money. I thought it was a scam, I knew everyone would be let down, and if one game is going to be good at spaceflight, it'll be Star Citizen.

Here we are today, with No Man's Sky, being one of the best games on the market. Giant worlds, full of actual things to do, it was a long time since I felt "overwhelmed" with things I can do in a game. And this time, it's absolutely top notch, for I have longed for a game, where you can explore the unkwown, and the unknown is actually interesting, something worth exploring.

Oh boy, I have spent hours on one planet. With several bases on nice locations, practical locations full of resources. I am just starting with another planet. I will probably spend less and less time on them, as I know what I'll be looking for. But the fact that there are underwater places to explore aswell, ones I've not yet even gotten to, makes me excited!

Next thing is - VR. I've never before seen a game, that wasn't made for VR from the ground up, to be so excelently represented in it. They saw the opportunity, and they took it. Most of the actions you performed with a simple press of a button have been translated into simple gestures, like pulling, grabbing and moving. It's VR integration done right. My room is now stuck with an armchair in the middle of it, because that's where I sit and fly my little spaceship, that can be operated with controllers, as if you had a hotas, it does feel kind of weird not having the base, but all you need is to gid the end of the controller (Vive controller) into your thigh, and it works just as well.
That was probably the most pleasant surprise, standing on a moon with orange hue, looking at the sky, where a giant planet looms over the night sky with a ring illuminated by the star's sunrays was probably the most beautiful sight in VR I've had, partly because it wasn't just a background, it isn't just a painting, made to look pretty, it's all accessible and ready to be explored!

A game that was pulled out of a ditch, repaired, cleaned, polished and detailed. And it's not going to end there? They announced more updates to come? I am surprised, baffled, bamboozled. I will be spending more and more time with this one.

It was nothing but a piece of meaningless carbon, but under extreme pressure of the angered gaming community, it slowly turned into condensed carbon, a diamond cut into a beautiful brilliant. Give this a go and support the devs, this is how it's done.
I tip my hat to you, Hello Games, one legend to another.
Keep it coming.

WHEW has this changed since I got it refunded 4 years ago. 

Long story short, 4 years ago I bought it and it got lame real quick. After about an hour or two I refunded it.

I had heard a lot about how people were saying that the game had changed and there was a total redemption, but I didn't believe them. I had a friend of mine tell me to play the game and buy it, and boy was I surprised. Yeah It's got it's flaws. Scale isn't super realistic. Freighter mechanics seems unrealistic. The only thing to fight on the ground is the Sentinel things. There aren't any cities (yet). Building multiple bases seems somewhat pointless. 

But it's got PVP now. The game has an actual story. You can easily meet up with friends and join a system together. If you want to LARP as an admiral you can literally own a sizable fleet by yourself. Worldbuilding is actually decent. There's space battles you can participate in. The grind is well done. You won't find yourself stuck at any point. There's apparently base raids of some kind. There's tons of variety when it comes to planets, each with huge oceans, caverns and so forth. Seeing all the different animals and plants are interesting. The game doesn't FEEL unfinished now, it's got a lot of features, and tons of content, lots of which I haven't encountered anywhere close to on my small playthrough. Vehicles, crafting, the works. In the few hours I've played this since last time, it actually feels like there's something to do compared to back in 2016 where it was pretty barren. Now I honestly feel overloaded with stuff to do, which is great. 

I would give it a recommend, I think it's a little overpriced at $60 but honestly you can't go wrong if you buy it on sale. Get a crowd together and you'll find shit to do. Play with friends for sure. 

No, it's not Grand Theft Auto in space, but it has it's own quirks that make it a game I would like to spend more time with. But it's damn close. And it's probably going to be similar to that in the future.

I, among some others, was waiting for the right time after a patchy launch. As of the Origins update, this game is now worth a look if you want a bit of survival exploration and a bit of mystery travelling across vast galaxies of space.  Now, I will admit, I trialled this using the XBOX Game Pass and was so satisfied with it, that I purchased it on Steam.  It's also very close to Sean Murray's original vision of how he wanted the game to be.  

You are an unknown entity, possibly an Anomaly who is seemingly stranded on some random planet on the edge of a vast Galaxy, and the only thing you seem to start off with is some limited supplies and a Multi-tool that can mine elemental components.  From release, the main goal is to race to the centre of that Galaxy and to see what lies there. However multiple updates have happened since then which added base-building, Frigate micromanagement and even the unknown with derelict frigates. Finally, the developers have added a "story-line", should you choose to ignore the original game's main objective.

It also runs modestly well on a GTX 960, but there are options to make the game look moreso impressive on higher-end graphics cards.  It can also be played on a DualShock 4 or a XBOX 360/One controller, with rumours that it will get Series XBOX controller support once it's released. There are, as of right now, no confirmations if there will be support for DualShock 5 controllers.

I would however say if you don't like the thought of survival, there is a Creative game mode that does away with the story content, and there are survival and permadeath difficulties for those who enjoy the game and want a more rewarding challenge, on more limited resources.

When NMS was first announced I was skeptical and decided to hold off and wait to see if they'd deliver upon their promises.  I'm glad that I did.  Some four years later and following many free updates I decided to give it a try while it was half priced.  Am I ever glad that I did.  It seems like they finally caught up to what they had been hyping up back in 2016.

The game does suffer quite heavily from consolitis (the menus and control schemes are pretty awful) but the game itself is absolutely massive and seems pretty darn stable.  There is so much to see, so much to do, so much to learn and unlock.  It's incredibly accessible for solo, up to four player co-op, and non-PvE playstyles.  I've started my space-faring career hunting down crashed ships to scrap them for resources and have branched out from there.

Worth noting is that the first few hours of the game are very confusing and frustrating.  It took me a couple days of playing to settle in and figure everything out, they throw so much at you without allowing you time to absorb it all.  Still, during this learning curve the game kept drawing me back in.  I wanted to return to it and understand how it worked.

That said, this is the space exploration game which I had always wished for but it isn't just space.  There are terrestrial vehicles (why can't we have standard throttle and brake gamepad controls for these?) and now submersibles for exploring water planets which is a game all of its own.  There's always room for improvement (waterfalls?) but the team behind this title has created something amazing and have proven that they'll stand behind what they've made and continue to make it better.

I can lose myself for hours in No Man's Sky and look forward to what Hello Games comes up with going forward.  It's taken a while but the stories are true, NMS is the great comeback story.

You haven't lived until a sandworm has erupted from beneath your feet.

This game's gone from one of the biggest examples of game devs misrepresenting final deliverables (no idea if the publisher had anything to do with it) to one of the few examples of a game developer going well above and beyond to correct their huge misstep. Most devs would just move on but Hello Games stuck it out. With each free update, the game got better and better. There were still weird glitches and sometimes frustrating bugs but piece by piece, repetitive worlds became exotic worlds. Basic survival expanded into amazing base building and exploration opportunities.

Today, the Origins update came out. At this point, you can do a ton of stuff: base building, exploration, trading, pirating (to a point), etc. It's not X4 but X4 isn't NMS really. There's still some grind but the best part is that grind really isn't necessary. Need to mine a ton of stuff to fuel your trade commodity production farm? Auto-miners will cover that for you. Want to build the base of your dreams? Most of the component materials can be bought/traded from trading platforms and stations. Looking for that special ship? Well, that could be a grind if you want something incredibly specific (like some exotic S class fighter with four fins and blah blah blah). But if not, grab that hauler from that guy (seems everyone wants to sell their ship to you these days) and upgrade it. Found some crap ship and you can't sell it because despite everyone selling their ship to you, there's apparently no ship market? No problem, break that puppy down for parts worth as much as it was worth (plus grab a storage augmentation here and there) and you'll soon have the money you need.

Whether this game's for you really depends on what you're looking for. Looking for a space shooter? Eh, there's always Star Wars Squadrons! Looking for an exploration game with base building, decent trading, and a lot of weird species and vistas to discover? You're good. You've got billions of worlds and there a bunch of universes to "upgrade" to in order to find another billion worlds. 

There are some weird places and some amazingly beautiful places. You'll find yourself standing overlooking a valley that leads to an ocean with a ringed planet in the sky and the sun(s) setting at the horizon. There's a trade port over there where all sorts of ships are flying in to and out from. There's some weird building guarded by robots that may just have something interesting. You see a twinkle in the sky that turns out to be your main freighter where five other ships you've found and upgraded are sitting, waiting for you. You can send out support ships on missions to find and collect materials and wealth to feed your empire as you build bases on frozen worlds and weird worlds with crystal creatures. 

There's a ton to do and while you may do enough that you'll get bored one day, it's not a big deal. You can always start a new game or just come back once in a while to warp to a new system and find some new planet that's all hot pink with purple trees and some massive creature is hopping around right next to you. Hop into your ship, jet off the surface and warp to the next system with another set of randomly generated worlds. Billions more to go!

Reviews.123094: With every fiber of my being, I wanted this game to be the messiah of the industry.  I love little in this world more than open-ended science fiction, and this certainly appeared to be everything I had asked for.  But after I became an owner of a functionally infinite universe, I realized that it was riddled with limits.  Setting aside its frankly abysmal release, credit must be given to the developers for their tireless efforts to completely overhaul the flaws of this game.  Yet even still, I remain incapable of recommending that you buy it.  As many updates as the developers release, they cannot ever fix the basic fact that open world games of this type don't mesh with the procedurally generated, survival-centric gameplay loop that NMS encourages.  You start the game by spawning on an alien planet, and are immediately consuming resources.  The mere act of standing around diminishes supplies, meaning that you are thrust into the world not by the desire to explore, but by the necessity to grind.  Procedural generation doesn't help either. I personally prefer my game worlds to be crafted with specific tonal shifts and pacing in mind, and random world creation strikes me as wildly unnecessary, and so too does the sheer quantity of generated worlds.  However many billions of planets the game will tell you are available, you will only ever be able to get explore a handful of them.  This makes me think that a game featuring a single solar system with 3-4 densely populated planets would be a much better use of everybody's time.  In short, the game was a valiant and ambitious effort that fell flat in too many ways to be worth your money.

NMS is a good exploration game, and I like it well enough. The worlds are interesting, if a bit uniform and predictive after the first few, which is a shame. The characters are nice enough, and the quests are well written if a bit rushed.
There isn't much character building for the NPCs in the quests. But the lore is nice and it's intriguing.

It's irritating and a hassle that you can't save from the main menu, I get the extra "survival" point of having to find a place to save, but what if I'm an hour in and the game crashes or the electricity cuts? All progress lost.

What makes this an INFURIATING experience however, is the fact that every two to five minutes, a little interface pops up to remind me of the current quest. There's no way to turn it off without disabling the entire HUD, and it really tears away from the game experience. If I'm exploring a planet I don't want a message constantly telling me to go to a different galaxy.
Related to this is the guide messages. I've played for over 50 hours now, I think I know how to use the jet-pack without it reminding me every. single. time I use it. 

These issues may seem small, but when a message pops up for every single little thing you do and there's no way to opt out, it becomes a major irritant. I like exploration-survival games, I love the concept of NMS, but these issues take A LOT away from the experience by ripping me out of the immersion every second minute.

If Hello Games would give me an option to turn it off, and an option to deselect quests, I would recommend it wholeheartedly. 

If you like an exploration-survival game with a lot of options, and possess the ability to ignore "helpful" messages for every action you take, then by all means, go ahead. 
If, like me, constant interruptions irritate you, then I'd recommend you look for something a bit more considerate.

No Man's Sky has come very far. from it's early days as a complete mess of a project, to what we have now, and trust me it's much better than day 1.
The team behind No Man's Sky, Hello Games, haven't given up on this since it first came out and have constantly listened to the community and completely reworked how everything works. The crafting, the ship management, the base building, and the multiplayer, all added since launch. they didn't forget about this project like other developers (cough cough anthem) have, and infact doubled down and got to work on their game. they wanted to fix the game and for the most part they've done very well.
The introduction to the game is a bit rough i must admit, but once you're up and exploring the universe, it's addictive.  There are so many random encounters, interactions ( both npc and other players) and objectives to do. The mere fact that you don't understand the other alien races and actually have to go out onto other planets and learn their language through mystic stones is amazing to me. it's almost organic how you're so new to everything, and you have to learn it all to actually talk and do things for the other races. Each of the races have their own unique Dialog, mannerisms, and characteristics is astonishing. If you're not into talking to filthy xenos, you could always work for them. there are three Guilds which you can do missions for, usually quick, small tasks as you first go in, that lead into bigger, much more influential acts such as literally destroying a frigate. luckily the frigates are usually pirates, so you don't have to feel bad for having killed the 1000~ crew members aboard. 
This game, like a butterfly, has came out of it's cocoon and shown it's beautiful colours to those willing to stay by Hello Games side, and truly it has paid off. they have put non stop work into this game and it has become what it was always meant to be. an open world space exploration game. This is a good example of if you work hard enough on something, it really can become something greater than originally planned.
Thank you Hello Games, you've blown me and many of your other customers away with your astonishing work.

Reviews.123290:
Like many others commented, its a game concept that unfortunately isnt fun compared to available alternatives. You get a big empty world to explore. Yet, a big empty world is the downfall of most multiplayer games. Now, multiply the big empty world to a big empty universe. Exploration is monotonous unfortunately as once youve seen a couple of different planets, they start to look like mild variations of one another. Furthermore, there is not much to do at these worlds... you point a mining gun at various objects to mine for materials and then try to build a box-standard base. The whole base building part seems fun on paper but it is very grindy and repetitive to first (1) unlock the build tree (for example you need to salvage tech by walking around the planet to identical looking buried caches and collect them... then you need to pay X amount of 'salvage tech' for each building option, such as a wall or a roof or a floor... they dont come unlocked together, which is just prolonging the tediousness of it all). (2) collect materials to build (yes you go around point your mining gun at the same repetitive objects spawned around the planet(s). (3) collect money to buy more materials and cosmetic options (by selling your mined/salvage materials... yes more grinding... or completing daily quests... grind grind).   To top it all off, there is little accomplishment once all is said and done, as the storyline is nonexistant and not fulfilling, whilst if you just ignore any story.... then you are just building a very boring looking sandcastle with limited options in a big empty universe.... in the amount of time that could be better spent in other more engaging indie games or AAA titles sitting on your shelf.    

I think for the game to work, there needs to be a more compelling storyline that ties in neatly with the game mechanics and aimed as a 6-10 hour single player experience.... then for those who are interested, a grindey multiplayer formula aimed at exploration and no-barriers customisation.... not space weapons or boxy basebuilding. it just seems like the concept is infinite worlds and then they realised its not fun so they latched on some gaming mechanics that work for other games. 

there are so many storylines they can work with - an ai drone that's set out by humankind to establish a colony only to realise that its eras too late at the end and then philosophies about sentience and the freedom to choose henceforth. or a drone thats also set out but needs to find its way back after unintentionally travelling through the multiverse rather than said distance. or an alien probe that is looking for humans after seeing an advert from the 1960s. or a research vessel thats supposed to reach a certain 'research quota' before being able to return to its parent vessel. there are many formulas that work that do not require guns or repetitive tasks in the genre of an 'exploration' story driven game and they tend to do well. allowing custom customisation also tends to bring out beautiful and awesome player creations (minecraft/planet coaster/planet zoo/etc). rather than a space station with set stalls, it could be much more, like a social hub, ticket booths for entering other weekly highlighted player built sites, photo sharing, competitive base building, etc.... why does the game incorporate mechanics that does not fit its core??? it tries to be a little bit of everything and does little in the end. sandbox mechanic but limited boxy customisation/building options. trading mechanics but grindey, exploitable and not very interesting, space battles but poor shooting experience with subpar graphics and feedback for a shooter, unlockable cosmetics  to enjoy mostly in the company of one. its a rabbit hole with updates as devs continue to try to make the gameplay work. i think the gameplay should have been thought through from day 1 and the new updates should be about adding more variety to the scenery/building themes/interactive environmentals +/- story.
 i think its too late for a complete rework, but hopefully the developers take this concept to the next level in a new game.

Reviews.123292:
HOW DO YOU HAVE FUN IN THIS GAME????

That is the crazy question I used to ask when I started flirting with the idea of playing it.  I played it years ago, got my ship to lift off and had so much freedom and so many choices that I decided to….not play it. Huge mistake. That’s the game's biggest problem, there are so many things to do and so many choices it is easy to become overwhelmed. Looking back it kind of reminded me of when I first played Skyrim...I recall the feeling of “what the hell do I do now”.

I recently started again, watched a few videos, focused on a few things and now I am enthralled. The game is fantastic with endless things to do. It's set up to do a good job at appealing to the people looking for groups/community AND/OR the people that just want solo games. They have an in game mechanic to go to a mobile space station where everyone goes, so you can play with existing friends or start groups with new people (with an MMORPG feel) OR you can play solo without issues, changing settings so people can go to your base or you can lock people out (so they can’t find it). You can mine in space, mine on planets, be a pirate, go on missions for skins, even set up complexes to generate money for you while you are doing something else like mining complexes or grow plants (for that huge market section of virtual green thumb gamers), tons and tons of endless things to do. In fact, I’m sure there is great stuff I missed.

I found myself surprised by a lot of awesome vehicles and weapons. I don’t think they advertised what this game can currently do (or maybe I just wasn’t paying attention). For some taste of the visuals, check out “Mech Battle No Man's Sky Beyond 2020 (The Minotaur)” by GenjiGear on youtube for a look at player operated mechs. (this is NOT me, I swear)

It is impossible to describe the sheer size of this game. I made a base on my starting planet and just explored. Whenever I get new vehicle tech I go to that starting base and try it out. I’ve spent hours finding trading posts, ruins, sentinel storage facilities (enemy places you can raid and runoff with costly goods), crashed ships, and on and on...I could spend hundreds of hours there and this is only on ONE PLANET. Each solar system has several planets/moons, thousands and thousand (if not millions) of solar systems, and I just found out that there are ~5 or so galaxies where every planet can be explored to the extent of my starting planet. It is truly mind boggling.

Do yourself a favor and get this game.

I got aboard the "No Man's Sky Hype Train" well before the game came out; I don't remember whether or not I pre-ordered it back in 2016, but I probably did.  Then it came out, and boy was I underwhelmed. This was partially my own fault, because I didn't have the best computer.....the game was playable, I could tell the game was pretty, but my system was just not good enough to truly enjoy it...so, I shelved it. 

...a few months later, I got myself a new graphics card and some more ram RAM and came back to it, it was a much better experience. I think at this point they had brought out the freighters...It was a better game than when I had originally bought it, and subsequently, I put in a good hundred hours of game play over the course of I don't know how long.  In my algebra, that means that the game is a good one. But, ultimately, other games came out, distractions, life...the game got shelved later...

Now, years later, the game has continued to evolve and, more importantly, I have a much better computer...so, I decided, "what the heck, it's basically a new game...let's...start a new game..."

...boy, am I glad I did.

The Story Line: It is convoluted and ephemeral...it barely exists, it is fleeting, it's complicated, and you only ever get brief glimpses of it...this isn't helped by the fact that you spend the first few dozen hours not understanding much of what any of the aliens are saying...the story line isn't straight forward, it is bits and pieces, here and there.  The story line is more existential philosophy than anything else. But you are probably not interested in the game because of the story. 

...although, on a side-note; I bought a map from a station that took me to an abandoned facility on one of the local planets....after breaking in and scouring the database, I was given the location of an ancient ruin; I thought, "eh, free money..." When I got to the new planet, it was basically a waterworld with superheated rainstorms. I find the ruin and land, and what do I find?  Some weird energy being...I approach it and it proceeds to narrate what I swear is some kind of monologue about yearning for the sea that you would expect coming from Ernest Hemingway....yeah, that happened.

The Universe: Back in 2016, the universe was a mile wide and a meter deep; it has evolved into something vast and deep. Obviously, this is the meat and potatoes of the game; exploring vast, uncharted worlds, seeing the animals, seeing the trees, seeing the interesting rock formations, building a outpost and mining the hell out of the planet because, guess what, you hit the jackpot....that desert planet you landed on? Turns out it is absolutely LITTERED with Gravitino Balls....and that's easy money. 

At it's core, it is the same as every other procedurally-generated survival/exploration game...the difference is, the biomes are crazy and the amount of stuff you can build is vast...and you have dozens of different spaceships to find, customize, upgrade, and collect.

Let's face it...if you are even reading this right now....you know what to expect in this game...it's 4 years old, for Christ's Sake... 4 years later, is it still worth $60?  Well....that I cannot say for anyone else, but or me, it is. At this moment, I have over 150 hours of gameplay..  $60/150hrs=$0.40/hr.  That's better value for dollar than renting a movie.

I recommend with a big but....

The game is a good "time waster" and a lot of fun ideas. but......

There's a lot of systems that are placed one over another that make each other obsolete. The devs clearly did not have a clear idea of where the game was/is going to be.

As example: In the game there's a beacon where you can use a data chip, that's consumed in the process, to summon your ship to that location...
Or you can simply use the quick access menu to summon your ship to where you are for "free".(as long as the ship has fuel to get off the ground it can get to you)

Another example is base blueprints, where initially you can "research" them in your base panel, later on you find a place that you can buy all the blueprints that can be "researched" and more. Also there's quest chains that unlock a good portion of these same blueprints

You can clearly see that the game had a system and the devs later on in a patch released a new system that have all the functions of the first one and more, without bothering to touch the initial system.

And stuff like that is all over the game.

You will play and clearly see mechanics that are old, are redundant and for all instances and purposes should be removed from the game but the devs did not bother to.

They clearly added new content without taking old content in consideration and to some extend you can see that they develop stuff because "they like the idea" and don't bother to work and fit the new content with the older systems.


While it's not a HUGE deal it's clear that the devs don't have a long term plan and instead are just adding stuff they think it's cool right now.

Also. The game suffer from being online. I could see this game being SO MUCH BETTER if it had support to mods in a single player experience.

No Man's Sky is a non-linear ("Open Universe" as I'd like to call it) video game with the hopes of being an adventure game with no limits. Its respective to say so, as the game starts you off with you having to fix your ship and than to that point you are (mostly) able to fly to as many planets in as many star systems as you would want. Of course, that has its limits in the beginning depending on your play style and what you choose to do for the first many hours you begin your game.

 It has its paths, some being linear to an extent while others are just smaller goals. However, you can go and fly wherever you want when you have the suitable resources to do so, but you will never visit not even 1% of all the solar systems in this game even if you played it constantly so you are going to be spread out. That's what I like about No Mans Sky, and to the best of my statement, there is no other game out there that delivers the amount of quality that is remotely relating in comparison to No Man's Sky and its core values and game design. 

The game can be beautiful at times, and some things are so unique you wouldn't ever expect to see something like it from any game you've played. I've only encountered one system in which someone else had visited around 3 years ago after me playing for more than a hundred hours.

I strongly recommend that if you get this game or play it to focus on the story paths while enjoying finding new worlds on the side. Without many spoilers, if you decide to do so, you can get schematics and necessities for creating a base, making modifications to that base, and having the ability to make the more complicated things that make the game much more fun.
When I started my first game I notice basic lifeforms and planets in my first few star systems were bland and not really a beautiful sight to be seen or a suitable planet to store my base on within my standard. 
Its worth noting that not every planet will be necessarily unique, and you may find very boring lifeforms on the planets you start out in, or at least, I did when I just recently began my first play through. 

Yes it can get very repetitive finding some of the same basic elements and mineral extracts from flora, to inorganic or biological species. I can say that the game is considerable enough to be an artistic statement though as well as a fun game with a lot of grind. The amount of variety is ever changing however, and with each update it keeps on growing. The Origins update gave a new amount of things to see and explore from storms to planetary uniqueness and more exotic life to beautiful scenery.

I have sold or scrapped so many of my ships only to fall back at a low amount of money in the game for my 1st hundred hours as well as investing in the type of weapon, base mods, freighter, fleets, and necessities to upgrade to something better each and every time. Its very fun, and the fact that they update this game for free is the reason why I will consider this game to anyone interested in sci-fi exploration with adventure and open world gameplay in the mix. I may continue to edit this as I keep playing, but as its set right now, I'm glad I didn't say no to this game.

I've been wanting to play this game for years but definitely wanted to wait until it's relatively playable.

In my view it's not. Yet?

I can't really judge any mid or late game content, but in the 16hours that I've played this with my friends we've encountered a large number of bugs (most are probably related to multiplayer):  NPC merged sideways in floors, NPCs not responding, spaceships parked inside each other, base objects not synching among players (bases half rendered for one player), random teleports into space, NPCs walking in place, alien creatures and objects vanishing into thin air, quest system buggy when playing with friends, etc etc.

I think however, the experience could be far better if only playing it single player, maybe even in VR. For a true co-op experince however it was quite disappointing.

Also, some horrible design decisions:
- No real spaceship feeling when inside the cockpit. No real navigation system except point and pressing space. Nothing to do in space, there is no satisfaction on learning how to master a ship. Literally every single space game since wing commander did a better job here.
- Wood as basic building material? Do space tools replicate earthen tree-like wooden boards from collected carbon? Quite immersion breaking. Why did this idea survive the first brainstorming meeting? How? Why not making it a "carbon compound" thingy?
- Teleportation is basically God technology. It makes the game boring and trivial, What's the point in having a cool ship? Why not making this very late game tech instead of handing it out in the tutorial?
- no real feeling of achieving things in a group when playing co-op. Astroneer does a far better job here.
- Asteroids are just everywhere and are seemingly in abundance all around when decreasing speed?  So they have been here all the time? No need to fly there? In space..? Asteroids..everywhere..really?
- One of the weirdest and most un-intuitive inventory aproaches I've ever seen in a game. Also the menu system isn't intuitive. Discoveries..log...catalogue..and then an extra menu for inventory? Really? One opens with escape and the other with tab?
- Only 3 Alien races
- Clunky dialogue system, repetitive and boring.
- Spacestations could have been so nice, yet are lifeless and empty.
- The no man sky friend code thing didnt work for us or is broken. 3 experienced gamers couldnt figure it out. After typing our code again and again we gave up. Who thought that was a good idea?
- Why not making the player's ship the actual base?

Of course there are some good things as well..most are best checked on youtube.Things I liked in particular:
- beautiful graphics.
- the idea of exploring things for the first time, identifying and analysing compounds.
- the idea of learning languages word for word. It's a funny idea..though it doesnt really make sense in such a technological advanced scenario.
- the multitude of elements, crafting materials and blueprints.
