I especially enjoy this game because of the amount of exploration you can do. For example, there are over 4 quadrillion stars in each galaxy iteration, and with each star comes with 2-5 planets, and each planet has 1-3 moons orbiting it. Then, there's the fact that if you keep walking around a planet, you wouldn't be able to get back to the point you started at within your lifetime. I guess I should probably stop babbling about the exploration, so i'm going to talk about something else. The economy system is pretty nice, vendors have a limited supply of stock, so you can't spend all your units (the currency of the game) in one place. There's also the inflation and deflation of a product, so it sort of works just like the real world. There's also a sub-currency called Nanite Swarms, which can be used to purchase blueprints and upgrades for your exosuit, multi tool, ship, and freighter. The game also has a intricate building system which allows people to make unique bases with tons of different building parts. There's also the fact that you have to make a power system for your base, otherwise it wouldn't function.

   All in all, its a wonderful game. I would recommend this game to people that enjoy exploring new worlds, trading with others, and creating unique places to live. With each world in the game being different, there's always something new to explore.

If this is the redemption story everyone is raving about, I don't even want to know what the original version must have looked like.

NMS might have regained a lot of ground - but from someone who never played it before the most recent Origins update: its a terrible game.

You cant play for five minutes without something important breaking. The controls, the scanners, the interface, the terrain, you name it. The game is broken beyond hell and lacks polish everywhere.

It still is incredibly empty. What good is an infinite universe if there is only like two or three (I'm being literal, not even a hand full) of village models, a SINGLE space station interior, a SINGLE "alien ruins" type architecture etc. etc. to fill that universe?

The core gameplay loop is entirely pointless and self-defeating. You only ever get fuel to jump to get fuel again to jump again. There is no tension, no highs, no lows, no goals, nothing. 

This game is the epitome of "width of an ocean but depth of a puddle". 
Its empty, broken, ugly as sin and boring beyond belief.

If you want this game's core experience but, you know, working - get Empyreon.
If you want the spaceships, flying, exploration and combat - get Elite: Dangerous.
If you want the base building and construction, suits and a whole heap more - get Space Engineers.

This game lives off the promise of combining all these factors and fails spectacularly. SO, as it stands, every aspect of this sh*tshow is outdone tenfold by these alternatives.

No Man's Sky and its developer are the golden example of how to fix your fuckups and go beyond to make it up to your community. It took a lot longer than expected, but after getting bullied into releasing far too early by an overexcited community and oppressive market forces Hello Games had a choice- take the money and run, leaving a broken game with half of what was promised, or keep developing. For years, largely without thanks, No Man's Sky has seen continued development and is now a much deeper and more engaging game than was even imagined at launch.

If you're someone who refunded this game, or who heard of the controversy- I've kept the game all this time. Hello Games has made up for their mistakes and more, and No Man's Sky is now one of the games I just keep coming back to. With continued updates and a sub-genre not quite matched by anything else out there, it's definitely worth another look- and with how much work has been put into bringing the fan dreams it shattered at launch back to life, the developer 1000% deserves your money and support.

This game was a pain in the butt to get to work right, I gotta be honest.  After a bunch of driver updates and configuration changes, I got the game to finally run smoothly.  In fact, it runs smooth as silk now.  I have a AMD Ryzen 5 2600 CPU and Radeon RX 580 4 gig card w/ 16 gigs of system ram.  Definitely install this game on a SSD if you have a choice between that or a mechanical drive.

As far as gameplay goes, this game is incredible based on my limited play time (under ten hours).  Did you love Freelancer?  Did you wish you could explore entire planets in that game?  I did and this game is that imagined game come to fruition! You will build, mine, create, fly, negotiate and hunt down mysterious signals in the single player mode.  If story is not your bag, you can just play creative which has zero story, just play.  This is a few hundred hours of gameplay for $60.00.  I was lucky and got it half off, so wait and watch: the game goes on sale often!

Just be ready for long load times when you first start the game.  Some people take 10-15 minutes to load a game and start playing.  It takes me roughly 4 minutes, tops, and apparently I'm one of the lucky ones.  At first I had a couple crash problems but, as I mentioned at the beginning of this review, after driver updates and configuration changes, the game hasn't crashed since.  I don't get too much time to play games but this is the first time in over a decade that I've found myself daydreaming of this game while mowing the lawn or working.

I highly recommend this game.

Understanding what you are getting into with No Man's Sky is very important to enjoying it.  Right up front, when you launch a new game and your iteration is initialized... there's no handholding to tell you how to survive, how to recharge your shields, or how to tackle the basics.  Your starter world is likely to be harsh, and you're probably going to struggle to get through the first hour of game play if you haven't paid attention to controls and watched someone else playing.

Then the challenge changes.  You need a better multi-tool.  You need more inventory slots.  You need to collect resources for both of those while very constrained by both of those challenges.  Your first ship has the capacity of an eScooter.  You get mission objectives on worlds that are very unfriendly to spend time on.  Etc.  There is a lot to learn and do, and you're going to need to reference the wiki to get clarity on how to do it or what you're even supposed to be doing.

To No Man's Sky's credit, with the latest release land, sea, and space are all alive.  There's a lot to be aware of even if you stick to the ground to gather resources and get accustomed to the pattern of the game.  "Procedurally generated" means there are patterns - lots of permutations and variations on a theme - and you can take advantage of that while building a base, establishing your inventory of materials, gathering knowledge, and trading to fund your expansion plans.

However, "procedurally generated" also means there is repetition.  There are objectives for learning words, working with factions, discovering flora and fauna, etc.  But there are plenty of times when you're endlessly working the terrain, hunting for the next "unknown building" or digging up loads of "salvaged data" to trade for construction blueprints, etc.  There are times when you just slowly chew through the asteroid field nearest to a space station so you can run from any threats while stocking up on gold, silver, tritium, and hope for the platinum you need.  There are times when you're stuck poking everywhere to find a newer, more capable multi-tool, ship, or just drop pods for fast upgrades to your exosuit.  

In short, there are highs and lows in No Man's Sky.  The adrenaline rush of pirates in space or battling rapidly escalating sentry drones on land is rare unless you seek that out.  Most of the big wins are finding a 2 million credit artifact at an "ancient ruins" site or finally finding the last mineral and animal to complete the roster for a planet.  If "collect them all" is a big thrill for you, you're going to vanish into No Man's Sky trying to figure out if you must complete every planet in a system or just friendly planets.  If "adrenaline junkie FPS" is your preferred play style, you can find that in No Man's Sky, but it's not super rewarding.

This also gets into modes of transport.  Ships come as they are.  There are more (very expensive) options for improving and expanding space ships, but you don't get to design your own per se.  Freighters are also basically about finding the best ones and hoping you can afford the exchange your current freighter for a better one.  Modules are far more common, so that helps a lot with getting the most out of more limited space ships and freighters.  Exocraft (land and sea) are an interesting challenge.  Terrain and hazards can vary dramatically, and I've wrecked more rovers than I care to admit.  And what you need for, what you do to enhance, and how you configure your exosuit has a huge impact on walking/running around.  TBH I find the controls for space ships to require a lot of sweeping maneuvers because there's a lot of drift in the handling.  It's even worse in atmosphere.  Rovers work best on flat plains - good luck finding that.  I don't spend a lot of time in nautical vessels, so I can't comment on them.

So what are you getting into with No Man's Sky?  Single player or multi-player, there is much more time involved in exploring with purpose (whether that's resource collection, financial need, mission objectives, or simply checking out what's over the next ridge) than following a scripted path.  And once you get on the scripted path, it's going to force some decisions on how you proceed, so keep that in mind.  There is a ton of content, but it can be repetitive content.  For example, the loop of "build X at your base" just to get the "base computer" to do more archive analysis and unlock the next thing is frustrating.  Same with requests to install things on your multi-tool or exosuit or ship.  There should be a better way to tackle that, but the pacing is important to encourage players to go deeper into the game versus just build everything from the start.

Also... fair warning... don't build too many bases.  You'll hit some bizarre construction cap, and that sucks.  I've changed play style from one epic base and small lilypad bases where I thought they'd be useful to using Space Station teleporters and dropping save beacons at crucial/extremely useful spots like planetary archives or very rich fingers/floating crystals/rare minerals sites.  Once you have a freighter, you can use that as a forward base.  Keep a throwaway ship for wormholes (which can damage ships), a ship for exploring/missioning, and then as many ships as you need for storage.  Melt the other ships down for trade goods to sell for credits.   This helps streamline the game somewhat, but it is frustrating that you can't permanently flag locations you want to return to (without using a generic save beacon).

Hope that helps.  I've enjoyed my time in No Man's Sky, and the latest improvements are pretty sweet.  But this is not a game for everyone...  and that's important to understand.

I really want to like this game, and I certainly don’t hate it. I’ve played this for about 36 hours now, and while I am definitely impressed with the originality of much of it, I am also frustrated with it.

The tutorial missions are good for learning the basics, but there doesn’t seem to be explicit instructions about how to expand player inventories (had to go to YouTube to learn), how to build a good base, and how to efficiently do things.

The story is very vague and not that interesting. In 36 hours, the story has been mysterious messages from someone we don’t know if we trust or not.

There is just so much running around and i’m not at all sure what my purpose is. Run here, get a thing, warp back, maybe fly. Go to space station. Learn single word. Fly back. Get more metal. Ok? Why? Is it about survival? Is it about making money? Is it about discovering who I am? It’s all so vague and same-y.

The UI for building is so frustrating. Give me a full screen or full pop up menu. The scroll through hologram is a cute gimmick, but it’s about as frustrating as using a Rubik’s cube as a dinner plate. 

The game is not explicit in what it’s trying to show you and kind of demands you explore some of the menus that pop up. Found a derelict ship? Ok, can I take it? The answer is yes, but it was not obvious. I realize that exploration is the theme of the game, but I never want to feel lost in the menus or for direction.

That said, there is a joy in discovering the unique worlds and thinking “I’m the only person to ever see this planet”. It’s kinda fun to catalogue all the stuff and give them unique names. I like seeing the unique creatures. 

Overall, I kind of just want more handholding and pushes in certain directions so I know what my goals are and what I can do. The story is so vague it doesn’t really teach you more than the basics, and the lack of loading screens (while great) also means there’s no quick tips to show while waiting. More tips would be a huge help. An improved building UI would be great. And a stronger arc for the story would be helpful (see Brandon Sanderson’s YouTube class on writing for some ideas on story promises). There’s a huge potential here, and I understand it’s a huge improvement on the original release, but there is much to be refined still. Right now it’s ok, frustrating, and seemingly a massive case of quantity (X quintillion worlds) over quality (frustrations).

This is it, this is the time to jump into No Man's Sky once more, or for your very first time. Origins, while Hello Games considers it a smaller update, has expanded the game in so many much needed ways. No, they did not add a load of new weapons, new quests, or new vehicles. No, they did something much more simple.

The quality of the planetary generation and sheer variety has be vastly improved. Skipping right over the fact there's now volcanism with actual eruptions, lightning, tornadoes, firestorms, meteors, etc, the very core of the generation itself has been expanded. They have allowed previously singular generations to mesh with others, for example.

Remember bubble worlds? Well now bubbles can appear on other world types. I had a Bioluminescent mushroom forest (with glowing grass) and bubbles. It was a verdant moon around a massive planet. The planet was a "temporary" one. According to the descriptor. No, that doesn't mean they remove planets. It's just a type, a bit of game lore mystery. Like a decaying nuclear planet. This one, is apparently unstable. Across from said verdant world (which had tornadoes) was a world I named The Boneyard. A world made entirely of... what appeared to be meat and bone, even its creatures were made of bone. One was a type of like, sandworm, that was just a collection of surfing bones in the dirt. Ever see the movie "The Bone Snatcher" before? Think like that. Pretty cool, pretty creepy. 

They have also expanded not just the flora, but fauna. There are now new types, like Dune's giant sand worms, or creatures that are both air and ground creatures who switch between the two modes. One world I had giant butterfly serpents that would slither around on the ground and then fly into the air when you got near. They glided like kites, I named them Frosted Butterfly Dragons. Since they looked like eastern dragons with butterfly wings, were blue, and found in the tundra. 

The clouds look amazing now, and I've actually gotten some screenshots out of the game that look better than what I would have gotten in Elite Dangerous or Star Citizen. 
https://cdn.discordapp.com/attachments/365850341591220234/761004285256531978/unknown.png

Terrain can now vary much more greatly. Huge ravines, colossal mountains, new and interesting shapes that aren't particularly outlandish. (Though if you're into Avatar type generation, there's still some to be found out there.)

While they didn't add any new ships or anything for the casual pew pew person, I wouldn't write this update off. This is actually one of the best, if not the best update No Man's Sky has received in years. The game looks so much better, and so much livelier now. When you go exploring, you won't be greeted with the same 5 planets anymore. I have been stuck exploring for days. It reminds me of my early days of playing Elite Dangerous, only instead of barren worlds, there's actual  stuff to find to give me awe. Like I found what can only  be described as an underwater city from a collection of ruins all in the same spot at the bottom of a giant chasm in an ocean world. I made a base there. New Atlantis. Also the planet had the descriptor of "haunted by green." I assume that's why the surface is always foggy, and green. Also feck you abyssal horrors. You're not helping my fear of the deep. 

In summary, 'small' update is the best update the game has had because it changes how the game creates everything you'll be staring at, which makes it much, much, better. Far prettier worlds, less jank, more variety. Check it out. This is why it's being called "No Man's Sky 3.0"

Although I heard about this game when it released, I didn't buy it because it was $60. I heard my friend who did buy it say he got burnt out on it, and after it's release I watched a couple people on YouTube reviewing the game, basically saying it was incomplete. Fast forward to a few days ago, the friend who bought the game on release told me about a new update, saying basically that they completed the game, fleshed out with more story and all that jazz. So here I am, and what do I think about the game?

-minor spoilers ahead-

Pros:
I enjoy it. There are some unique and interesting mechanics in the game relating to movement, combat, and world manipulation. There's also some interesting things that happen when you leave and come back to a solar system (especially when your base is right next to a crashed ship spawn). I really enjoy the Artemis story line, albeit linear. There's also plenty of environmental storytelling, from ruins of ancient origin, abandoned modern bases, and currently occupied bases. Travelling from planet to space is very satisfying, though if you have a weaker graphics card you are bound to experience lag spikes when you do this. Combat on the ground and in ships is thrilling and fun.

Cons:
Yes, it's a walking simulator. Most of your time will likely be dedicated to following the breadcrumb trail that is all the goodies on the surface (ruins, ore deposits, outposts). Yes, it is grindy. I don't particularly mind the grind but I know for some people it is a total turn off. It's a survival game: it's going to be grindy. Travelling from solar system to solar system tends to become boring, and journeying to the galactic core just seems downright impossible and an immense challenge. So far, it's the Artemis story line that's kept me playing.

Summary:
It's a survival game where you have a ship and you mine for resources and search for loot and fly around in a fricking space ship, IN SPACE. It's a cool game, and I would recommend buying it when it's on sale.

This is my favorite game. For real, it was made to be so. It's a space game about exploration and surviving with a procedurally generated galaxy. Even when the game launched I had a good time with it, though I ran out of stuff to do fairly quick. The freedom this game offers is unprecedented in gaming. Some games like to pretend you're free to do whatever you want but have a very set path for you to take (Far Cry, Assassin's Creed, Red Dead Redemption, Grand Theft Auto, etc.). Not in No Man's Sky.

You can make units (the game's currency) by doing just about anything, and if you upgrade the right pieces of equipment you can make a career out of doing nothing but scanning rare animals on other planets. Or you can become a scrapper, locating wreckage and artifacts using the navigation data you can purchase from the space stations, and make bank pretty quickly. Or you can do a scan for hostile systems, hop to each one and collect high bounties for a living. Or DON'T AT ALL. Units aren't required to have fun in this game, you can just spend your time drifting to the center of the galaxy and gather the necessary resources to move on without spending a single unit. You could establish a hub that other players can fly to using your galactic address. Stock up or plant rare resources for them to gather, or make a disco room for dancing and exotic drinks (you can craft drinks and food for your very own club/bar as well as make custom music to accompany a lighted dance floor). Farm some animals, kill some animals, kill some NPCs, explore oceans, build in oceans, become the Indiana Jones of space, do whatever you want. Truly.

It's true, the multiplayer wasn't here at launch, but Hello Games has made up for it by making a no fuss jump in/jump out multiplayer options. You can either join a random person straight from the start menu, or summon "The Anomaly" a multi-dimensional space station with warp capabilities captained by two enigmatic NPCs named Nada and Polo. From The Anomaly you can interact with other players, scan their sweet rides, chat it up, purchase upgrades for everything you may need in the deep darkness of space, talk to a space version of Gordon Ramsay and feed him your prepared dishes, and many other things. The main draw of The Anomaly is to be a multiplayer hub of sorts, a bit like The Tower from Destiny. The game doesn't change at all when playing with another person other than some things might be easier to do as a group. Things like attacking Sentinel Walkers or collecting Larval Cores from infected outposts. There are also multiplayer missions that can be initiated from The Anomaly where other players in the hub can join you and embark on a journey to a distant star system to complete a simple task. These tasks are great ways to learn how to explore the galaxy and teach you what to look for when you want a specific item. Completing these missions rewards you with Quicksilver, a currency used for purchasing cosmetic items in The Anomaly's Quicksilver store. You can get such crazy things like jetpack that emits rainbows or some badass bounty hunter helmet for your character. Multiplayer wasn't available at launch, but after many important updates, it is here in a big way.

On top of all the new content, necessary updates, and complete overhauls to gameplay, the developers and the community are the stars of the show. Hello Games have been absolute champions in supporting the game for years after its rocky launch, and the community is some of the nicest people you will ever meet. Somehow, through the absolute toxicity of the terrible launch, we, the community, have successfully filtered out most of the trolls and abusers that used to frequent the forums and subreddits, leaving us with a wholesome, and surprisingly large community of dedicated players from around the world, even bridging game console gaps and encouraging production of the game on as many platforms as possible. Hello Games promises to continue giving gigantic updates for free and the community have all agreed to pull in even more players to help support their monumental efforts.

No Man's Sky, in its current state, with its update model, ethical monetization, community and developer support, and positive view of the future should have been the standard for this generation of gaming. Instead, we have games like Anthem, Fallout 76, Madden 2021, and a whole plethora of unfulfilled promises by devs or publishers that refuse to innovate or give back to the community without heavy, egregious, and unethical money grabbing schemes. Because of this, No Man's Sky stands out as the standard we should all be looking for in games, a complete 180 from their launch of broken promises and lacking features. I say reward them for not giving up and sticking to their ethics. Come join us and count yourself among the stars. Call of Duty comes twice a year and dies just as quick but the No Man's Sky community will be exploring the galaxy for years to come.

No Man's Sky is an interesting and fulfilling proof-of-concept type of videogame that tests the strengths and weaknesses of a procedurally generated videogame. For those who are fans of survival, space, exploration, and seeing whacky things - No Man's Sky will be just about the right game. No Man's Sky is a multi-layered game that rewards those who devote and work towards achieving their goals, this is showcased throughout the game in all the vehicles, weapons, bases, pieces, modules, and upgrades you can get for nearly everything you can use in this game. The possibilities for loadouts and playstyles are endless - you wanna just build a base? Wanna just get a cool dog-fighting space ship? Wanna explore cool planets? Want to discover new plants and species? Want to be a trader, or even crash the economy of a planet? Want to just follow along the story-line? Want to go explore underwater in a submarine? Want to do mini-missions and side quests? Want to just get the best gear in the game? Wanna be a space explorer, an alien, a small bird-like raptor, a robot, a shark, an iteration? All these are possibilities in the game.

No Man's Sky, despite it's lacking launch, is nowadays a very complete game full of possibilities for those who seek it and get past the initial steps of gameplay, which leave a bit to be desired and isn't very welcoming to new players, but it's extremely rewarding to those who invest into actually seeing the full picture of the game. COOP & Multiplayer implementation could be better, and it's OK once you unlock the missions, or if you just wanna explore together, but mostly it seems to be a singleplayer game with multiplayer elements. Nonetheless, aside from that being one of it's only downsides, the game is very solid. And for sure I'd say it's among the best in the genre.

I love this game.  It's now my second favorite game of all time (after ARK).  I've played for about 60 hours at this point, and I still feel like I am not very far into my journey in NMS.  Despite that, I don't feel like I've spent those 60 hours doing grindy, unfun things.  When I want to explore, I go exploring.  When I want to work on my base, I do that.  And I can do my quests when I want.  I don't feel this constant PUSH to progress, but neither is the game so open-ended it's without goals.  

Pros:
Massive, massive, massive world that literally can not be fully explored.
Discovering planets, naming them.
Discovering animals, naming them.
Base building.
Incredible screenshots / photography capabilities.  NMS is made for screenshots.
Cool language system where you really feel like you've learned the alien language.
Multiplayer, but you can go off on your own too.  Not really any griefing because of size of universe.
Wonderful customization options for player looks.
No microtransactions.  You can earn "Quicksilver" in game and no way to buy it.  Quicksilver unlocks what would typically be covered by microtransactions.
Constant wonderful updates from Hello Games
Main plot quests and dailies.
You can tame animals and ride them (I have not done this yet though).
Lovely community.  

Cons:
Sometimes a few graphics glitches (may be my card though)
Takes a while to unlock the anomaly/portal glyphs via the storyline, so you can't immediately go into multiplayer.

If Hello Games reads this, these are my ideas for things that might be fun down the road.  They're not exactly requests so much as...just things I thought, "hey, wouldn't that be neat"?  

1) Ship color/component customization, to allow changing the look or just paint of your ship.
2) More community support via inworld things.  Maybe guild or clans you can join (hopefully the ability to join multiple of these) where you can talk in a guild or clan chat.  
3) Opt-in PVP.  I am not sure I'd like total global PVP, but something like PVP-enabled planets or PVP-enabled systems where you can do dogfights.
4) I'd love a way that you can rent out spaces in your base or town build to others.  That way when you invite people to your planet, they can really take up part-time residence as part of your community.
5) More buildable game elements.  The race stuff is neat.  What about something you can bury on your planet to do a scavenger hunt.  Or...an object that rolls (functions as a ball), can be picked up and thrown, or kicked...and a sizeable, positionable goal.  What about a buildable track with a cart that you can set up and ride to give tours?  
6) Ability to add art to the game.  I'd love to hang screenshots of my explorations in my base.  Or to make my own banner.
7) Mail boxes / mail.  
8) Ability to capture/display animals - build your own zoo for people to visit.
9) Grah!  Grah grah grah!  GRAH!

Anyway, I'll edit this and add more of I think of things.  And some of this might actually already be in the game.  Like I said, I'm only 60 hours in and don't feel like I've gone very far...so these might just be things that exist but I don't know about yet.

Reviews.123872:
(VERY LIGHT SPOILERS IF YOU CARE)
If you like space exploration, this might be the game for you. This game has a few new bugs with the Origins update. First of all, crashes can happen every hour or so, if you're playing with friends and they edit terrain for their base, when you rejoin it may be restored to its original shape, submerging the base. I have also had a planet where the ground wasn't loading in when I got closer (it was like I had a "un-render circle" around me.) 

This is where I compliment the game. No Man's sky is a game about you, a Traveler waking up in a unknown world to him with only one thing in mind, the one thing you hear over and over again. 16. I will not reveal the importance of that number, but all I can say is No Mans Sky does an incredible job at delivering cosmic horror. I personally enjoy game that are more story based rather then gameplay based, such as Red Dead Redemption 2(not saying these two games are similar), but I am not saying that No Mans Sky lacks gameplay, I'm only saying that the story is very good in my opinion. There is also three different species, or at least main ones, that all have their different language, and are more dominant in separate galaxies. These three are the Gek, the Korax (my personal favorite), and the Vy'keen. The Gek are mostly traders and merchants, the Korvax are mostly scientists and mechanics of the sort, and the Vy'keen are mostly meatheaded brutes, not to says there isn't some bright heads in their race. 

The gameplay is mainly exploration, combat, and resource gathering. The resource gathering part isn't always that fun but how fun can you make it? The exploration is where this game is stellar. Whether it be the random anomalies you can find in space or just the pure dread or beauty a planet can overcome you with. Then there is combat which consists of dogfights and on-foot combat. On-foot combat is nothing to write home about but the dogfights are where it gets fun. There's a lot of ship types too, some are meant for storage, some are meant for dogfights, and some are meant for exploration. The dogfights are honestly a lot of fun, especially when you've pissed off an entire species and everytime you go in their galaxy they're gunning for you. 

So, my final thoughts. The game is fun, I do recommend playing it with a friend or two, the tutorial is a little long. I just think this game is in kind of a rough patch right now, but certainly much better then it was at launch. If you have this game in your library and happen to see this interview, consider replaying. You might like it. If you're interested in purchasing it and looking at the reviews, I'd say go for it, you'll get your moneys worth especially with the deal going on right now. My overall score for No Mans Sky is:

7.0/10

So I was on this mission, see? Digging up a few ol' dinosaur bones. It was easy, they said, just dig and deliver "for science". They didn't mention the radioactive storms, but what happened after was much worse. 

As soon as I finished the job I rang up my contact. As soon as I heard his voice, I also heard unnerving chatter behind me. The call had been traced by Sentinels that immediately opened fire. Luckily they were only the two of 'em, so I took them out with my trusted blaster.

After I caught my breath I rang up my contact again and we agreed to meet, so that he could do his lab thing. A twenty minute walk? I'd much rather have flown there. Dumb of me not to check first if my craft was fueled up before I ventured out. Seeing as I couldn't use the autopilot to have the ship come fetch me, I just started trodding, grabbing whatever I could to stay alive as I wandered.

The night is mighty beautiful, with a big orange ringed planet looming overhead, like a ginormous moon. Coincidentally there was a meteor shower, having me jump sideways a few times so as not to have my head cut off by flying space rocks. Deadly, but beautiful. Like that women I once knew...

Eventually I reached my man. He was done within a few seconds, barely even looked at them. Was he really interested in the bones, or have I just been part of some spectacle for invisible viewers? Either way he didn't want the bones. Took them to the market and guess what? I'm a millionaire now!

I want to recommend it, since Hello Games put so much effort into making it the game they really wanted it to be from the start, but the starship physics, controls and space combat in general fall flat far too much for me to really say it's worth it. It's easy to say that if you want a space sim there are many out there to play, and that's true, but a game as big in scope as No Man's Sky would only benefit from having a better set of systems than what are in the game. Not refined, just plain different. 

It always feels like my spacecraft, no matter where they are, is lethargically trying to breathe air. I try to do some manoeuvres you'd expect of a spacecraft, and it stalls, falls backwards and starts banking in a random direction I didn't want. Spacecraft don't stall, so I don't know what on Earth is going on there. In-atmosphere is frankly worse; they don't control any better, making this aircraft flight model nonsensical still, and if you try to get close to the ground or pitch your nose anywhere, the game doesn't let you! It's like we still have the training flaps on!

Instead of just yawing the ship in either direction it actually banks; that might mean nothing to you but since it imbalances the ship's keel, you actually end up having to do a weird dance with the roll/pitch controls to do anything advanced. Combat may as well not exist too;  the UI is not tailored to it at all. While I could forgive an exploration-focused game for that, since it's not the focus, there has to be more than a random arrow that's not even pointing to the closest aggressor, but rather some hostile out of range. It's all a bit of a mess, but I'm willing to say that's on me for not trying hard enough to understand it.  I've used my ship to fight sentinel walkers and I'm not aiming my weapons, nor can I tell where their firing arcs are, so I miss 90% of the time!

The game is about more than that, and aside from being told to explore then instantly pinned down being nonsensical at best, I've enjoyed puttering around in it. I expected a more complete and accessible Elite Dangerous, but maybe that's on me.

Reviews.124096:
No Man's Sky is... weird.

I would say it's an amazing game at what it tries to achieve, the exploration in this game almost never feels tiring, and especially not after the recent Origins update. And really that's all the game is, exploration. Being the main selling point, it should be expected for it to be fleshed-out, and it is. Does it bring anything else to the table? Well...

You play the game to explore a vast and expansive universe, filled with rocks to look at for 3 seconds to get money. Is that all the game has to offer? No. There are procedurally generated quests in the game that resemble the ones from Skyrim, I.E. Go here and do this predetermined tasks that repeats itself a few times. The game also has a story arc, although i have yet to finish it in my 120~ hours of playing, which is a sign that the exploration of this game overshadows everything else that it has to offer and by a long shot. Although the storyline isn't bad, if you don't do it all at once you'll find yourself 100 hours in in the middle of the main questline with no idea what the hell even was going on, and not feel like completing it. It'll always be there though, that is more content for you to do in the game and by all means that's a good thing.

The game itself doesn't really set any goals for you other than to "Reach the center of the universe", which is the main quest for the game. The game never really sets many restrictions in the course of the game, other than at the very beginning. You're free to explore the universe with little to stop you from doing so other than some upgrading you have to do to get to the higher-tiered systems, which really isn't hard to do. 

An issue i've found with the game though, is that after some time of going around exploring the universe you find less and less things to do other than explore. The content that was in the planets in the beginning of the game start to become redundant, as they're just fronts for you to get more Units and Nanites (in-game currency), and if you're already satisfied with what you have you'll see very little reason to collect these optional resources from the planet, considering all it'll do is make your wallet even bigger.

That's not to say monetary gain is the only reason to explore, no no no. In No Man's Sky you have 5 races (technically species but i only noticed this midway through and i'm not gonna replace every word sod off), the Anomalies, the Travellers, the Korvax, the Vy'keen and the Gek. Each has their own unique quirks (although they don't have much if any effect in gameplay), you can be whatever race you choose to be via the Appearance Modifier, and because of that you are never truly any race other than an Anomaly, which is your starting race. Currently they are purely visual for YOU, but you can find the many races naturally exploring the universe, be it in space stations, trading stations in planets or the new archive buildings (which are just glorified trading stations but with more pizzaz and some lore-content), you can also find them in the Space Anomaly which i will get to shortly. Each race has their own backstory, and most of their stories directly interact with eachother, be it past conflicts or current beliefs. The exploration of planets will award you with tidbits about the races and the universe itself. you also spawn in with no knowledge of their language, and you must slowly learn how to speak their language by interacting with knowledge stones or asking them directly for information. The three main NPC races (Korvax, Gek and Vy'keen) can be befriended or dissuaded, and each have effects on trading with the respective race affected. How good your relationship with the race is affects also what kind of interactions you can have with them, they can give you locations of valuables or items that can slightly aid you through your journey (although useless in the endgame). 

Another aspect of the lore are the Sentinels, the main threat of the game. Through exploration you will learn about why they are here and their previous interactions with the aforementioned races. You will commonly see them roaming the surface of planets, scanning the fauna and flora constantly analyzing every inch of the planet's body. They will attack the player if they catch sight of you "impeding the balance of the planet" and will shoot at you from a distance. You can either hide at this point or continue being stubborn and slay the thing. When killed, they will call for backup, that comes in four tiers, each escalating the conflict, until the last tier is called and after that, tier 4 will repeat until you either escape or die. Sentinels will also attack on space, with their own spaceships that are tiered aswell, although as far as i know, the only change in tiers is the ammount and the last tier calls upon a Dreadnought to help kill you.

Other than sentinels, the only other threats are some specific fauna and flora, the envornments of the planets and pirates (which can be of any race). But this aspect of the game is still rough, combat feels short and unbalanced and untouched. The only time you'll feel actual threat is when you poke the sentinel nest early in the game and get destroyed by the fourth tier. Space battles never feel like they are actually threatening, and it is unpolished AT BEST. Ship movement overall is kind of wonky and hard to get used to, and space battles become a struggle of slowing down to a halt or reversing, looking around for a few seconds and shooting a circle until the enemy is dead. Nothing that they do feels challenging, they'll mostly only try to get out of your sight, and they can't really use much cover considering most asteroids explode in one shot.   The game gives you a lot of options for ways to damage the enemy though, and it even features some upgrades to this very thing! although if you upgrade them once or twice that's enough to destroy everything on sight with enough effort.

On this sense, No Man's Sky falls short. But these are action segments and that was never what this game was about. And still, the game is very regularly updated and this is bound to change. The only other shortcoming i see with the game is a lack of things to do at the end-game, which is understandable. At that point you are fully decked out and nothing will pose a threat to you, so all you have to do at this stage of the game is explore the universe and find a nice place to settle in and build a base. When it comes down to this, the game feels relaxing if anything, and it becomes more like a snack that you eat from time to time to help relieve stress. Speaking of base building, the one in this game can be very nice, you can build an assortment of awesome-looking bases with the hundreds of decorations you can place in your base, which have to be unlocked periodically by finding buried treasure on the planets. Bases can be uploaded and other players can see them on the Space Anomaly, the in-game hub for online multiplayer.

On the Space Anomaly you can do quests with your friends, meet up new people and learn a bit more about the world. You can visit other player's bases and interact with the playerbase in a 16-player lobby. Multiplayer is essentially just exploring the universe with your friends, and doing some tasks in the Space Anomaly together. You can accept tasks at The Nexus, a glorified billboard where you can earn various rewards for doing said quests. Most importantly Quicksilver, the third currency in the game. This can be used to purchase various cosmetics in the store of the Space Station, mainly new attire for your character, new decorations for your base and gestures. 

Overall, the game has a lot of good things and a lot of under-developed things, which will eventually get touched because Hello Games has been hard at work for the past 3 years making free content for the game, and improving it each time.

I have always loved the idea of No Man's Sky: a sandbox experience where players can explore a virtually infinite amount of worlds and live out their sci-fi fantasies in any way they wish. A game where you had total freedom to become whatever you wanted. I avoided it for a couple years, however, because of how it overpromised and underdelivered. I had a feeling it'd still be a fun experience but at its price tag, I wanted to wait to see if it would get any better. Thankfully, No Man's Sky ended up becoming one of the greatest comeback stories in the entire history of the games industry.

At first, this game will overwhelm you with information, gameplay systems and the promise of limitless adventure. I think this overwhelming sensation may turn some people off and I can absolutely understand that, but if you stick with it, take your time and learn the way the game works, you literally can do whatever you want. I also think many people expected this to basically be Skyrim in space. If you want Elder Scrolls-level of gameplay in sci-fi, you're gonna have to wait for Starfield. This game doesn't have a huge amount of story content but it definitely offers a similar level of sandbox freedom. However, you do have to make sure you do what you can to survive. It's not just about running around in a playground. Instead, you're freely surviving in a galaxy that is rough and difficult, but equally matched in beauty and wonder.

Again, this game is not about making you a chosen one hero who makes the universe his playground. It's about setting you free in a universe that lives indifferently to you. Whether you live or die, life goes on. However, this creates a natural sense of adventure when you're exploring because you are, quite literally, coming across places that no other player (or the developers) has ever seen before thanks to the procedural generation. Everything present in the Steam description of the game is 100% true, it has virtually limitless freedom. What's amazing about this level of freedom is that you're just as likely to spend countless hours of adventure in a single planetary system as you would just hopping from system to system and exploring every bit of the galaxy that you can.

It's also quite a beautiful game, with stylized graphics that aren't too cartoonish but will certainly age well as time goes on. The color palette is also extremely beautiful, even more so since the most recent update, Origins... which brings me to another thing. This game has, since day one, received 100% free expansions. Part of this may have to do with how the game underdelivered so much on launch but it's still extremely commendable that Hello Games continues to give us huge content expansions entirely for free. I can't guarantee they won't start releasing paid expansions eventually, but considering how much content we've been given, I wouldn't mind that one bit.

One of those updates added great multiplayer systems to the game. Now, you can team up with friends or random strangers to explore, undertake missions, build, etc. This is made better by the fact that the game has crossplay on all platforms. There really aren't any limits to you and your friends exploring the cosmos together, other than the game's base fee, and it's worth every penny.

This game is one of the most ambitious games ever imagined and, in its current state, it's wholly worth the cost because its original promise has been fulfilled. What makes this even better is that it continues to get bigger, better and even more ambitious. If you've ever wanted to freely explore and live a sci-fi life in space, if you've ever watched a sci-fi show or movie and thought, "Man, what sort of adventures could I have if I were in their shoes?", then No Man's Sky is absolutely the game for you. Don't let the haters keep you from enjoying this phenomenal game. It's amazing and it's only getting better.

The current consensus about NMS is 100% correct: it has rebounded from its failed 2016 launch and, via a steady train of massive updates/free expansions, been transformed into an extremely impressive/epic exploration game; arguably the biggest comeback story in game dev history.

Free expansions have included: underwater/sea cave exploration/base-building including a mini-sub, various vehicles including a mech suit, derelict spaceships to explore, a chance to encounter massive dune-style sandworms, working coop, VR support, and an across-the-board variety/quality upgrade to its planets/weather/visuals.

The original selling point of seamless travel between different planets/galaxies to space to space stations etc + encountering endlessly randomized environments/weather/fauna/flora now works as intended as is extremely impressive/immersive. Also, unlike most survival games, there is a constant sense of purpose thanks to the underlying story/quest elements & various mechanics like technology discovery, alien language learning, upgrades, etc + the journey to the center of the universe.

If you want a spacefaring, world-exploring adventure this is it.

I found a neat little island that looked perfectly like a gyoza, on an arid planet with gigantic mutant trees. It was even complete with the little crimps on the circumference (which actually turned out to be the shores of the island). While building a small home to tuck myself away from civilization at, I decided that I wanted to grow some plants, and out of an aesthetic interest I picked Star Bulbs, plants with the most elegant blue flowers. 

Unfortunately, I needed saplings that were not to be found in this system, so off I went in my living ship to another system nearby, where pirates immediately attacked me, noticing precious items in my inventory. Dealing with them swiftly, I proceeded to the nearest planet where Star Bulbs could be harvested.

As soon as I landed, my breath was taken away by how gigantic this planet was - the hills and valleys and even caves dwarfed my character, and even as a raging storm deafened me and battered my Hazard Protection, I could not help but stand in awe at the vastness and beauty of it all.  If I could post screenshots I absolutely would, and I probably will at a later time. The most incredible maroon grass and calcified plants dotted the landscape, and creatures that look like a prototype of some dinosaur-rhinoceros hybrid wandered the land. I fed them and collected some Faecium from their droppings since that would allow me to plant Gutrot, if I recall correctly, in my little base.

As I prepare to leave (since the storms really hammer away my sodium reserves, as I have chosen to not include any Thermal Shielding to challenge myself in-game), I notice a beautiful valley overlooking the sheer cliffs and tremendous vistas this planet has to offer. I land there, and gaze in awe at the misty fog and the strange airborne creatures that leave behind puffs of blue smoke as they fly around. The temperature is relatively cool, and the sun peeks at me from behind the moderate cloud cover.

Of course, all thoughts of home have vanished. Nothing else remains, but the beauty that stands before me.

I stand, as but a dwarf before this alien land and its beauty. And what is the point of life, if not to feel awe at how this vast universe dwarfs us throughout our lives?

Only two things remains - the first, to thank Hello Games and Sean Murray and the whole team for not giving up. 
The second, to thank you for reading this far.
I have found home, and it is not where the heart lives, but where the heart soars.

The first few hours of this game feel quite grindy and unintuitive, to the point that I very nearly quit and would never have gone back to it. I started out with a couple of close friends who were also new to the game and we found the beginning quite frustrating as we encountered quite a few bugs, including never being able to get rid of our Sentinel wanted level (think GTA police). 

However, that being said, we managed to persevere through some rather annoying quests bugs, crashes etc and after 3 or so hours progressing through the main missions, we started to see what the game really had to offer. After that, it's truly felt quite difficult to put the game down, there's always something to work towards or work on and never a dull moment exploring new planets and what you might find. 

I do still have some gripes with just how many bugs, glitches and exploits there are in this game and when I look most of them up, they've been known about for a very long time. Years in some instances. There's even a bug that essentially allows you to keep trading ships you find, claiming them back and trading them again, essentially allowing you to print money. Fortunately it seems as though lots of the important game upgrades and unlocks are behind a few different currencies that appear to be less broken than the games main currency. It would also be nice to have ways of purchasing ships that doesn't involve just trading them with NPC pilots landing in space stations and trading outposts, as well as being able to fully customise the interior and exterior of our ships.

Whilst the game really needs some extra TLC around bug fixes and a little more depth in certain areas, overall it's truly a game with brilliant scope that keeps you feeling like there's always something to work towards, in the most enjoyable way possible. The perfect game if you have a few friends to play with, but even solo it's incredibly addictive and far less buggy. Would highly recommend it!

Had this since day 1. Yes it was rough at first but overtime the verse got even more fleshed out. I mean cmon guys it was a small team being pressured by a massive corporation. With Beyond, NEXT, and now Origins, this game has become much more than what was shown initially.
Pros:
Fun to play with friends
Easy to learn
You choose the way you wish to live in the verse
You can live out your Firefly or Cowboy Bebop dreams
Non-Linear story line
Cons:
It's easy to get stranded without fuel (Just plan ahead and have backup fuel)
Making money isn't easy (If it was easy then it wouldn't be fun)
Story is confusing (but you're not locked on a set story)
Good stuff is expensive so the game is a bit grindy

Tips for starting players:
GET A FREIGHTER AS SOON AS POSSIBLE SO YOU CAN OWN MULTIPLE SHIPS
Chlorine so far has been the most profitable resource to mine for me (found as massive underwater crystals on oceanic planets)
Focus on upgrading multitool first and then your exosuit.
AVOID BOILING, CORROSIVE, SCORCHED, TOXIC, IRRADIATED, AND VOLCANIC PLANETS UNTIL PROPER SUIT PROTECTION IS ACQUIRED.
Learn your languages quickly by searching for lost ruins or by asking around space stations for language help.
You can find abandoned ships that can be claimed but only do so after you buy a freighter, these ships can be scraped and can give at least a million units in parts to be sold. (Not the most efficient business but it can rake in extra cash).

Have fun and remember.
Always know where your towel is and DON'T Panic

Whilst pottering around scanning rocks, you stumble across a distress signal, so you track it to the source. There you find a crashed ship, the occupant long dead.

Its a better ship than yours- much better; at least it would be if every part of it wasn't critically damaged. You want this ship, but how to fix it? By a combination of collecting nearby resources, refining them with a portable refiner, and cannibalising parts from your existing ship, you get the drive systems running. Now able to take off, you fly to the nearest space station where you can purchase parts to get a few more systems up and running- shields and basic weapons.

Finally, 8 hours of playtime later, you finally repair the very last broken component. You've been getting on with other stuff during that time, and this 80% functional ship was still better than your old one, but gradually, as new planets provided new resources, you were able to repair each bit over time.

You are now so invested in this ship that you almost dread the inevitable point that you spot another crashed wreck in the distance whilst exploring, and this time a much, much tougher decision.

This is just one example of the compelling gameplay loops at play here. There is always just one more thing to get done before bed.... If you like space trading, fighting, exploration, survival, base building games, you should play this, and in doing so support a dev that 4 years after launch is still dropping massive free updates to show their commitment to a playerbase who were "somewhat disappointed" with the game at launch!

[This review is being posted directly after the Origins update, September 2020.]

Is No Man's Sky any good? Resoundingly yes. It's worth full price and if it's on sale you should absolutely pick it up, though there's some caveats depending on your playstyle preferences.

A lot of the joy revolves around grinding/farming resources, so if you don't enjoy games like Starbound or Minecraft it's probably going to bore you. I loved both of those games so No Man's Sky is a fantastic fit for me. There's also roughly zero forced combat in the game and what I've encountered has felt pretty easy, so if you were looking for an action-packed adventure you'll have to make your own trouble (which is a genuine option). Base building exists and is actually really enjoyable, but it isn't an immensely in-depth or complex system - it mostly excites through the different alien vistas you can build on and generally neat outposts you can come up with, as opposed to being able to build anything you can dream of.

For myself though, No Man's Sky is amazing. I usually can tell a game is great when my complaints are so minor they become nitpicky, and that's squarely where this game falls. Things like not being able to put a building foundation strut just how I want it, or wishing I could paint my ship but being pretty satisfied with how it looks anyway is about the extent of my problems, and that's a pretty good place for a game to be.

I've played this game for nearing 100 hours since release, and it has definitely delivered on the promises made back when it was initially shown and then some, however it is not without its problems and is by no means a perfect game.

As for the pros of this game it delivers on being 100% procedural and having a variety of planets almost never looking the same however they all do follow a set of rules such as the type of planet whether it's earthlike or more akin to the likes of mars which always have appropriate rocks, trees plants and such however creatures rarely match the environments properly although they are similarly mostly procedural but following some rules.

The multiplayer since release works well for how much the game has to offer with small issues such as the possibility for item duplication and other things, you can share bases and items some containers and talking options are also shared but some are also not. Freighters also work somewhat although i haven't tried recently you can usually warp to new locations with players inside your freighter and they will come with you though when i tried it a few times you wouldn't teleport and just die as a result. A few things you cannot change is the owner of bases as such, no ability to trade ships, frigates or freighters. And lastly warp stations allow people to travel across the galaxy to either meet up on galactic hubs or find rare looks for ships, multitools as such a nice feature that brought the community together.

The space exploration in the game is in my opinion a hit and a miss at the same time, initially travelling to a new system seems exciting with fresh new planets to explore potentially a new race of creatures inhabiting it new types also with the inclusion of a different economy and aggression levels. The systems can also include different types of recources ( Copper, Cadmium, Emeril and Indium ) which require different warp drive upgrades to access, personally i think this system falls flat as a progression system as they give you access to just more metal which is a generally lackluster resource and can be obtained fairly passively without mining at all. The other problem is that after the first few warps warping around feels more like a burden and you'll end up passing by many systems and not exploring any of them because they don't have many unique things to offer or wait around to find, you'll likely end up just passing to high economy systems and ones with the better resources.

As for ships there are a few notable variants ( Shuttle, Fighter, Explorer, Hauler, Exotic and Living ) Which all have different pros and cons such as haulers starting out fit with lots of slots to carry more items, or a fighter which has higher damage potential and maneuverability but less slots. All ships bar a few come in different classes reflecting their stats. ( C, B, A, S ) These however do not make much notable change to the ships since their looks are procedurally generated within a few parameters and the slots are seemingly random as well it doesn't feel rewarding or satisfying to own a higher tier ship as it doesnt change much once you own it.
Ships also do not vary much in how they feel, all the ships act the same they don't feel faster or hit harder personally it feels like ships are only notable on slots and looks needless to say this is one of many systems that fails to feel rewarding.

Base building was a nice addition to the game allowing you to setup a place to return to rather than wondering around aimlessly in space with the inclusion of mechs which allow you to explore your world in various different methods like cars, mechs submarines and more. While this system feels okay to play it doesnt feel entirely necessary as it doesnt have any exclusive content where it is required, if they added new fauna or resources only available to the exomechs it would give them some use outside of just wondering aimlessly on the planet.

Lastly the space stations are fine as they include everything you need like quests, pathfinding, upgrades new purchasable ships and multitools with plenty of npcs to talk to and gain knowledge. The nexus is a variant which is a player hub with a few npcs including quests, daily quests a unique currency shop, some quest npcs and research stations, nexus ties a lot of the game together as its a main point for quests throughout the game, allows for the upgrading of weapon types of your multi tool and ships, allows you to research more base items.

TL;DR:
The game has a lot of individual systems to explore and enjoy can easily put 20 hours into a save and potentially much much more depending on what you enjoy. The game is grindy but i feel like the grind never really pays off to anything notable, there are lots of expensive ships and freighters to buy but it never feels like any notable changes. I think the one thing the game suffers from is the addition of new systems which dont often compliment the old ones with no real end game in sight throughout the game grinding for small unnoticable changes to ships doesnt feel so rewarding.

Nonetheless the devs turned an empty game into a fun playable one.

Buy on sale for sure, pay full price depending on what you enjoy.

I remember playing this game briefly at launch, at a friends? Yeah.. anyway. I basically rushed to the center of the galaxy, as there was little else to do at that point once you had seen the nth variation local flora/fauna, and had upgraded your ship enough that jumps were trivial. I got to the other side and promptly lost the will to play and did not bother again for a while.

Every so often I heard about the updates being pushed, and was really glad to hear the game being fleshed out. However, no single improvement really attracted me enough to sit down and purchase the game.

After a few years of hearing about updates, I finally grabbed the game a few months ago. I've been captured by it. Whatever reputation this game had at launch, this is now a very freakin' solid sandbox. It's far less serious and technical than Elite Dangerous, while seemingly accomplishing more with less complex systems.

There is lots to do, but this is a sandbox at heart. It's about exploring. It's about cultivating your little slices of a handful of planets, and idly exploring the randomly generated beauty the game readily feeds you.

The most recent (as of Sept. 27th 2020) update contains an overhaul to how planets are generated, that generally has made them far more interesting. While I had some cool planets that were unfortunately made substantially less useful, it has overall done little but improve the game.

I would say the game is in such a state now, that if you left it at the beginning, disappointed with the fact the game did not live up to its own promising nature, you might want to come back. If you stayed away because of early controversy, try it now.

It's fun, and it's more fun with people.

Yet I am always interested to explore a new planet for a while when I discover a new solar system. 

Only thing to watch out for is a fair amount of stuttering and texture load-in. Although I am using a second drive to play this game, other games don't have that issue nearly as much, so I'm guessing its a limitation within the engine (ground texture randomly goes blurry and back to normal). As to stuttering, I am using a Ryzen 5 1600, which is above the minimum requirements, so I blame the engine for these issues. I am curious to know if people will better processors have the same issue. The game does receive a decent amount of updates so I expect these issues to be ironed out soon.

In conclusion, No Man's Sky is a fascinating project with hours of potential. The potential gets sapped from technical issues, but I don't think they outweigh the fun of the game.

Credit should be given where it's due. No Man's Sky can be a beautiful game and the procedural universe is gorgeous.

However, there are many issues that totally stop immersion:

First off, just about every interaction requires the player to press and hold a button, from selecting menus, entering ships, speaking with NPCs; I have never played a game where this was implemented. The fact that this hasn't been fixed after years is seriously concerning. The UI is incredibly frustrating.

Then we have the issue of just about every star system being very unrealistic.  Planets loom over each other, asteroids float in dense clouds around every celestial sphere, there are no gas giants, or moons, every system is just a collection of terrestrial planets which really doesn't help with an already repetitive game.

The flight controls aren't very good either. Just about any flight simulator has better keyboard controls, I don't understand why the mouse is used to steer spaceships.

The updates that have been made since release are commendable, but so many basic quality of life and variety issues have kept me from being able to really jump into the game, which has the potential to be one of the best out there. So close, yet so far.

Why I can't recommend this game:

1. The grind/difficulty curve is bizarre. Right off the bat you're doing little grindy fetch quests to get materials to build things to process materials to build new things with new materials and so on and so forth - that's all fine, and to be expected with the genre. But as soon as I get off the first planet and head to the nav point i'm directed towards, I land on a planet almost entirely devoid of carbon and oxygen - two elements that you immediately need to progress any further in the game. How are there no checks and balances in place to prevent this from happening? Don't send me to a planet with almost no carbon at a point in the game where carbon is a necessity to progress. Same goes for oxygen - you need it for life support - yet the amount I can gather from the few shitty plants on my hellscape of a planet is basically only enough to keep up with basic burn-rate of existing and moving around - certainly not enough to actually use to progress through the story/tech trees. Absurd. You need to safety gate people from this kind of worst-case scenario - it's stupid and frustrating and makes you game look worse than it probably can be.

I'll acknowledge this is probably just a run of bad luck. Most people probably aren't sent to some total shit- pile of a planet devoid of the super basic starter elements you'll need to make any progress - but it's dumb that it was allowed to happen to me, and has put me off the game.

2. This game, 4+ years on from launch, runs HORRIBLY and suffers from some of the worst pop-in I've ever seen in any game yet. Shit will just suddenly load in beside you after you've been standing there for 10+ seconds already. It's not even distant stuff, it just seems to load in in chunks even if you're literally beside the stuff. This is running on an SSD on a relatively high end modern system. Seriously unimpressed by performance.

Ultimately, the game disrespects my time and is unrewarding to my efforts. I don't need everything handed to me ez pz, but this is ridiculous. And again - maybe that's just shitty RNG luck on my part, but the game shouldn't give you such shitty odds right off the bat. It hasn't earned my interest enough to make me fight to play the game yet. Throw the curve balls further in, not right off the bat.

Summary: A fun open world game, with a great blend of exploring, fighting, researching, and building. Many beautiful landscapes and cool ship designs.

The good: controls are generally intuitive, and the intro provides a good balance of introducing new game mechanics and challenges, while ramping up the difficulty. The procedurally generated worlds, multi-tools, and ships are the best part of the game: they provide for great repeatability, and you have the ability to play the game in your style- you can focus on exploring or building or fighting, and aren't generally forced to do what you don't want. The landscapes are gorgeous, with very alien looking plants, creatures and mineral formations, in lots of varieties. Devs have chosen inventory as a limiting factor, (progression slowly gives you more inventory space) which may annoy some, but I find it well-implemented, and not so restrictive as to be annoying.

Bad and/or ugly: Bugs. While this is not uncommon among AAA games, a lot of these are not related to the procedural generation, or new content but are quality control things that should have been fixed four years ago. Some are merely amusing: On a mission you help an alien repair their ship. The ship takes off, the alien disappears, but the shadow under the ship remains, and an invisible alien walks around the crash site making alien sounds, and periodically removing an object from their pocket (which is not invisible.)  Some are more annoying, such as objects at your base not being saved. Enough said about that. I also find issues with game balance and scaling. Normal mode is great for chill game play. Combat is generally pretty easy. Want a challenge? Sorry, but the increased difficulty level is more annoying/punishing rather than challenging, making the already annoying inventory limits worse, and overwhelming you with numbers rather than interesting challenges. An ARK style difficulty customization would be welcome. Additionally, there are lots of things that just don't scale well as you get further into the game, with a lot of the exploration activities that were fun and interesting early game yielding rewards that by mid to late game are completely worthless.

Yet overall, it's well worth it if you like building and exploring, and despite many dozens of hours of game play, I still see planets, creatures, and ships that are new and interesting.

In short this was the game that I hoped Elite Dangerous would be.

So let me start off by saying that I have seen very minimal gameplay or footage of the original, supposedly "bad" version of No Man's Sky so this was my first genuine experience with the game. I bought it because everyone insisted that No Man's Sky had really turned around on its bad release, there was hype surrounding the most recent update, and it was on sale for $30 at the time of this writing. I went into this with high expectations.

Unfortunately, the new player experience is simply god awful.

As soon as the game starts my health starts draining because I've started on a radioactive planet. There's no time to get acquainted with the controls or explore the menus because I'm immediately on a countdown to die. However, there is a nice little pop up informing me that I can scavenge sodium from the surrounding plants to recharge my radiation suit. Great! I scan my environment for sodium deposits around me and I find... like 3 plants. I ended up dying around 4 or 5 times before I said screw it and quit.

Maybe I was just unlucky with the procedural generation? I deleted my old save and started up a new one.

So this time I'm not being bombarded by radiation, instead the planet is extremely cold and yep, I'm constantly losing health due to the lack of heat. Apparently it is intentional design that the starting planet will always have a hazardous condition that slowly drains your health. My question is why? Why make this the starting area for new players who are just learning the game? Not to mention, it doesn't matter how fully charged your environmental suit is, you are constantly losing health whether your suit is at 100% or at 10% capacity. That's just annoying that I can never be at full HP.

I die a couple more times while progressing the tutorial and I don't care anymore, just get me off this planet so I can go to a different one. I jump in my space ship and fly away to find somewhere more habitable. Except there's no where for me to go. Out of the 7 planets in my solar system, none of them have conditions that allow me to just exist peacefully; every planet wants to kill me. Look, I get it, space is a dangerous place and in reality, it would be incredibly rare to find a planet with earth-like conditions. But this is a video game and video games should be fun. I don't want to spend the rest of the game having to micromanage these two meters on my screen that I can never get full.

I feel dumb and stupid because I've died around 10 or so times in what are supposed to be the tutorial missions. In fact, I didn't even finish the tutorial. I got as far as setting up a base computer and placing it down because it was at this point I realized the core gameplay loop just wasn't for me. I don't normally leave reviews for the games I play, but I felt like I had to for this one to warn other new players what they're in for. I expected way more from a game that sells for $60 retail price and my only regret was that I kept trying to stick with it and now I can't even refund it.
