Brief Review : Played since Launch, Dropped a few times, came back, Iteration 1 player.

Game Play : 4/5
Story Line : 4/5 (3/5 in some cases)
Mechanics : 5/5 ( Simplistic but gets the job done. )
Overall : 4.5/5 ( in year Four )

---- In-Depth Review -----

No Man's Sky at launch was, well a tech demo. It was interesting to fly around and see how Hello Game's systems designed planets and systems, but beyond that, the game lacked any real engaging depth. Beyond mining for resources to continue your race to the middle ( Before the Atlas Rises DLC ) there was little reason to spend more than a few minutes on a single planet. However as many have stated, in the four years since it's launch, NMS has become a real redemption story of gaming. Beyond the Pre-Order DLC of the Omega Ship ( It's honestly just a ship with a hyperdrive, that's it ) there are no paid DLCs. You get what you pay for, a singular, no bull payment. That's beyond rare in gaming these days, and really stands out in the current market.

Game play ( as of Year Four - AY4 ) : 4/5

As mentioned, there was no real gravity to the game at launch other than to reach the center, for the sake of moving to keep reaching the center. Atlas Rises added in a new story line regarding the universe of NMS (16.16.16.16...) and from there on the game only got better. However while the story improved, so did the game play. Objectives became more varied, from building exo-crafts and bases, to repairing damaged ship components, to digging up rare fossils for profit ; All in all, the game continued to grow and expand bringing a new sense of life and purpose to the game. Game play has only improved since launch, along with great UI improvements, and new hazards and planetary elements giving purpose to the grind. There is one small problem here however, that there is a small ceiling. Once you have your S rank Ship ( which now can be improved once you find a shell you love, for nanites and units. ) and your S Class Freighter the game begins to wane somewhat. Perhaps the rush of the struggle makes everything more weighty, but in my S Class Viper-esque fighter, I fear no sentinel or pirate in space, while on land my S-Class max upgraded scatter blaster absolutely nukes walkers and leaves me to become a nigh unstoppable criminal scrap maker of the galactic caretakers. 

That's why I have to give NMS game play a 4/5, beyond the perma-death mode, difficulty in game play can take a backseat in late game. However if anything, Hello Games have proven, they are committed. Perhaps one day that'll change.

Storyline : 4/5 ( 3/5 in some cases ) AY4

Hah. Oh boy, this is a spicy one for me. I was appalled at the sheer lack of story in the beginning. It was...weak and there is no talking around that. I remember just trying to make sense of who the hell the Gek were ( other than adorable ). However as the years went on, this as well, got a considerable amount of love. Where as the original base game did little service to ATLAS or the races, the new story lines with Artemis and Apollo do an amazing job of introducing you to your new world as a traveler. The revamp of the Anomaly as a public hub as well has shown some hints to the strangeness of the NMS story, and now make it beyond charming. However there are some big bumps here, namely in some of the fringe elements of the game beyond the main story. You have the infestation that is never -really- touched upon ( though with the derelict ships they have some neat side stories.) You then have the Abyssal expansion, which gives a fun distraction, but was a little underwhelming to me.

All in all, NMS has some neat little flavor to it, and if you read close enough can be thoroughly enjoyed.
However beyond the Main Storyline, I have to bump it down to above average. It's fun, but shallow, though in time who knows. After all, I already wrote off Hello Games once and I don't like to make a mistake twice.

Mechanics - 5/5 ( Sweet and Simple )

There is not a lot to say here, NMS has a clear vision. Explore, catalogue, discover. The mechanics regarding that are kept very straight forward and bare bones. There are some exceptions to this rule ( the new system introduced for "simplified" repairing is still taking a good bit of time to get used to. ) however from the standpoint of time investment, don't worry ; You're not going to have to set up a new fuel mining operation base every few hundred light years. Grab some base materials, slap in some fuel, and get back out there. You are the universe observing itself after all. ( 16.16.16.16 )

Overall ( AY4 ) 4.5/5

After all is said and done, for what NMS wants to bring to the table, it does it well. It's not perfect, but it's a fairly well obtained vision from Hello Games now. I could write an entirely unoriginal entry about Hello Game's fantastic rebound, and Sean now being able to come out of the bunker and not be hunted for sport by rabid disappointed customers, but there are plenty of those reviews out there. Hello Games wanted to give us a galaxy of random chaos and beautiful creation to explore and discover in, to catalogue and define, to make our own.

They have only made that dream all the clearer and more lucid as the years have gone on. I'm excited to see how much further it goes. Oh and the game has a fucking Synth expansion, Beats by Atlas ( Retro-wave grooving on the paradise planets ). Also Space Worms now, the Spice flows.

Well done Hello Games.

I only played VR mode so far, so this is what I'm gonna complain about. The controls are horrible and while there are different options, it seems none of them really are viable...

The game practically depends on you using their analog-stick-rotation feature to rotate your body around. For example, the mining tool is located on your right shoulder, but if you turn your physical body about face suddenly the mining laser is on your left shoulder. This game is practically made to be played standing or sitting in a single direction - which is incredibly boring for a VR experience. There doesn't seem to be any quick recenter option either, you have to go to the options menu every time.

Ironically, when you turn on the body VR mode (your entire body is shown and you only have an arm's reach) playing sitting is practically impossible because your arm reach is shortened because of the way your body works in VR (the game thinks you're still standing).

I wish there was some kind of feature for an into sequence for ships so I have time to sit down and stand up instead of just teleporting me instantly, but I guess that might just not be for everyone.

Movement is fine, supports teleport and constant movement move, with three modes for moving in your body direction, head direction or controller direction. Sprinting is also pretty intuitive. However I kept getting stuck on stuff on the ground and always had to manually stop moving and walk around which was incredibly annoying.

Based on the other reviews I'm sure this is a fine game itself. But it just was not enjoyable to play in VR, which is the only mode I bought the game for.

This could have been a great game, but a bigger team needed to be working on this game, and several core design elements needed to be drastically changed. Everyone speaks on the "comeback" of this game, and if people feel this is warranted of praise, then I cannot absolutely imagine the poor state this game was in at the beginning.

These are the elements I have serious issues with (and you'll see a lot of these things overlap):
1) Survival mechanics
2) Progression
3) Resource management
4) Controls

Survival Mechanics
Your seemingly never ending tutorial is dragged out even longer by constantly having to fight your environment protection and life support systems. As soon as you load in, you are immediately greeted by a blaring voice telling you your environment protection system is depleting and your stuck fumbling around trying to figure out what it is and which bar corresponds to that system. You keep seeing these bars ticking down and that voice continuing to yell at you, but the poor semblance of a tutorial is trying to get you to change your multi-tool instead. Once you fight your way through the supposedly "revamped" UI system you start carrying on your way and collecting resources you need to progress, but nope. Those resources you collected get spent on refilling your life support and environmental protection systems. So you go back through the menus trying to figure out how to refill them and then ok, you can keep going, but nope.

Progression
You'll very slowly start gaining resources to get upgrades for things, but for every two steps forward you take, you go one back. You want to upgrade your multi-tool to the advanced mining tool? Cool here's the things you need to collect. You look through and see the resource you need is 1 planet away. So you try and get in your ship and it says the thruster engines are out of fuel. You grumble and try to refill your engines. Nope you need to make fuel. So now you go running around finding resources to make fuel and you finally refill your engines after 30 minutes and you're like "ok finally I can take off". You take off, but nope you cant move at all because your pulse engines are out of fuel. So you spend another 30 minutes getting resources to make pulse engine fuel and you finally can take off and move. You finally get the resource you need after another 45 minutes of constantly refilling your support systems and scanning everything you see to hopefully find something that will give you what you need. You better hope you don't need to travel to a different system, because guess what, that takes a different type of fuel. Progression in this game is an annoyingly slow snail's crawl pace because every time you start working towards something, you have to do 5 other annoyingly stupid steps that feel like it's trying to cover up it's shallow system of exploration.

Resource Management
Very quickly you'll realize you don't have enough inventory space to carry all the resources you need to manage the 30 different systems in this game that constantly need your attention. Eventually, you discover a blueprint for a storage cache, and they're pretty easy to make as well. You feel a sense of relief, FINALLY, something starts going your way to help you make meaningful progress. You put it down and walk up to it and it says... it needs power. A box to hold things... needs power.... Well you already made a generator to power your teleporter so you hook it up and dumb all 1000 units of carbon you were saving to power your mining tool into the generator only to have it tell you thats enough carbon to have 13 minutes of access to your storage cache... 1000 units of carbon... let's you access a literal box for supplies... for 13 minutes. I know some keyboard warriors have wanted to start typing in the comments already "well there's solar panels, and there is this item for this system, and this item for that system, etc. etc.", but here's all I will say to that. My ability to start having fun with a game, shouldn't be dependent on me sinking dozens of hours to get access to the items that make the game fun.

Controls
They suck. Especially flying. It plays like a 90s arcade game.

I have to make the Elite Dangerous comparison now. Coming from that game, looking to experience a new space exploration game, I'm seeing now that this game is more about acquiring resources than actual exploration. There are so many barriers to the actual exploration part of this game, it is infuriating. On Elite, you start out with a simple (albeit still super horrible) tutorial on the basics of the different systems in the game, and then your ship STARTS OUT with everything needed to get around the galaxy. You could stay in the starter ship the entire time you play this game if you wanted. It's not a good way to play the game, but you have the freedom to do so. This game does not give you that same freedom. You are forced to play the game on the developer's terms, having them dictate when and what you can do at all times. You cannot do what you please without getting the game's permission first. With Elite, your progression comes from finding bigger and better ways to accomplish the very diverse sets of activities possible in the game. You can be a pirate, miner, trader, bounty hunter, explorer, and so many other choices, but with this game you will always first and foremost be a miner, regardless of whether that's what you want to do or not. The "depth" in this game starts and stops with how long you can left click on a rock, plant, or animal, but Elite gives you the breadth and freedom to explore the intricacies of the different play styles, which makes every accomplishment feel like a true success, whereas here, your accomplishments let you exhale a deep sigh of relief as one source of unending frustration is relieved. It also can go without saying the graphic polish of this game, even after over 4 years of post-release work, is just not comparable to most other games of it's lifespan. It's still poorly optimized with an uninspired minimalist art style, with loads of texture bugs. What little immersion I do get to experience is constantly interrupted by slow loading textures despite this game running on an absolute powerhouse of a computer.

If you're ok sinking dozens of hours to left clicking the procedurally generated environment to make little to no progress, shallow progression and depth that is covered over a derivative base-building system and annoying at best survival mechanics, then this is the game for you. Otherwise, save your money and buy something else.

Reviews.124899:
No Man's Sky is still more sandbox than game, but Hello Games has packed it full of activities and "things to do". Many blissful hours of exploration await. It is worth some time.

On the minus side, there are still fundamental design problems. The game is arguably as much about shooting rocks and staring at your inventory as it is exploring a beautiful, infinite procedural universe. You will grow to hate the sound of the words "inventory full".

The "normal" game mode is almost trivially easy, while the "survival" mode is punishingly difficult, particularly at the start (before eventually plateauing to trivial difficulty). 

The game ultimately remains a great experience, and an example for developers about what "ongoing support" can mean for a game.

The base building in this game is incredible as well, they give plenty of options and creative freedom and when combined with the variety of planets that have beautiful vistas to behold, you can build yourself an awesome collection of bases whether they be imposing fortresses, cozy cottages, or large mansions. I've built a large resort on a crescent shaped island surrounded by crystalline blue water complete with guest bungalows and an outdoor bar, and a base built vertically along an ice cliff, the game gives you the setting and the tools to be creative. I've seen bases online that would make Frank Lloyd Wright blush.

That said, the plot is meandering and almost useless, there isn't much narrative thrust, but that's not really the point anyways.

Get this game if you like your games to be relaxing and pleasant, and/or if you're interested in base building. Don't get this game if you care primarily about action and/or a cinematic story experience.

No Man's Sky was rough when it initially released in 2016, missing a variety of core functionality and features (such as multiplayer) that had been promised to the fanbase in the lead-up to launch. Despite the missing functionality, I *still* enjoyed NMS, sinking in numerous hours on my PS4 and later doing the same on my PC. The variety and scale of the universe has always been awesome from the beginning.

When NMS released and a veritable shitstorm descended upon Hello Games (developer) over the missing features, the dev team hunkered down, went silent, and started working hard on fixing bugs, performance issues, and working towards a series of large updates to the game to provide features and functionality that were missing from the start.
After 2 years of steady updates, NMS had already undergone some great changes. Now we're at 4 years since initial release, with even *more* ongoing updates that have been released. The game still resembles what it was at original launch (at least when you start out a fresh game), but *so much* has changed. Since launch we now have first & third person, we have VR support, even more planets and biomes have been added. Weather is more dynamic and versatile. Caves, mountains, volcanoes (added), oceans, are all more extensive and varied. Lighting has drastically improved.
There are new modes to play in (Normal, Survival, Permadeath, Creative), full-on multiplayer exists, full-on base-building exists, ship customization is more versatile, more variety in flora, fauna, materials, colors.

The depth of building and construction in the game approaches almost the depth of Space Engineers, but unlike Space Engineers, that's not even the focus in this game. You can build on any planet / moon / whatever. Exploration is awesome fun, and the amount of ridiculous views you'll see almost everywhere will make you want to constantly take new screenshots and create new video clips. It's so easy to find a view that resembles what you would see on the cover of a sci-fi novel, which is amazing (and really was one of the goals / inspiration of the developers).

I highly recommend this game. The only thing it's missing is PvP, but that's fine, there's plenty of other games where that is a focus, and really PvP could end up ruining the experience of this game for the explorers pretty quickly.

The fact that the game supports cross-play means you can have friends or family playing with you, regardless of what device they're on (Xbox One, PS4, PC), which is great fun.
Definitely a must buy.

This game is a lot of fun if you're into space and sci-fi. It does a really good job of really giving you the sense of just how big the universe is, while also giving you tools so you can travel that distance (and not spend 6 hours running in a straight line). There are a lot of really awesome features here, and it's come a really long way from when it first launched.

There are a couple drawbacks to this game. First, the UI/UX is hit or miss in a lot of places. Sometimes it's great, and other times it's really hard to use. It can be overwhelming at times with the numbers of different types of objects, resources, etc. The controls for UI/UX are often not intuitive. But if you can get past that, you'll probably find this is one of the best space/exploration/survival games out there.

My only other complaint is that the game can often be buggy, especially if you're playing multiplayer (and let's be real, multiplayer is the best part). So if you're the type of person that gets extremely frustrated when a game hits you with an annoying bug, maybe avoid this one.

The last thing I'd like to mention is that the developers regularly release big updates that include bug fixes, huge new features, and all sorts of other surprises. And they don't charge you anything for these updates, they're totally free. For me that means a lot, and makes me way more satisfied with my purchase. (I stopped playing this game for a year, came back a year later and there's so much more content now that I feel like I just started again.)

tl;dr: Do you like survival/crafting games? Are you a bit of a space/sci-fi nerd? Have you always wanted to pilot your own spaceship and explore alien planets? Check out this game.

TL;DR: Procedural space exploration game with an enjoyable crafting/survival gameplay loop, potential for breathtaking randomly generated discoveries and satisfying base building that is ultimately slightly dragged down by very noticable pop-in, nasty bugs, uninspired 3D models and very apparent glitches. Recommended regardless.

Pros:
+ Terrain generated by the game can look amazing, especially after the Origins update
+ Wide variety of possible creatures, plants, minerals, ships and star systems that can be named and uploaded for a satisfying kick of "This is mine".
+ Satisfying and expandable base building with all the good stuff: power grid, decoration, upgrades, customization galore. Reminiscient of Satisfactory.
+ Incredibly content filled free updates years after launch
+ Atmospheric and serene vibes and an ever expanding assortment of possible environments make for astounding photo opportunities and the occasional wow-effect.

Cons:
- Lost potential in 
- An assortment of graphical glitches and general jankiness
- Lack of systemic gameplay drags down the game's vision: variety is there, but interaction isn't
- Variety is there, but the lack of interaction and multiple components make it seem like there isn't much variety after all. It's like rolling five dice; each die has a 20% chance of getting X result. If they interacted with each other, they'd have thousands of different results each with only fractions of a chance to happen, for the same development cycle and the same five dice as presets. NMS has lots of dice, but they do not interact wiht each other.

Overall, this game is pretty great. It's always fun in a single player/multiplayer game to add a bunch of mystery and wonder, especially in a game where you explore space. Reviews.125325:
No Man's Sky, what is there to say about it? Everyone knows about its infamous and terrible launch, and most wouldn't think to give it a second glance after such a terrible first impression. But we're entering a time with video games where developers want to make good on the products they deliver, and more and more you see success stories of games turned around, most famously Final Fantasy XIV.

So what of No Man's Sky? Well, it's been at least three years since their launch, and things have changed since then. I can't speak much of the early days, but I do know multiplayer was a feature they failed to deliver on, and have since implemented. There's not only a player hub, but featured bases you can visit, entire communities of players living together in their own corners of space. The various alien animals native to each world are not so gawky (comedically so) as they once were. But these don't really serve to impress.

What does impress me, is that for these three years, they have pushed content update after content update FOR FREE to everyone who owns or buys No Man's Sky. A Mech, space freighters, underwater base building, content and a submarine to top it off. Group content where you explore derelicts in space overrun by hostile alien creatures with a horror-esque vibe to it. Base building in general has become incredibly robust, but even then, if you so choose, your freighter can essentially be its own mobile base as you travel the galaxy. And with the latest update, new types of planets to explore, star systems with two or even three stars, visuals that have been improved yet again, new biomes, and mega-structures to explore, an exploration guide for those of you who want to chart the stars, anomalies and weather conditions of all kinds (volcanoes and meteor showers, too now), and (most excitingly for me) giant, freighter sized sandworms that roam certain planets!

Can we write off the initial poor launch of the game? No. Does this game deserve a second look? Yes. There's a nice feeling when you play a game where you collect a bunch of resources. This game scratches the itch pretty well. I haven't played on anything but survival, so keep that in mind.

Game starts out pretty tough, with you having to keep your protection recharged or die horribly. As your progress, you will worry about these less as you gather more resources in abundance to recharge the protections easily. 

The starship controls are okay. Personally, I find them a bit confusing, at least when you have to spin around in space combat. I stay stationary and just turn my ship to find the enemy ship, so perhaps I'm not doing it right. 

Base building is pretty good. You gather salvaged data as a semi-rare resource which is used to unlock new buildable blueprints.

There are several bugs I've noticed, but none of them are completely game-breaking.
*Oxygen capsules can't be used in the current update, make life support gel instead
*The three people you talk to on the space station around the midpoint of the tutorial will be permanently locked, so make sure they are random wandering civilians you talk to, or you will have to travel to another space station for specific merchants
*Sometimes "trees" will not be breakable, as if they lack any hitbox at all
*Ships and multitools are sometimes free when they should cost units (ingame money)

I'd say it's worth $30-40, so get it whilst it is on sale. Have a lovely day, whoever reads this.

This review is short and simple. 

No Man's Sky is not a game of clear objectives. There is a guide system. There are missions. There are even story missions. But there is no streamlined experience. You will be moving from planet to planet, hoarding some materials, compiling others, trying to figure out the best way of getting more units, etc. 

I have 30 hours in the game. I have played off and on, slowly, for a long time, coming back whenever there is a major update. What I have just described is my entire experience for 30 hours. I know there is base building, and cool upgrades, and even a cool biological spaceship you can get for yourself. But I haven't seen any of that. 

The devs have clearly invested in this game. This game gets better and better all the time. But it is a bit long. Don't want to give a bad review though for what is obviously only my very occasional cup of tea.

Side note: This game is one of the few that makes me nauseous after a short play session.

Absolutely amazing. Zero cons. If you like to explore, build, craft, design, gather resources, create from scratch, fly, discover... this game is absolutely for you. You'll have to make difficult decisions throughout the entire game, such as how to upgrade your tech / weapons systems / starships / bases and how to coexist with AI-based races that inhabit the universe. Some are hostile, while others are quite friendly. Every action you take has consequences that stay with you. Make a mistake? No problem - your character is able to make amends by assisting those races with such tasks as learning about their lore and taking on quests for their guilds, or helping them to defeat space pirates. Find undiscovered planets and create a home of your own, taking the time to map out and discover every inch of whatever your heart desires. From land-based biomes to underwater habitats, this game has quite literally everything you can think up. And it just keeps getting better. The graphics are stunning, the gameplay is unrivaled and you'll soon find yourself losing hundreds-to-thousands of hours, marveling at the endless possibilities that No Man's Sky offers each player.

10/10

Ok so... I am impressed with the amount of content Hello Games have been pumping out for this game. First of all, the fact that they keep releasing new "DLC-sized" updates every few months is huuge! I have already bought this game long time ago, yet they keep adding more and more stuff, for free! Not all updates are as big, though, as some are more bug fixes and QoL changes, but the big sizes ones add a ton of more gameplay and extend its life well past the point of "end game state".

Based on this, the amount of things you have on your to-do list is pretty big... which keeps you occupied for a loooong time. Some can be fun, some kinda boring, depends on what you like and what you are looking for in a game. So there's content for everyone.

The story is pretty cool. I have completed about 90% of the game (I think) and IMO its a pretty immersing solo campaign. In addition to that, the new Anomaly Nexus missions you can do w friends add an extra layer of replayibility, as it lets you experience a more cooperative game.

There are a few cons, though. There are bugs and glitches here and there, that are sometimes triggered out of the blue, like terrain issues w the base, and sometimes falling through things or getting stuck, but nothing that can be easily solved. For example: my base was loading up slow and had lots of parts, so I would sometimes fall through stairs cause it wasn't drawn yet. I ended up increasing Base Complexity in the menu and that fixed the problem! Some others can only be fixed via patches though, but still, not really game-breaking for the most part.

All in all, I definitely recommend this game to anyone on the fence. The fact that the developer keeps adding more and more content, which has a decent quality, is something that keeps you entertained and can be a lot of fun as well! (which is the ultimate goal of a video game, to let you have fun, entertain you, tell a story). And its also a pretty good comeback story, as some of you might remember the backslash the dev experienced back in 2016. But boy have they given back to the community!

Hello Games has earned my respect.

No Man's Sky is a game that is broad, ambitious, and varied. 

NMS was initially a victim of it's marketing, promising the sky and failing to get off the ground. If you check the review graph, you'll see that the VAST majority of the negative reviews, and the only reason the game remains mixed, is negative reviews from launch. Any review from that period ought to be ignored, given the massive number of updates since.

What it's become since is impressive. Major updates providing large scale changes include: VR, base building mechanics, harvesting and farming, animal taming and mounts, organic ships, fleets and carriers, exploration, faction wars, raids on derelict carriers abandoned in space, superbikes, hovercrafts, underwater bases and submarines; and now, doubling the size of the random assets that get drawn from to build worlds, adding in 'dune' worms, volcanoes, etc.

NMS provides incredible breadth and is slowly building depth. It has a unique art style, and a neat scifi story/lore. If you want a game to just kind of drift in space, get lost in a world, and wander, this is that game.

Reviews.125770:
Wow, they really pulled this one out.

First impressions are really positive.

Congrats on sticking with it, Hello games.

TLDR: No.Man's Sky feels like a game without limits.  The experience is very much what I hoped for 4 years ago when I saw those amazing trailers.

One of the most addictive games I have ever played...  I put in over 120 hours in 2 weeks, I haven't done that with a game in years.

Normally, I tend to follow story missions, side missions, but NMS is strongest in the elements that aren't planned out for the player, the Random Encounters, the purely visual Intrigue, the sense of exploration is wonder that you feel as you move on to the next alien world.

I've never played anything quite like it.


Elaborating further:

No Man's Sky has gone from one of the most notorious examples of over-promised content in gaming history, to an underwhelming dissappointment, which rightfully incensed legions customers, many of whom swore they would never pre-order a video game again, to something completely unexpected.

A labor of love.

The team at Hello games clearly had passion for their project and despite being put in an awful position by their mistakes and the relentless pressure of the retail gaming promotional machine, they accepted their situation, put their heads down, and got to work.

I was rightly skeptical, because I could probably count the instances where a game launched to broken promises and disappointed customers, and was subsequently reinvented buy a determined team of developers on one hand, and I'd have a few fingers left over.

Hello games did it.

Not only is No Man's Sky every bit as exciting as the game we saw in those fantastic trailers in 2016, I'd have to say it's more than they promised at the time, and far more than I'd ever expected.


I stumbled back onto the new promotional material, because I was looking for a space game, (there are several good examples on Steam right now, in addition do a few promising titles in development.) Something new that I could pick up right away.

The good now?
1. EVERSPACE
2. Star Control Origins
3. Starpoint Gemini 2
4. Rebel Galaxy Outlaw (mostly)

The good forthcoming
1. EVERSPACE 2
2. DEEP: The Battle of Jove
3. Star Point Gemini 3

Redout Space Assault looked good too, but I'm afraid it might be stillborn.

Notably, there are a couple other AAA space games forthcoming, which look absolutely awful. (Squadrons, Chorvs)

So I ended up taking another look at the promotional trailers for No Man's sky, it was also 50% off.

Utterly blown away.

Not merely that, because NMS is more than just a space flight Sim, it encompasses the complete experience of space exploration and commerce, flying spaceships, visiting space stations, walking, driving, flying, on planet surfaces.  Building bases, piloting mechs, sub Oceanic exploration and habitat, mining, crafting, combat...

You can do it all.

Coupled with that, there is a pervasive sense of wonder about everything you do and everything you find, the systems are intuitive, easy enough to figure out, that you don't need the game to Hold Your Hand.

I'm not sure if it's because of the procedural generation, but everything you encounter feels like something new.

You can choose how you want to play and what you want to do, and so far, I feel like I enjoy everything.

I spent hours piloting my craft around an asteroid field, harvesting rare resources, flew to the space station, parked my vehicle, sold my Wares, went shopping for system upgrades, haggled for a ship, and then decided I wanted to go sit down on a couch.... and every bit of it was fun.

And I'm only a few hours into this game.

Hello Games may have taken time to make good on their promises, but they did it.

More than that, in my opinion, they have created a Timeless masterpiece.

Without mods, or any knowledge of what narrative content the game May contain, with my character's still hanging out in my first system, in the back Waters of the Galaxy, I can see myself sinking thousands of hours into this game, and I look forward to it.

Notes:

Now over 100.hours in, I want to point out some of the experiential highlights.

-Undersea exploration: I ended up settling on my main home base on a fairly safe world, habitable, glasses and oceans, lots of goodies to discover.

Initially I swam in the water looked at all the sea life, I absolutely loved it.  It motivated me to unlock the "Nautilon". (Pro-tip- you can unlock goodies a lot earlier using the anomaly, instead of waiting to expand your base, all you need is Salvage data from the buried modules)

Once I got to submarine, I was able to explore deep water, hundreds of meters down from the surface, there were even cave that were big enough to be navigable with the small sub.

In one of the larger oceans, I found a crashed Starship, I swam through the tropical see among the wreckage.

Not far from that Starship, as I was harvesting resources to make more fuel, I encountered a school of massive under sea monsters, which one bigger than my submarine.  Just epic.

I highly recommend at least checking out the first person camera on the submarine, it's not as easy to navigate, but it's an incredibly immersive experience, and one of the coolest things I've ever seen in a video game.

-Base Building: full disclosure, I am not a fan of survival games, or pretty much any other game that centers around building bases.

When I've played Skyrim and Fallout, I didn't even attempt to build bases, I just lived where the game with lightning, ( with my beautiful wife Lydia.)

Something about the utility of bases, the overall sense of Frontier exploration, and the unearthly settings made base Construction in no man's sky absolutely addictive for me.

I had to spend at least 10 to 20 hours of the 120 that I played in the last 2 weeks building bases.

They run the gamut from the prefabricated high-tech units, which allowed me to build a looking installation, perched high on a precarious Mountain Ridge, with a view to die for.

I built a custom structure, which starts on the coast of an ocean, bridges across the water do a building on a small island.  Because of extreme weather on the planet, I made sure I had plenty of space for everything, with the exception of my landing pad...  not content with merely fantastic, I decided to excavate a cave into the ocean underneath one of my buildings, and build stairs allowing me to access my submarine while never leaving the building, at some point, I will add an underwater portion to the structure.

I also built a more simple desert Hideaway, perching on Foothills, it has a great view off the porch, and since I was feeling a bit silly as I was finishing the project, I decided to build the jump ramp as the main egress for my exocraft.

And as far as I'm concerned, I'm just getting started.

I've put a lot of time into this game, and I've seen it evolve over time, and I just can't recommend it.

The one thing I like is the spaceship design. That's it.

As for the rest of the game, the choices they've made make no sense to me. In a game where exploring infinite space was the entire point, they've decided that making a base is the most important thing you can do. A stationary base, on a planet. In a space EXPLORATION game. And you have to go back to it over and over and over again. It's a core mechanic. So forget about exploring the galaxy, and welcome to "fetch and bring home" repetition. 

The whole thing is a pointless drag. Starting a new game requires at least an hour or more of being forced to do things that aren't helpful to the main game. You can get the "use the laser to get resources, use resources to repair/make stuff" in five minutes, but instead they force you on several, non-optional missions - including making a base (yes, it's required). 

If you can get past all of that, the universe is as dead and shallow as ever. All the bases are still the same, even though they're nicer. NPCs are cardboard. All the quests repetitive and uninspired. The planets are uniform, even with the new "weird" ones, you see all you need to in the first two minutes of landing anywhere. 

Basically, the only fun part is the ships - and even then, most of them are too damn expensive for a casual player to reasonably afford. It's just a parade of generated ships, most of which look kind of cool.  

If there's more to this game, I haven't discovered it with well over one hundred hours of play. 

I keep wanting more from this game. Every update I check it out, hoping that it became the awesome EXPLORATION game I was told it would be. But every update only locks things down more, adds ridiculous new stuff no one asked for (DJ booth for your dance floor in the city you built - in our space EXPLORATION game?), and is still, at it's core, a boring grind for resources and money so you can endlessly upgrade, so you can grind more.

There's better space games out there.

ORIGIN UPDATE: 
Maybe all the new stuff they added in is cool, but just from trying out the beginning again, I can tell the core gameplay hasn't changed, and I didn't want to spend the hours getting off the starter planet. 

Look, I don't want to rain on anyone's parade here. It's fine so many people like it. I came close a few updates ago - I discovered that if I tried to NOT play the game, and just cruised around the galaxy in my starter spaceship checking out new planets, it's a fine way to waste a few hours. 

But it wasn't very fun, and it got boring. The game itself (quests, jobs, grinding for money, etc) wasn't fun at all. And it has the WORST writing of any game I've ever played. 

tl;dr
The best parts of this game are just decent, and the rest are still, after all of this time, not fun or engaging, but it might be worth trying out if you get it on sale. I tried everything I could to enjoy this game, but in the end, I just don't think it was worth it.

EDIT SEPT 26: Needless to say I was able to dig into the update sooner than I thought. As my previous update was already pretty extensive given what I feel was missing, I will attempt to keep this as concise as I can.

[b]Just not good enough[/b]: Everything about Origins feels like a push in the right direction, away from "samey"ness and towards a more diversified and exciting universe. But much of the issues that existed before are really just as prevalent, simply with a bit more polish. I noticed in the update notes that Hello seemed to almost dance around the word "biome", seemingly using every conceivable synonym without actually coming out and saying it, I can see why that is. I have traveled and explored at least 50 new worlds since Origins release, and I can say beyond a shadow of a doubt, they are all nearly the same. I will give big credit to the new rendering process, that looks great. Mountains are indeed taller, textures look better, clouds are hugely improved, but there is still no diversity to speak of. Further compounding this I found that several planets actually looked more unique from orbit, swaths of red with streaks of green, giving the sense of a varied world. But alas, on the surface there is no such luck. I wanted to like this, I really wanted to be surprised, even just enough to change my mind on recommendation, but this is massively short of the magical varied worlds that, I'll say again, would be more than possible without the dozens of diluted planet types that all seem to stick strictly to a singular theme. 

[b]Some light revisions[/b]: I'm leaving my original review up, because unfortunately most of it, if not pretty much all of it, is still relevant. There is the illusion of biomes, without actual biomes. Combat does feel tighter, I didn't notice anything from Hello mentioned in patch notes about combat so I can't explain this, but its better... magically. It still lacks variation as with most of NMS, but is very passable. Everything else is pretty much accurate to how I feel about the current state of the game.

[h1]ORIGINAL REVIEW[/h1]

I know everybody has a bucket list of features they feel would really tip the scale here but there are three things I'd like to see and one other I really must to see to recommend NMS.

The must is a tough one, I realize this isn't an easy update, but its SO important.

[b]PLANETS NEED BIOMES[/b]: Exploring the vast expanse of NMS becomes stale at such an accelerated rate without this. Once you've seen the dozen or so planet types (and many are essentially duplicates with ever so slightly different environments or atmospheres), you've seen it all. There just isn't enough variation between worlds to hold that deep sense of wonder for very long. It's a shame because the game does have that for a time, but it falls off incredibly fast due to the nature of, "okay, well that's what this one has to offer, let's go check out the next one". I can say quite confidently had the developer simply created 5 or 6 different planet types fully fleshed out with unique biomes and natural phenomena (how about some mountain ranges and canyons instead of 60 caves?) this would have had a [i]much[/i] better effect. For one thing, due to randomization, it would never [u]feel[/u] the same. Even if you visit a dozen different paradise worlds, when they all have unique oceans, mountains, poles, etc. you end up finding the one that you really like. That spot between the tundra and the wilderness that's just perfect. And for the record, leave a couple of the gimmicky ones in, why not? The weird ethereal space magic hedral planets more akin to moons with floating obelisks? It's fine they don't have biomes, they're neat, leave 'em. But really put some work in the others. This game really needs this, and I hope the developers listen to the at least half a dozen high profile reviews that have already said this. Also, space stations could gain a lot from this same point, and should be included as well. This was not a good idea for the copy paste formula, and at least half a dozen different layouts would have been greatly appreciated. Maybe even some grungey space bar type deals, make a couple barely working stations where the lights flicker and the bartender only serves space bootwash. IDK. so much you could do with this.

The remaining 3 points are more nitpicky and hardly required for a recommendation, but the biomes (and to some extent variation on space stations) just straight up need to happen. It would take a mediocre to okay exploration experience and amplify 10 fold.

[b]Asteroid sprites suck[/b]: This is a beautiful game. Beauty is important to the experience of this game. Graphics aren't always everything, but they are deeply meaningful here. Why is the one thing you see in droves when exploring space so overlooked. Asteroids need a refresh, more variation, and better destruction visuals. I stay in impulse as much as possible to avoid the nasty looking rocks that fly by every time I boost. Also, having different asteroids in different systems is a neat idea, but again, had they all just been mixed up and implemented wherever, with a bit better look and feel in general, this would have made for an experience that didn't grow old so quickly. The, "ahh the asteroids are different here" moment is novel, but fades after 3 or 4 systems, and since they all look bad, not really selling it. And you're stuck with seeing whatever nasty asteroid graphic you get over, and over again in your "home" system.

[b]Combat could be better[/b]: It's fun, but some variation here would be nice too. Real pirating would be amazing but probably asking a lot, not that you run across other players very often anyway, still something other games of similar context have managed to do. More interesting weapons particularly on ships would really sell this for me. Which kind of leads me into the next point.

[b]Hubs that bring people together in more dangerous context would be huge[/b]: The only hub points in this game are safe zones. Why not make a hub that's well, [i]not[/i] a safe zone. Pirate real players, interact and work with others. Here's one thought to really reach out to scifi fans: implement a WORKING hailing system. Let that freighter (who is a real person) know he needs to pay up or your fleets gonna blow him away. Or maybe he'll just ignore your hail and shoot first ala han solo. A "live" space hub zone would have a lot to offer with already existing mechanics or relatively easy to implement new ones.

And one bonus -- [b]Cities[/b]: I don't think this is ever going to happen and where I find all my other suggestions reasonable this is getting pretty intensive. Regardless games like X4 have made it work, so it can be done. It would certainly add a tremendous layer of wonder to this entire universe to interact with civilizations in all different parts of development, and to be honest, even if it were just a couple different types copy and pasted, as this game does a lot of anyway, it would still be deeply meaningful. This could well be implemented in a biome update anyway, although I get this is some serious work. Still, I can't imagine the pay off.

TL:DR or more [b]summary[/b]: sorry my review is what I'd like to see instead of what already is, but in a sense that's a lot of what this game feels like to play. A few hours of glorious exploration digging through an enormous space for all there is to see followed by many hours of disappointment as you realize, rather early in, you've essentially seen it all.

Honestly I don't get the reviews saying "Hello Games really turned NMS around." It still feels fresh out of alpha with a thin story slapped on it, though I'm aware of and respect the technological hurdles and various other difficulties that HG had to overcome to make NMS.

I did buy the game 2 years after it came out, and maybe that influenced my opinion. From my perspective though, the improvements do not justify the $60 price tag. Apart from some nice additions, the game still has bad visuals, long load times, and unimmersive worldgen. Base building is honestly the most fun part of the game for me, because the story and quests are really shallow and the visual issues make exploration and resource gathering a bit grating.

These visual issues include the utterly nasty clouds, harsh edges between foreground and background elements (probably where render passes overlap), antialiasing that just doesn't work, bad HDR tone mapping, and huge quality differences between basically every 3D thing. Apparently very few people seem to notice these issues. These are technical problems, not artistic choices, and have existed ever since the game came out as far as I can tell.

But it's not really a matter of looking good. I still play some older games with horrible graphics, and the content and the feeling of accomplishment when doing things is enough to feel immersed. I expect a lot of grinding and resource gathering from a survival game, but I don't expect immersion-breaking game mechanics and glaring graphical issues.

On a more positive note, HG quietly fixed ultrawide support recently - this was "added" a while ago but the UI was still stretched to hell and back. I checked in a few weeks ago and it seems they finally fixed this.

I know NMS isn't a great example of photorealism, but it really does seem like the devs have little experience programming visuals. Things like blending issues should be fixed, and massive quality differences between different areas and even different parts of a scene can be smoothed out. Not saying it's easy, but it can be done.

I wish I could recommend this game. The number one limiting factor is price. It's not a terrible game, just lackluster in content. I would feel much better about recommending it if it were $20 cheaper.

I'm having to update this review because my previous one was done with a kiss of irony, but as this game rapidly approaches by #2 all time played game, I think I need to give it some justice.

No Man's Sky is a masterpiece of gaming well deserving of your attention. It is a testament to what is possible if a developer (not the community) actually sticks to their guns and sees their project through. I purchased this game 1 week after release, well aware of the controversy. At the time, I'll be honest, I didn't see what everyone was upset about. You flew around and looked at things, that's what I came for.

I'm not sure how to describe precisely how far this game has come in the last 4 years. World of Warcraft doesn't feel this different in the last 4 years. Minecraft doesn't feel this different. There is no comparison to how much this game has developed and how far it has come in the last 4 years. It is staggering the amount of things that can be done. There are certainly drawbacks, there are definitely bugs, but when you truly get a sense of the sheer scale of this game, you're more than willing to put those aside to just gawk at what this game really is.

It's a space exploration game. You fly around, sometimes there's pirates, very rarely there's other players, sometimes there's derelict freighters, sometimes there's planets made out of hexagonal plates of metal, sometimes there's tornadoes that fling you into the ocean and now you have to swim back. Sometimes, you bring your friends along and you establish a colony, sometimes that colony expands into multiple star systems, sometimes you spend 500 hours building bases, trading with each other, sharing experiences, seeing so many different things you can't believe they're all in the same video game. Sometimes a $30 game shocks you into realizing exactly how much gaming can be. 

This is the most comprehensive VR game on the market today, bar none. You don't get the interactivity of something like Boneworks or Blade and Sorcery, but No Man's Sky is open and you can do literally anything you want. There is not a single VR title on the market that can challenge the ludicrous amount of things that you can do on a daily basis in No Man's Sky. This game is truly incredible. By now I doubt you need me to convince you of that, but if you haven't been convinced by now I'm telling you to change your mind and experience the greatest comeback story in gaming history. 

If you ever make it to the centre, there's a little Indium star called Sun's Hollow, come and see us all some time. We'll be here.

Ok this is important, No one gonna let you know this unless you dig really deep on the internet.

If you are having FPS problem/stuttering, you need to go to game files and find "TKGRAPHICSETTINGS". Open it with Note Pad. Ctrl+F and find "NUMHIGHTHREADS". Set it to half your CPU's logical processor. And set "NUMLOWTHREADS" to half minus 1 of logical processor. It will make your game smooth as butter. This is not overcloking.

I couldn't find any solution until I made a reddit account and ask for it there. I don't know why game developers not fixing this easy problem, yet very common and really having big impact on game experience.

Also there is this another problem, my game kept crashing when I tried to finish "The Purge" quest. Couldn't find any fix for this too, until I went deep on google. Turns out you need to finish "Find Black Hole" quest first.

Hello Games really needs to focus on these problems first,

After 180 hours of gameplay, I decided to write an updated review for this game and changed my recommendation. here is why:

NMS is a beautiful game in a vast and endless universe but it is ALL procedurally generated with the exception of players' built bases. Planets and star systems often feel the same with lots of repetition. Missions are pretty much the same in every star system and are there as fillers. They don't really have any affect on the game. NMS is not really an MMO but more like a limited Multiplayer where you will likely NEVER see another player unless you visit the hub or join a private group. Even then, the hub is limited to a max of 32 players who never talk in the chat and the game doesn't really have a sense of a community. No guilds, no organizations to join, nothing. It feels like you are just by yourself.

The space flight model is very limited. Ships are cookie cutters with very small variations. NMS is mainly played as a 3rd person on foot. The ship is just a mode of transportation but has no other real purpose. Space combat is super aracdy/catoony and limited. PVP is non existent.  If space sim is what you're after, NMS is light years away from that. In fact, it classifies itself as a survival game so I guess that's fair. 

If you are an explorer at heart and don't mind a game with no real objectives or progression , then this game is for you.  There is endless stuff to discover and with the recent update, they supposedly added even more stuff.

Launch controversy aside, what this game should have been called for the longest time is 'Early Access'. Around the time of the Beyond update is when I'd say would have been the true 'launch'. 

I didn't get this when it first came out, but even when I did it was a fragmented mess of a game. Now, finally, with the Beyond and Synthesis updates there's a solid game here that's almost (but not quite) like what Sean Murray promised way back at the beginning.

Performance on PC has dramatically improved with the switch over to the Vulkan API, and it finally supports Ultrawide and various other PC-specific options. The game itself provides a significant amount of variety, offering a combination of Elite-lite and 'Minecraft in Space' mechanics. There's plenty to see and do, and the exploration aspect is enjoyable - if a little bland. The planetary biomes and overall game could still do with further diversity, but there's plenty here to get to your teeth into.

Hello Games show no sign of slowing down their support for the game either, having just recently released a bizarre in-game music synthesizer of all things, and going by the evidence of their progress to date I can only see the game improving further as time moves on.

EDIT - 24/09/2020 "Origins" Patch: well, you can ignore the previous comments about diversity being a bit on the low side. They already added things like living ships, derelicts, space creatures and robots since I made this review, and with the Origins patch the variety of experience on offer is on such a scale now that I don't think I'm going to be lacking for things to do for some time. Also, impressively, the game runs even better than it did when I originally posted this - and the rejigged UI looks fantastic on Ultrawide. 

Brilliant work by the team at Hello Games. I can't think of any game I've played (and I've been indulging since the late 80's) where I've ever gone from "I can't stand this" to "this is one of my favourite games". It's taken a while to get here, but No Man's Sky is definitely one of the greats.

UPDATE AFTER ORIGINS:

Still not enough. They've changed the way planet looks and added a bit more of scale on things. Also a bit more of variety such as natural disasters and events. It's cool to find you landed in a volcanic planet with a volcano active and such. But the almost all of the issues I mentioned before are still there, except for the inventory management. They fixed that and now you can split stack of items in quantities, or quickly get half of it.

But:

- There is no sense of loss in this game. And for me this is a killer. Sure it's nice to explore but at least make it optional then. Look at Rimworld, Factorio or even Cities Skyline. Those titles are games you have to manage your resources and build stuff to survive, but you can lose what you did, so you give more attention to it, to "care" more. 

- Gathering resources from flora and small minerals makes no change on planet sustainability, meaning you can gather all the stuff, flight out and in again and everything is there back again. It would be awesome to have a planet sustainability meter where if you don't care on how much to gather from it, you can make it a desolate planet or one of those dying planets, for example.

- The dialog and story is pathetic. And at this point I don't think they can fix this, besides getting rid of all dialogues or rewriting the whole story.

- There is almost no ship customization. You can now change the color, but there is no ship dealer shop for example. Adding it as a NPC on each station would be awesome but having to check with each NPC on its spot is boring and tedious.

- Blueprint progress is confusing. New items are added without me expecting them. They should at least add a placeholder with the item greyed out or a huge item tree with which quest you can get it.

- There is no automation at all.


--------
Original:

I tried. I really tried to like this game. Flying in and out planets and system seamlessly sounded amazing and is done amazing in many ways, but the lack of reason to play and the variety of planet content was and still is a problem. There are so many bugs and inconsistent behaviours that takes away all the efforts from the developers to fix this game:

- There is no sense of loss in this game. You can build and build and destroy all life that is current rendered in your current planet that it causes no problem. There is no penalty for killing fauna or harvesting flora too much. You go out to space, in to the planet, and everything is there again.

- Following the same idea, when you clean up an area to build your base (like removing small rocks and plants), if you go out to space and return it will be filled with all those rocks and plants you just removed.

- The dialog and story is pathetic. It's not just bad, it is filled with generic meaningless dialog with no voice-over and with no sense at all. It is slow, you have to smash buttons to fast forward and sometimes you have to take actions that makes no difference in the end, the NPC will behave the same way and the outcome of a dialog is always the same.

- It is way too repetitive. Quests are always about: Killing life in any planet, with no reason at all; Delivering item X from A to B, with some generic space pirates in your way; Scan mineral/plants, again, with no reason at all, with no specification about it. The game must have twenty types of planets yet it quests are not really engaging enough; Destroy supply depots that have either a walker or some sentinels.

- [strike]There is no ship customization. You will have to patiently watch random ships landing and taking off from a space station until find something you like. Races, sectors or planets have no influence about what you will find.[/strike]

- [strike]Inventory management is poorly made. Once you put your items from inventory to storage, you can't get a fraction of it, you can split in packs, you either get all or none. That's one of the basic principles of stacking items.[/strike]

I spent a dark few decades searching for the perfect game for my play style and I always knew that a space faring game would be at the top of that list. In fact, I knew decades ago, while playing the original ELITE sci-fi game that I was destined to be entwined with this genre as the future unfolded for us. No nostalgia trip though. At the time, original Elite was a very fun game and I have just about played every Space Faring/Trading/Flight/Combat/Strategy/Kitchen Sink simulator that came down the pike. I enjoyed them all up to a point. Until now, they all had big pluses and unfortunately equal minuses. No Man's Sky brought me into the realm of what I like to think is as close to an Adventurous Life In Space simulation that we have been graced with so far. Now there are a large number of these types of games out there, but IMHO none of them brought it home, so to speak. NMS seems to be the only game for this genre that did not either fail at, or just leave out, some important aspect of this game type. It has every facet of the sci-fi action/sim covered in very well done approaches. Space Flight ..CHECK.. I believe the entire system of Flight from basic technology mechanics to in depth warp travel and endless destinations are a complete win here. This is one of, if not, THE most important aspect of a game like NMS. It keeps it interesting, exciting and intriguing without drowning you in ultra-complex stats and flight controls. As with all areas found in NMS, Flight is balanced perfectly between just enough depth and easily learned with plenty of room for mastery. The game passes on complete ship customization in exchange for a plethora of ship types and configurations with a large amount of add-on and upgrade selections to choose from. Not to mention all spread over just as wide a selection of basic ship types such as Fighter, Shuttle, Hauler, Scout and many more. Combat is likewise easily learned with enough to learn, achieve and master to keep you on our toes well beyond getting your own S-Class ship of possibilities. Let me cut the verbosity a bit here though. I could easily babble for hours about how much I love No Man's Sky and about all there is to do in the world(s) you discover. ..then name ..then explore ..then name the plants, the animals, the rocks, the trees and on and on. All of which you can hunt, feed, husbandry, mine, dig, refine, combine, craft, purchase and sell. All the while saving your money, your nanite rewards and more which you can use to obtain an endless number of items, structures, machines, resources, construction blueprints, machines, and on and on. Did I mention you can have as many or as few bases on every planet you wish to discover and then build on. Bases that can be as tiny or immense as your imagination and desire allow. So, did I mention I love sci-fi adventure/sim games since I played Elite on my Commodore 64 almost 40 years ago? I quite like a lot of this game, approached as a fairly peaceful walking simulator. There's a lot to see, and it feels like there's a lot to potentially find. I almost enjoy the base-building stuff, and could probably learn to like it, although it's a bit opaque.

Unfortunately it's largely gated behind a really infuriating inventory-management minigame which wastes my time by forcing me to manually discard things I (hope I) don't want.

Manually recharging my life support systems with a stack of gases from my magic gas pockets doesn't improve immersion, and having a single unit of Oxygen fill an inventory slot that could otherwise store a metric tonne of sheet steel doesn't constitute an interesting optimization problem.

Trading off suit slots between storage and functional modules actually [i]could[/i] be an interesting optimization problem, but I don't think it's well expressed by the current tile-shuffling inventory (weight, volume and/or power limits might work). There isn't even a way to swap the contents of two tiles, so you need to empty one before you can laboriously move things around, like a sort of rubbish Towers of Hanoi split over six or seven different tabs.

Changing this to a thumbs up even though the inventory remains a pain, because it's fun in spite of that if you're in the right mood.

2020 Origins Update: I have changed my review from a thorough No to a wholehearted Yes for a reccomendation.

this game has caused a lot of controversy for its lackluster launch, and many things missing. I now think that the backlash was deserved at the time, but they have throughly proved that they are committed to building this game up and are full steam (pun intended) on improving it. This wasnt the AAA scheme of chopping games up and pulling the "oh dear, we are sorry. we will improve it in the future" BS thats going on. I honestly believe this was a naive indie studio manipulated by big talking people and a very eclectic head who seems very gullible. And they flopped, and now are still trying to earn back trust 4 years later. 

I think they deserve our trust now. 

--Why? 

with the Origins update, THIS is the state of the game we wanted (and thought were getting) when it first came out 4 years ago. A lot of the questions are addressed that I had been concerned of from my original review (see below). This isnt a story rich RPG. It is definitely an exploration/open world crafting game but it has more storyline than Minecraft. I have not finished the main storyline yet, for full disclosure, so I do not know if we find all the answers we want but they smoothed out the storyline and introduction. 

--Which gets me to their improvements. 

I restarted the game to see what the new worlds were like and was pleasantly surprised that they had overhauled their tutorial. They HAVE a tutorial added now, so you know what element does what, how to harvest it, and what it applies to. AND how to refuel your things, upgrade them, as well as give you a reason to explore (to avoid spoilers). you also get into base building and the terrain scanner right away so you can mine for stuff, know how to search for materials, know how to base build, and start the process of upgrading your tech and materials right away. What once felt like a vast wasteland now has flavor and character. 

--Tutorial added

I've learned more about No Mans Sky within about 20 min of this new update than I did exploring multiple planets and solar systems during my first playthrough a year or so ago. I originally gave up and just went to creative as I was sick of not getting anywhere and realized that after i made my cool space station hut i was done and didnt have anything to explore besides plants. 

--Diversity of flora and fauna

But now, there are flying fish and graboids (see the movie Tremors), a weird spikey teddy bear, and a weird partying house size dinosaur that likes to gather amongst its kind and get krunked while they party. All in one planet. Now I am on the hunt for the legendary Dune Worm next.  

There is SO much variety. I never knew how to access the bestiary before and they overhauled their menus so things are easy to access. You find a weird animal, scan it, and then can view it and show it to your friends. I like to show my wife all the weird animals I see, and as she is a fan of the River Monsters series she enjoys them as well.  

As for memorable areas, theres just so much to see and it is procedurally generated that I've realized you won't have a single memorable planet as they change for everyone. But with the variety of terrain and fauna, you can tell where things are by the mountains (or lacktherof), the kinds of plants that are there, animals, etc. So you know there is a hill to put solar panels by the lake, and know that the planet with the psychadelic dandelions is where you can find lots of copper, but the one that has the goofy fish may have more oxygen. They are diverse enough to be memorable. 

I definitely reccomend this now as I finally understand what this game was trying to do and how to really appreciate it. 



Here is my original review:

Has this gone from One Mans Lie to No Mans Sky after 3 years? 

That question I still havent been able to figure out yet. This game is definitely lightyears closer towards their goal, so to Hello Games a Yes.  but it still isnt anywhere near our expectations of it. So for me, No. 

This game is only for those who want to explore for hours, mindlessly searching and grinding for resources so they can see the next pretty flower or weird animal. THATS IT. 

This game is not for us who like story, progression, and sensible goegraphy. This game is MASSIVE. Most likely the largest video game in history. However, I found myself getting much more involved in a map like Kanto (Pokemon) or in something like Blood Gulch or Ivory Tower (Halo) than in any planet here. There still really is no story, just lots of aimless wandering for resources.  The other games mentioned all had definitive features, wonderful memories, and some spirit that glued everything together. This does not. 

Who are we? WHY are we exploring? Where did this unverse come from? WHY are we exploring? Where did we get our ship from? Why did we crash? How did the individual species come together to form alliances? Are there any enemies like the Kilgon or is everyone just friendly?  None of these are answered.

To be honest. I am a person who normally gets bored with a game very quickly and moves onto the next.
There is only one game I have played for a very long while (10+ years so far), of which being Lord of the Rings Online.

Now this game, well, personally I think it is EXCELLENT.
Yet, I always ignore personal opinions when people post about a game. As we are all different and I am sure that every game out there has good points and bad points for everyone.
I look for comments with regards BUGS, DEVELOPERS paying interest in the game, etc, etc.
Personal opinions on games are like saying you don't like Marmite or you love it.
For everyone is different.

Just lately I have purchased a few games looking for the right one and this seems to be the right one.

It offers a hell of a lot more than most games in the same category.

Now, to the review.

The gameplay is very smooth on my machine, even on ALL MAX RES.
With regards bugs, played the game for 20 hours so far (intend a hell of a lot more), the game has crashed twice.
Yet, when I re-run the game up, no problems, straight back in.
There is a lot to explore in this game and a lot to learn.
The quests in this game are quite good. Of which also teach about the game and crafting, etc, whilst playing.
The worlds are varied and very strange :)
The starmap is very large. Of which there is a hell of a lot to visit.
The learning curve in this game is nice and steady, it seems to help you in such a way that your enjoying it and also achieving whilst learning. It kind of teaches you as you play. Excellent way of doing this.
There is not much PVP, unless you go around picking on things you shouldn't. Also run into a star system that has a conflict/battle going on. Which, makes this game a lot better for me as a personal point of view, as I prefer PVE games, with some PVP thrown in.
I see a freighter out there and fired at it. Next thing I know I am a hunted man. Starships came out and made a grave for me.
Yet, I am sure all the fast response gamers out there who like PVP, would not have been sent to their grave. But, I am not sure how long the conflict in space would have gone on if I had not had died. As, I got away, yet, when I went back into space, in a different area, I got clocked by one of my enemies, then I died :|


Now I have only played this game for 20 hours and I must say as a personal view, (yet, we are all different), this game is excellent.

If you like PVE with some small amount of PVP. (Unless you go fight things, then I would imagine it becomes more PVP).
Exploring, Crafting, Hunting and gathering, learning, etc.
Then this probably might be the game you are looking for.

Well I hope that helps someone who is wondering if they should buy the game or not. Of which was not to much rambling on.
I have reviewed is from a slight personal opinion and tried to give as much info as possible about the game.

All the best and see you in space :)

*** UPDATE

Nearly 200 hours into the game and still LOVING IT.
With regards BUGS & CRASHES.
Apart from the 2 early ones (mentioned above), in nearly 200 hours I have had one more crash/freeze. That's ultra acceptable as an opinion.

Well Well Well, Third time reviewing this game is a charm and im happy to say that after returning with the origins update and extensively playing the game i can happily say that no mans sky has finally, finally reached a state in my opinion that i can call...Good. I would even go so far to say that this game is amazing.

i have always been a fan of no mans sky even back during its initial release, I dont regret pre-ordering the game even back when it first released in its lack luster state, i still enjoyed what was present despite its shortcoming, fast forward to the next or the beyond update i think? one or the other the one that majorly changed the entire games existence and at the time i reviewed the game and said that it was good but still felt lacking and also felt boring after time. Now i can happily shove those opinions in the the trash heap where they belong because no mans sky has now become a survival game i would gladly recommend along other titans of the genre such as the forest or subnautica, a game i have always enjoyed paralleling NMS to because of both games sci fi setting, something i myself am a fan of.

No Man's Sky is much better now featuring lots of things to do with at-least one of which is surely to please you, the core game is the same, your still gathering space materials to fix your ship and fly all over the universe but the game has been fleshed out a lot, but not in a way that feel tedious or monotonous which was a big con i had previously with the game, everything felt like busy work, but having played the game i understand that the games takes great lengths to make no factor of the game tedious, nothing feels repetitive or boring like it used, the simple act of going from planet to planet is no longer boring, every planet is truly unique now I feel, I've seen a planet where there is nothing but gigantic flying space eels for as far as the eye can see and another which is a scrap planet littered with giant floating robotic balls, whose existence makes no sense but doesn't need to, in a game where your main loop is planet hopping it always feels fresh but without ever getting boring, as for the main game-play survival loop itself I can say its no longer a chore, surviving is not a issue if you know how to play, early on it feels harder because you don't know how to play and I will admit as a returning player I had to relearn how to play the game but once you get into the loop, once your understand the mechanics, once you understand and follow the games pacing and it gets it's hooks into you there isn't anything quite like it, the game has a lot of content now, maybe not vastly different amounts of content but enough to allow you to do one thing like questing and swap to another like base building without the switch ever getting boring, resource mining is satisfying and simultaneously intuitive, the game is really easy once you get it, the whole survival mechanics feel more like a extra rather than a annoyance, they flesh out the game extra without ever feeling like padding, there's always something to do whether it be quests, base building, upgrade crafting, Nanite farming, resource farming, farming farming, all that good stuff.

excuse me please I get that I tend ramble on a lot...so then, how is this game better now exactly, well for one the base building is easy satisfying and intuitive, the game never feels hard but it never feels like its holding your hand, it'll baby you and teach you how to swim but it wont refrain from throwing you in the deep end either and its this perfect amalgamation of difficulty combined with a simple and gratifying game-play loop that make it so good, learning new recipes and cashing in your units always feels good, the quest lines in the game interesting with quest lines like the Artemis path and the Atlas path telling a interesting story and attempting to flesh out the lore whilst also teaching the games mechanics and show casing some of the games best looking worlds the procedural generation has to offer.

the games inventory is a beautiful cluttered mess, it'll have you constantly fighting with yourself as you make the decision to use your valuable inventory slots of upgrades to actually survive, and if you play on the harder difficulties these decisions can be all the more renching, do you take extra health and shield or do you run the risk of being vulnerable but be a living pack mule able to haul large payloads, this quandary extends to your ship and freighter as well and presents an interesting dichotomy for the player as you explore more and more hazardous planets taking bigger and bolder risks as you attempt to complete your goal.

the game is pretty, its downright breathtaking at time, with the origins updating improving lighting and foliage and expanding the games repertoire of procedurally generated rocks, the game can look absolutely amazing as you stare out into vista's on a tropical planet, the ocean in the distance and the valley below you rich with foliage and fauna strolling around, trees swaying and this serenity is a great contrast to the games more frantic points, parts where your being chased by aliens, sentinel and giant alien sand worms, the games looks great, and there are many things that want to kill you. truly a great improvement over the early days of being stranded in a empty space.

anyway that is my really really really long review/opinion of nms as of the 2020 origins update and I apologize for the length, its clearly compensating for something, but thanks anyway.
