[h1]No Man's Sky Review[/h1]

No Man's Sky is a very fun game about exploration. The main focus is to get to the centre of the galaxy, and complete the multiple campaigns that the game tells you to do.

Although there are many selling points, the main one is the massive exploration potential. Although you can't instantly hop over from system to system, you can hop between planets inside the system. Each planet is largely the same throughout, but you can find some occasional points of interest. For example, you can find an abandoned starship or freighter. It used to be that the only way you could find this was by using the navigation beacon to scan for objects, but since the new update, all you need to do is talk to a dude in the space station.

The gameplay is largely repetitive, if your one goal in the game is to get into the centre. However, I'm sure that most people would try to get the best weapons, build bases etc [b]while[/b] trying to get to the centre. Each base can help you get valuable resources which you will need later on.

Within a few jumps, you come across one of my favourite additions to the game: Freighters.
These massive ships are not flyable, but you can summon them. Each freighter is basically the same, with the same core features (fleets, upgrades etc). However, you can actually build a base inside the freighter. This allows mobile HQ, and you can do all your trading in one place. Freighters also have their own personal hangars, which allow you to store up to 8 starships. Any spaces not used will be filled with AI pilots, whom you can trade with, acquiring trading items that you usually won't find in the trade terminals.

To finish this small review, we will talk about updates. Hello Games are constantly pushing out updates, each adding new features and places to explore. Bugs are also crushed each time, meaning for a less annoying experience. 

In short, if you are considering getting this game, I say: "Yes, buy it."
Thank you for reading my review!!

2018 REVIEW:

I've spent 140 hours with this game, about 90 of them since NEXT was released, and because of a recent bug that allowed me to acquire unlimited funds, I've got all the money in the world. Now, all there is for me to do is hop peacefully from star to star, looking at a bunch of identical planets... which I could have been doing from the beginning, actually. That's right: the ultimate of endgame play is exactly the same as what you get from the start, and it's critically boring.

Let's start with what NMS says it is, but isn't. It's not a game of exploration: yes, there are technically limitless procedurally-generated worlds, in the same way that a TV screen's static is a limitless series of procedurally-generated artworks. They're all bland and boring palette swaps of each other, with nothing to see. This isn't the rich procedural depth of Dwarf Fortress or Caves of Qud, because every "settlement" is one of literally 4 shallow pre-generated templates. It's not the secret-laden world of Fallout: New Vegas or Pillars of Eternity, because the "secrets" you're searching for are either strewn every 100 feet with big HUD arrows pointing to them, or they're one-per-system things that are a mechanical chore to find, and either way they're all pretty much identical. There are no lore-bombs here, just paper-thin systems hoping you don't try to dig too deep.

NMS also isn't a survival game. Every planet is like a garden of Eden, filled with all the resources you need to survive just kind of sitting around, ripe for the taking. Even the most brutal hellscape planets (there are 4 kinds of bad weather, and each planet might have one of them) can be easily trivialized with cheap and easily-obtainable upgrades to your suit, meaning the hardest part about surviving them is enduring the extremely ugly weather and boring palette-swapped wildlife. Of course, there's also a survival mode, in which all of the above is true but you have to do all these easy, boring things twice as often. 

NMS also isn't a game about story. There's some quests, but everything is so fragmented and spread out that it's hard to parse. Your quests won't change anything. There's no coherence, there's no rising action, there's no reward. There's not even a conclusion--the game ultimately just cops out and puts you right back at the beginning. You're not required to follow the story, and you don't get any rewards for doing so. And again, there's no procedural story, either--imagine playing a version of Skyrim where there are four palette-swapped NPCs, each of which speaks in a language you initially cannot read any of at all.

NMS DEFINITELY isn't a combat game. You can get into combat, but it's laughably simple, and yet also so incredibly clumsy that it FEELS hard without actually BEING hard: it's hard to do what you want, but even harder to fail in a way that matters. There are three kinds of robots that will sometimes get angry at you, but all of which can be defeated by the genius tactic of "circle-strafing." 

NMS isn't even a game about cool spaceships. Yes, there are cool spaceships, but there are hundreds of thousands of different variations, and each system gets a random assortment of 20 that land there. So if you find a cool ship, but you wish the wings were a little different, and it was red instead of blue, guess what? You're not 10/12 attributes there, you're effectively 0/12, because you can't modify your ship's appearance AT ALL: you have to fly from system to system, hoping vainly and insanely that the 12/12 ship will just so happen to randomly show up. Also I just want to note that this is not hyperbole: it's actually that bad, so bad it would be almost impossible to exaggerate [2020 note: still true even after another dozen updates]. Literally Armored Core 1 for the PS1 had better aesthetic customization options than this. You can exchange ship spawn locations on Reddit, but that honestly is even worse, because now you have to go to Reddit.

So what is NMS? What this game is REALLY about is grinding endlessly so you can have a big inventory. If you've always wanted a big inventory, and nothing else, then I'm sorry for burying the lede--this is THE game for you! You spend the game gathering resources, which you craft into items, which you CANNOT use for ANYTHING except to either sell them, or craft them into bigger items that sell for even more. And what can you buy with the money you sell them for? Either other crafting items, or spaceships with bigger inventories but that are functionally identical in every single other way!

Everything about this game ultimately helps you in this quest for capacity. You can learn words of an alien language, not to experience a deep exploration of conflicting cultures, but so you can decode puzzles so you can get more crafting blueprints so you can make stuff to sell to get a bigger inventory. You can fly from system to system, not to discover incredible inexplicable life forms, but so you can find more valuable raw materials to craft, etc, bigger inventory. You can command an entire fleet of starships that you can send on missions, not for glorious 4X domination, but so THEY can bring you crafting materials to etc. etc. bigger inventory. You can build a sprawling planetary base so that you can, guess what, farm plants that you use as crafting materials, and build vaults that expand your inventory. The core gameplay loop is more like 2048, trying to fit as many things in your little boxes as possible, than it is like a Fallout or Elite: Dangerous.

So you grind for 50 hours for your big inventory. You went on Reddit to find where the cool ship you want spawns, and you waited 2 hours for an S-class to land. What can you do with your cool ship with its big inventory? All that's left to do will be to explore this shallow, hollow universe, which--guess what?--you could have been doing from the beginning, with your tiny starter inventory, because space fuel doesn't take up that much room in your inventory at the end of the day.

I suppose, given how much time I filled with NMS, you could say I got my money's worth out of the game. But I don't feel like I've accomplished anything. Instead, I feel like I've been freed from the grind, and the illusion of progress which is, ultimately, just for the sake of more progress, like that Flash game where you clicked a button to get achievements. 

At one point in the main quest, you meet a character who's trapped in one star system, unable to escape, and they're angry that they'll never get to see the universe. I'm just sad that in all those trillion procedural stars, there's really nothing to see after all.

Summary, this is a phenomenal game. We had anticipated this game however at launch based on feedback from those we know and reviews we did not purchase it. We did follow the progress of updates to the game. It is now the game it was advertised to be at its inception. I purchased copies for myself and my two sons.

This game is not for everyone, it is an open world space exploration game with a plethora of other features, so if that is to your liking then you will appreciate this game. There are a number of other space simulation games out there, I have a number of them, but they do not compare to what No Man's Sky has become.

Why do we like this game?

First the game is well balanced. It has a space combat capabilities but it is not the games primary focus. This is something I respect about the game. There are plenty of good space combat simulators (although I wish we could get a modernized Freespace, but I digress...) and I am glad that this is not the focus of No Man's Sky. You can collect bounties, eliminate pirates, or raid freighters for resources. There is a also a well balanced element of space craft missions. For example you can acquire freighters and frigates to complete space based objectives. I personally would like to see this aspect expanded. It would be cool to be able to travel with a group of craft on assigned missions, to leave and join the convoy at will. All you really can do is send them in groups on missions and wait for them to return. There also is a space station in every star system, which is a very smart choice on the part of the devs for obvious reasons. We also can greatly appreciate being able to use the teleporter to travel cost free between previously explored star systems via space stations.

Space flight controls are arcade style. You have several engine types depending on whether you need interstellar travel, travel within a solar system, or in a planets atmosphere. This is well developed and balanced, not being cumersome at all, except perhaps that you can not hover (you are always in motion when not in space) and your craft can not perform strafing motions.

The game focuses on exploration. The universe is truly yours to explore as one could never visit every star system in the game's universe. In addition to exploring and travelling between star systems one can also explore the surface of the planets in each star system. Planets have unique flora and fauna. There are incentives to 'scan' and archive these aspects of each planet giving detailed information. 

The game also has a construction element where you can build bases on planets of your choosing. This aspect is well developed and functional. We have found a few glitches but nothing we have not been able to work around so far. This leads us to one of the primary goals of the game...grinding...

In my opinion grinding is of aspect of a game that requires very careful consideration and design, such that it is challening enough to the player to not become bored but not difficult enough that one loses interest or becomes frustrated. At the current moment the balance in the game is very good. There are a couple of modes to adjust the difficulty of the game and the grind. As for myself and most people I know, we really want to focus on exploration and do not want to grind excessively having families, jobs, etc. One must grind to provide raw resources to produce finished products via blue prints to build fuel, structures, and basically anything that you need in the game. Once again this portion of the game is well balanced and I would caution the devs be very careful making changes.

The game also has a functional economy that works well in my opinion. You can buy and sell goods in the markets, purchase upgrades and blue prints. There are a few forms of 'currency', although each type has a different purpose.

There are three primary civilizations in the game. Diplomacy (although not directly called as such in the game) is an important factor in the game. You can improve or ruin relations in the game by performing missions for a given civilization or raiding their freighters. This is a fairly well developed part of the game as well.

One thing that really surprised me is the story lines. The primary story lines in my opinion are amazing. They are amazing because they are genuinely unique and well thought out. In addition it has taken me quite some time to get through the missions that I have and I still have not completed all of them or even most of them. Each stage of the story lines does not take to long, which is a good thing because you feel like you are making progress, but rather the stories have depth and a very large numbers of stages. It is not unusal to have 3 to 7 simulateous missions. I think it is very cool that at the end of the primary story line you can basically start over and because of the open world and breadth of the game it is very replayable. 

If you like space and a lot of freedom to explore, and enjoy both being in space as well as on the planets surface, construction, with grinding not being to intolerable, etc. get this game. If you want a space combat simulator do not bother getting this game (you can not do the equivalent of strafing in a space craft, and many other maneuvers that are standard in space simulators, the HUD is under developed, etc.)

The game crashes on occasion, currently we have no idea why as it happends to all of us, but it is infrequent, and the most recent update seemed to alleviate this issue to some degree.

Here is what we want:

1) The ability to add content to the game.

2) The ability to host our own servers. As multiplayer is currently set up in the game you can find players on your own lan or join some random server on the internet. There are NO provisions to query who is on your game, kick or ban, etc. If you really want this game to thrive we need the ability to host private and public servers our selves WITHOUT needing the run the game, that is, stand alone servers.

3) We want to be able to hover, strafe, and rotate (yaw) spacecraft. A more realistic and functional HUD would be nice. There is a bug in the game where the position of the HUD/cockpit overlay is misplaced and that is really really annoying.

4) We do not want the difficulty of normal mode or grinding in normal mode to change.

5) We want the base computer to be able to be placed in a structure.

To the devs:

Well done! and do not screw up the game by making major changes to the well balanced systems as they currently exist.

One last thing: the graphics are beautiful especially considering the kind of dynamics and complexities the game has such a deformable terrain/meshes.

Reviews.171534:
*sniffles* Oh No Man's Sky... you've grown up so fast... *grossly sobs*

Okay, so this is No Man's Sky.

It used to be a game about loneliness.  You're traversing the universe on your own, with the space suit on your back, units in your pocket, and bucket of bolts you repaired.  You weren't traveling to find anything in the beginning.  You were just... traveling. You didn't know who was where or why or what they were doing.  Every space station was desolate save for the pilots you conned out of their ships.  Even the planets were barren.  The abhorrent nature of RNG-esus created quite possibly the most grotesque "animals" known to man that could have God's creator license revoked and his universal HDD wiped.

But as the years passed No Man's Sky matured.  Slowly you came out of isolation.  You planted your roots down on those barren planets.  You made something for yourself.  After awhile you could have vehicles, missions, and then - suddenly you were traveling for a reason.  All of a sudden you were secretly fighting for the approval of factions, doing missions for money and trade, and seeking out the mysteries of the universe we've had four years to master.

Within the past year NMS gave us literal *alien ships* , a chance to explore abandoned freighters.

... it gave us the Space Anomaly.  It gave us a home in the beautiful, fucked up wasteland we once explored.  It gave us a greater purpose.  We're still travelers, and for our own reasons, but Goddammit we're traveling *together* .  Researching.  Dogfighting.  Still conning aliens out of their spaceships but that's not important.  Building bases.  It's home.

And Hello Games, even after four years - which by now most devs would give up on their game and go home - is STILL updating NMS.  They're putting in so much effort to give us what they promised and THEN some.  I gotta give these guys a helluva lot of credit.  They've done well <3

Pros:
+ The Space Anomaly is a wonderful mix of multiplayer and goal-oriented play
+ space stations have more meaning
+ missions may be bland but it gives an excuse to explore
+ trading in map data for coordinates is my favorite part; exploring a planet has never felt better
+ the crafting system is linear and relatively easy to grasp
+ flight has been drastically improved
+ the game runs like a dream now <3
+ ship class/parts upgrades are a nice incentive to keep your ship but also hunt for your perfect starfighter

Cons:
- sound design is still a little meh
- creature RNG is still hit or miss but they're getting better
- Missions are bland
- Planets still look a little flat and clay-like, mildly empty

Overall?  Even with the cons I have and the ones I've yet to encounter, NMS keeps pulling me back in for another few hours.

And I hope that it continues to bloom <3

2016/2016: gg, Hello Games.

I came back to the game because I had heard it was updated (again) in good ways and yes, IMO it has been redeemed. The game has become pretty much everything that I had personally hoped it would be originally. There are some quirky issues but nothing that can't be endured if you're wishing for an immersive (and breath-takingly beautiful) space fantasy. There are different difficulty styles to choose from so I've noticed the game has a lot to offer to a variety of players (my 10-year-old plays this in Creative Mode, for example.)

Wow, I was mad when I wrote the old review. I'm glad I gave the game another chance.

----------------------------

What’s the point in discovering new planets (and plants and animals), plus naming and uploading them, if there’s a good chance that the next time an update comes along they won’t exist anymore?

I remained a fan of the game even back when the pendulum was on the side of "hugely unpopular". Yes, I thought it was expensive and was disappointed in the lack of multiplayer. However, I defended it because it was a great experience. 

I had the most beautiful home planet. I was so fond of the animals that inhabited it. I spent hours immersed in the place, developing an attachment to its inhabitants and "story". My entire game experience was tied to that planet because it was my base, the home I looked forward to going back to after space exploration. I had hoped that if there would ever be multiplayer, I could share it with friends.

Then the new update came along and my home is gone. The planet is technically still there with the same name but it's been replaced by an unrecognizable frozen wasteland. The plants, animals, and resources it once had have also completely changed. 

It turns out that this new update has altered the game so much that our already-procedurally-generated planets have been "rerolled" to be more challenging, even if you’re playing on Normal mode like I had been. I spent hours reloading a new game, trying to generate another habitable planet like I once had, but every single one was a hellhole. 

This game used to offer an amazing dreamlike experience focused on exploration and some survival. Now it’s just another survival game but with fancy filters and the promise of very limited multiplayer. With my beautiful home taken away and with every new planet trying to kill me the experience just feels depressing.

I can no longer recommend this game because I’ve lost the trust I had left in the developers. Hello Games needs to sort out what the hell their vision is and develop some better business practices.

TL;DR: 
If you like exploratory/space-opera/survival games, do yourself the favor of playing this one. It's definitely niche, but it's worth the experience at least, and its being given a lot of love and attention.

[Main Review]:
I won't say I owe Hello Games, or its captain an apology, but I am obligated to recognize that they grappled with just about every problem that can beset a developer, or person - and overcame them. 

They fixed, then improved upon, then continued to improve upon the experience they promised. While I still have my personal issues with the game, such as:

1) the pace still feels unnecessarily slow, especially at the beginning (which is the *worst time*, guys!) 

2) arbitrary restrictions on inventory space and other mechanics (at least at the start) force a very specific, restrictive play style at the beginning

3) most aspects of shooting/combat while serviceable, still don't meet a baseline "satisfying" standard I've experienced in almost any other game

3) most importantly - the progression curve is a classic developer mistake - take the normal, functioning (enjoyable) game and then "hobble" all of those mechanics to give the "illusion of progression", rather than well, actual progression

  ...the fact remains Hello games has done something innovative, unique and special, and they've met and exceeded player expectations over and over. 

  NMS remains (sadly) not my cup of tea, but I highly recommend it for fans of the genre, and I hope the development team continues to wow us and has a long and successful career ahead of them. 

  Thank you for showing us what honesty, perseverance and redemption look like. Kudos.

Complete rework of this review on the 22nd July of 2020:

Look, i really tried to like this game. For 130 hours i tried to desperately find the fun in this game, over and over again.

Look, the basic problem that kills No Man's Sky for me, is the inane grind a player has to go trough just to actually play the game.

I want to fly and fight and built in the world. And i don't actually mind a grind if it is fun and adds to my progress or experience. I love games like Minecraft (untold hours), Terraria 280 hours), Conan Exiles (around 70 hours i think), Subnautica (probably also 200 hours at least) and many more. Hell, i even put endless hours in Dragons Dogma and Dead Cells just because the combat is so visceral and fun.  
However, when i dig in Terraria it either adds to my resources for building or it attributes to me conquering the world by cutting my path trough it and making it mine. Additionally i have to pay attention what i dig trough, because of the environmental dangers. enemies and resources around me. I don't just stand there holding the trigger, swaying the crosshair a bit to get all resources and be annoyed when a Sentinel comes around or because i have to wait to not overheat my tool or reload it.

In No Man's Sky you need to grind just to be able to go back to what you were doing. Your personal Spaceship ALONE has at the least 3 or 4 resource bars to keep filled up.

You need one resource for normal Flight, you need another resource to just start your ship, another resource for flying with afterburner between planets and ANOTHER resource to jump in between star systems. And THAT last resource you first need to craft from SEVERAL different other resources.

That is 4 resources just to keep your shit going, one of which you have to craft from at least three others which makes it 7 resources in total. And that doesn't even consider the resources you need when you want to recharge your shields or repair your armor (which you need to craft from other resources). It also does not consider the the three or four different sorts of ammunition you might need for your weapons.

AND THIS IS JUST FOR YOUR PERSONAL SPACESHIP. IT IS RIDICULOUS!

But wait! There is more! Because the same ridiculous situation happens around your personal spacesuit, your universal tool/weapons and its various modules. And it also counts for every separate spaceship, vehicle and the giant freighter you may get.
 
Your personal spacesuit has a resource bar for your health, a resource bar for your life systems and a energy bar for eventual specific shielding, like if you land on a planet that is extra hot or has an acidic atmosphere. 

This makes three more resource bars to keep filled given i have not forgotten something. And the grind to recharge all of these is not really contributing to your progress.

You only do these so you can just play the game. Do you see the problem here? There is a gem of a game under the grind here, but i can't play that because i am more busy taking care of this orgy of resource bars every four minutes then the actual game progress or even just taking in the world.

And no, Creative Mode isn't really what i want. I would not mind to have maybe one energy resource and ammunition to take care of. I also would not mind having to repair the the tools and the ships i use. I want SOME friction and challenge, not tedium.

What i would want is a game that properly balances these elements and does not make filling energy bars the main mode of the game.

 5 out of 10 for Animal Husbandry (Ark Survival Evolves Primary Game Mechanic) and Multiplayer (For its naming of things in the universe as well as Base sharing that was recently added in Patch 1.2.0, also for the 1.5 Next Update adding in Full Avatar Based Multiplayer 2.0 Beyond added in a better system of joining groups and more things to do with friends)

NMS 1.3 Atlas Rises updated review:

I am still unable to give a solid rating for this game for the same reasons I don't give Ratings to any game I review.  To each their own is my motto. 

If you love the Thrill of going someplace no one has been too.
If you want to meet people who are not stuck on MOBA's and RPG's with Levels and PVP.
If you have a need to challenge your inner "Explorer" and make the long Trek Semi-alone :)

Then No Man's Sky Atlas Rises is the Game for you.  But don't buy it at any price if you don't think you can answer the call of those 3 statements above.  I promise you that you will be more sad than Sean Murray during the time that people misunderstood his brilliant brainchild of a game.

The one thing I think has changed though is this:  No Man's Sky was a Massive Lake a Mile wide and an inch deep at release but over 3 updates, it is now about a foot deep and very easy to drown in :)

Give up on AAA 6 foot deep bucket's of water like games and come over to the really meaningful and large scope of NMS :)

NMS 1.5 Next Update Review Notes:

The Lake that is a mile wide has just gone to the 2 foot level with all the changes to No Man's Sky in Next.  We see the continuation of the development of Multiplayer in Next with Fully Realized and Customizable Avatars and 3rd Person Views.  A Universe Reset that ushers in better Planetary Atmospheric looks as well as Ringed Planets and better looking Terrain Rendering.  New Freighter Mechanics and Frigates for doing missions while you are offline or doing something in game.  

A revamp of Materials for Crafting as well as changes to Mining and Base Building without limits to where and a much expanded range of building and more parts to build structures with. New devices and systems for playing with your friends such as COOP Missions, Being able to build bases together.  Being able to carry friends in Freighters while warping to other systems. Racing Exocraft in a fully (Max 4 player) multiplayer way through crazy alien world terrains.

The full list of changes is far too long for me to include in this review and I think I will learn a lot more in the coming months while playing Next :)

Murray Nextmass To All :)

With Beyond the Game has reached its end of major developement .  A central area where people can meet.  More interactions with others through group quests and later in Synthesis more abilities to create things such as music and better looking bases.  Indeed the Lake that is NMS has gotten over 3 to 4 feet deep and is probably just as good as most games that also sell for 60$.

At this milestone in the game I would like to say something profound :)  A Game that makes its map ideas after creating its mechanics will surely fail.  A game like No Man's Sky with most of its map unexplored and Features made to work within it will last for decades to come :)  Happy New Decade in 2020 - 2030 and See you in The Greatest Exploration Game of the 2010 - 2020 Decade :)

Beyond to Origins - We are dead in the middle of 2020 and the pandemic has become the norm.  Games have become a source of safe entertainment and No Man's Sky keeps on being the game I turn to from time to time.  In Beyond we have seen various updates that have improved the overall game experience:

New Underwater Biomes in Abyss,  Byte Beat (Procedural Music Making), Exo Mech, and Procedural Derelicts in Space (Procedural Dungeons) .  Looking forward to continue playing No Man's Sky through the Origins Update 3.0.

// 2020 Update Review

I owe Sean Murray an apology. No Man's Sky in 2020, is exactly what he promised it would be in 2016. He might not have been the most astute, charismatic man, or perhaps the most comfortable under the limelight of the camera, but everything he said, at least, came true.

It's all there, and it's finally worth playing.

Best of all -- it's still improving.

Learn from this company, AAA studios. This is the bar we'll hold you up to.

/// ORIGINAL - 2016 RELEASE REVIEW (Old):

Okay, so.. open your wallet, and take out $60. You know, three crisp, $20 Jacksons.

Think about all the things you could buy with that $60. Think about it for about... 40 hours.

Now, walk over to your fireplace, and throw it into the fire.

Congratulations, you've beaten No Man's Sky.

Like many others, I was so hyped for No Mans's Sky. Watching every trailer and interview, reading articles, looking at screenshots and thought: "Damn, this is going to be so epic."

Yeah, I took the bait, I even took days off from work, so I can play this "masterpiece" when it's going to be released. When that day finally came, I was never so disappointed. It was such huge let down, there was so many missing features, blatant lies and bugs. I have refunded it and thought that this is goodbye, no way I am going to play this game ever again.

But Hello Games didn't do what was everyone expecting. They didn't take the money and run. Leaving the broken husk behind. They start working on it, keep delivering small and big updates, all for free.

From time to time I have stumbled upon trailer or news about No Man's Sky and thought: "This is cool. But I don't want to go back." Years were passing and I was getting more and more interested. Now here I am, four years later, buying it again.

In 10 days, I have played this game for 50 hours and let me tell you, it's damn good. There is so much things to do, you can spend hours just by exploring one planet. Collecting and building stuff. Then you take off and go explore the space. Visiting other planets, some are boring, but some are very cool and interesting.

Visiting space stations, learning alien languages, trading, owning a freighter, owning a fleet and send it on missions. I still didn't touch a lot of things that this game has to offer. I have only the bare-bones base, just got my first exocraft and haven' even tried multiplayer.

On foot part is well done and I can't say a bad thing about it. But space combat is not refined as in other space games. Flying is kinda clunky and battles are quite simple. Maybe it will get interesting later. But I hope that this part will gets some improvements in the future.

Yes, there are occasional bugs and stuff that irritates me, but overall this game is definitely worth a buy and fun to play.

I have to say that in my eyes, Hello Games fully redeemed themselves.

The variables are incredibly limited in my perspective. And perhaps more anoyingly to me, weapons. You have a mining laser and you have a rapid fire gun. I am not allowed to defend myself or mine a rock, but a giant gold ore deposit inches away from one is somehow perfectly fine?

I was expecting a lot from this game. Too much? Well, maybe they hyped it to be more than it actually was, and i kinda was expecting that to be the case. Yet from all the things i've seen and heard up to the eventual release, we barely have a handful of the things they said would be in it. 

Does it look pretty? Yes
Is it big? Yes
Will you ever get to see everything there is to see? Very unlikely

I have over 100 (>500 hours as of patch 3.0) hours lodged into this game, and I'm only several systems into the first galaxy so far. It should come as no surprise to say that I'm in love with this game. Sure it has it's faults, bugs and missing features, but what game comes close to the feeling of wonder and discovery.

I knew what this game was going to be, and I'm not at all disappointed, apart from the odd bug and procedural generation artifacts like buildings lodged half-way inside a hill.

I'm also a fan of games like Dear Esther, which had a weak story, but a ton of atmosphere.

I just love the feeling of being lost and alone in a huge universe, trying to survive and discovering new, interesting and beautiful worlds to explore. It has definitely scratched that itch for me.

Time will only improve this game, and I don't regret taking the plunge into the game upon release. This game isn't for everyone, but it is for me.

Update 1: I'm still plodding away at NMS, but at a reduced pace. I've upgraded everything, and now only have to 100% languages and finish the Atlas path before heading towards the centre of the galaxy to restart in another galaxy. I've now bought Elite Dangerous to fill the gaps that NMS currently is unable to. I'll head back to NMS more regularly once there are content updates.

Update 2: I somehow find myself coming back again and again. It's just such a relaxing game that I can jump into for a short or long session. I'm also beginning to unravel more of the story and lore of NMS, particularly when talking with Nada and Polo, which is beginning to explain why there are a lot of things which appear the same throughout the universe. It's all fractal patterns. Sean built a game with fractal patterns built into the simulated universe and as part of the story that goes along with it. Whether this was intended from the beginning or they brought it into the story due to the limitations of the procedural technology, it's still beautifully crafted. To really appreciate the game you need to delve deep and unlock it's hidden mysteries.

Update 3 - post patch 1.1: Loving the changes to the game. Has provided some extra purpose for visiting planets. Really looking forward to seeing what they will do next.

Update 4  - post patch 1.3: I'm even more in love with this game now. The changes and updates to the game are amazing! I'm now excited to jump back in and explore. Looking forward to seeing what happens next.

Update 5 - post patch 3.0: I am amazed at the dedication the developers have for NMS. The Origins update has breathed new life into the game. It's gone back to its roots by building on the exploration aspect of the game and improved on the amount of variation between planets. I'm looking forward to seeing what the future holds with further updates. This update has blown me away and I'm thoroughly enjoying it.

"They lied about many features for this game. They built the base for which a game could be built on, but did not finish. This game is not worth $60 let alone $20. Dont waste your money."

This was my original review.

I will stand by the statement that they lied. The situation has changed though, they have added many features and after a third attempt at the game, it now feels worth $60. 

The Positives:
Many of the visuals are very beautiful,  many of the 'existing' sounds are nice and fitting. There are multiple ways of doing things such as gathering currency (Units, nanites, quicksilver). You can take on many different self envisioned roles for your self, such as pirate, merchant/trader, farmer(to a degree), explorer, base builder,  etc.. There is a lot of options in the game right now and they continue to grow. You WILL get your money's worth for the game. Right now you will get about 2-3 hours per dollar you put into the game (about 120-180+ hours).

The Cons:
They lied about about a very larger amount of features in the game at launch. While the game maybe good now, their word can no longer be taken at face value, and its going to be a VERY long time before it can be with any or ANYTHING. There are minor graphical issues when mining terrain, such as large chunks looking like playdough, this will fix it self though after a few moments. While the existing sounds in the game are good, their is little that makes sound outside of player interactions; a few ambient sounds, very very very little music (Whats there is not all that inspiring), and there are a few audio bugs such as with your starship not getting quieter when you leave the atmosphere, but instead going to 200% volume, very annoying. Base building is nice, but the option that determines how many base objects are visible at a time seems to do nothing, causing a lot of pop in and fade ins and outs when in slightly more populated bases. Overall, while there are many different roles and routes you can take, many of them are quite shallow right now such as farming or space piracy.

Some things I fear will eventually be included:
Loot boxes, pay to win options, etc.. It would be very easy to convert some of the options in the game to these, such as existing cosmetics, changing quicksilver to be 'premium' currency, moving S class ships or making a higher ranking of ships premium/payed content, etc.

Somethings I hope to see added  or expanded:
-COLORS, I cant stress enough for those of us who enjoy base building, we NEED an expanded color pallet with better control of colors and not just presets. I want to control the main color and accent separately, similar to how you can for your suit/character. Don't just add customizability, but a full on color plate /wheel. The existing colors are pretty stale tbh.
-Starship Customization, such as color, models, etc. IT could get pricey, but a fully customized starship. I know its supposed to be a luck of the draw, but you could make it so certain parts could only be obtained after finding a ship with those parts, or make those parts a chance drop when scrapping a ship with them.
-More plants to grow and cultivate, add more depth to farming, and more variations for the same farmable resources. For instance instead of the vine shelf thing for carbon, lets do some trees or bushes. Fertilizers would be nice too, maybe some that make the next harvest grow faster, or yield a percentage more. Maybe allow us to harvest soil from each plants needed biome to make the plants grow faster or yield more. I mean, my ideas for farming are a bit lacking, but the current system for plant farming is a bit shallow in my opinion.
-Expand the base building parts. Wood, concrete, and metal need a bit more expansion, such as upside down triangle walls, or floor patterns, part of it comes back to the color options. Decals are few and far between, not to mention deleting them is buggy and tricky to do. SIGNS! For those of us who have larger, sprawling, and confusing bases, we would like signs for ourselves, and for other players. Something  thats not as clunky or unresizable as the message device.
-Better color control/options 
-Piracy, needs expanded. Sure, smaller ships get blown up, but make haulers bigger, so we can board them once we disable them, but let us board other ships and not just freighters! While combat is not the focus of the game, allowing a wider option in space would be nice, like boarding, or leaving a minefield.
-Deeper planets, bigger meteors. Remove the terrain edit limitations, make planets deeper, and let us make subterranean  bases. Make bigger meteors so that we can land/attach to them and make meteor mining/farming a thing.
-Better Color control/options
-Destroyed planets, RIVERS, canyons, etc. Also allow for water manipulation!
-Enemy NPC's.
There are so so so many options out there for them to add, like better color control/options : D

All in all the game is worth its price now and I recommend it!

I suppose it's time to once again update my No Man's Sky review. I purchased the game on release day and although I wasn't as disappointed as a lot of players (because I hadn't paid attention to any of the promos for the game so genuinely didn't know what to expect) I still shelved it after only 8 hours.

I played again when whatever release introduced base building but only for 2 hours before once again uninstalling and forgetting about it.

Finally, when I saw game play for the Origins update on YouTube, it was the first time that I felt I was looking at a game I would happily purchase again. I had roughly 10 hours in the game by that time and in the couple weeks since reinstalling it with the update, I've gotten up to 100 hours. It is simply a better game in every way I care about. Granted, I skipped a lot of updates so some of the things that I enjoy came out prior but I don't think they would have been as fun without the things added in Origins.

I happily recommend this game now whereas before I recommended it with many, many caveats. There's still plenty of things I wish were better but I can't think of any game I've ever played in which that wasn't true. It's a shame that it took 4 years for us to reach what I'd consider 1.0 of this game but as I wasn't waiting around with baited breath or kicking myself for buying it, it was worth the wait for me. There's tons to do and unlike most of the "survival sandbox" games I own, the survival difficulty of NMS is ACTUALLY PRETTY FRIGGIN' DIFFICULT at first. To the point that it isn't even fair, to be honest. My first time back I spawned in an area with absolutely no caves or sodium nearby and died twice from environmental damage.

The team seem to have given up on a lot of the ideas that made the original NMS idea seem to good to be true (and turn out to actually be too good to be true) but I think that was a good decision as they simply wouldn't have worked without redesigning much of the game from scratch. There is no persistent universe in which you can randomly encounter other people's planets unless you specifically choose to go looking for them. As far as I can tell, every time you start a new game you get your own private seed of a galaxy to explore at your leisure without having to worry too much about other players coming in and discovering all the planets before you can get to them. While I can appreciate that, I do somewhat wish there was a way to accidentally stumble upon abandoned player bases and such without actively deciding to enter multiplayer systems.

Even writing this review I am getting the itch to play some more even though I've been trying out other games for the past week. There's just so much to do. When the game was released in 2016, you basically could only hop from planet to planet, naming animals and rocks, and eventually finish the really short and unfulfilling plot which infinitely looped over and over. That's all been scrapped in favor of several plots going on at the same time (and much lengthier). You can command fleets of merchant ships and industrial ships, collaborate with other players on gigantic cities, or simply wander your own huge galaxy solo. Even the eerily empty private systems have tons to discover.

No Man's Sky is finally one of those games that everybody enthusiastic about space exploration games must own.

I have played No Man's Sky for over 100 hours now, and I can say without a doubt that it is totally my kind of game.

The problem is, it might not be your kind of game.  Read on, dear customer, read on.

The first thing you must understand about No Man's Sky is the gameplay, or more generally, the goal.  The big question of "what do I DO in No Man's Sky" is best addressed by, "explore and harvest planets at your leisure in an effort to work up to being able to warp to other planets and systems of planets to do the same thing".  This game isn't really about the survival, or the mining, or the upgrades you get, or the languages you learn, or the milestones you achieve, or the crafting recipes you find.  It's not even about the plants, animals, and rocks that you catalog and collect money from uploading.  It's not about the space battles you have, or the factions of aliens you meet, or flying in any realistic manner whatsoever.  And it's 100% not about leaving anything more than the most superficial of impact on the game world.

It is not about your personal power.  Sure, you can do more and go more places when you have more, but that's still not what this game is about.

This game is about cresting over a hill, seeing the sprawling mass of land before you, and just drinking in the place you are, right then, right there.  It's seeing those planets in the distance and either knowing as they hang in the sky, like some 70s sci-fi novel cover, that you could go there, or that you've already been there.  It's finding that cave that just sings, or happening across a great beast trying to climb that side of a mountain.

It's about moments, about the journey, about making up stories for the planets in your head.  It's about leaving a planet when you want to, and looking for something else.  The elements in the game that you can achieve are not the point, and if you think every creature and rock and plant are the same, you aren't really looking that hard at them.  Not hard enough.

This game is a love-letter to those book covers, those sprawling, desolate vistas, huge, strange columns of rock, and yes, even the occasional grassy, pleasant planet.  It's a love letter to the idea that you could not own, or even greatly impact those images, only visit them, and share them with others.  This is not your sky, that's in the name.  You own nothing but what you can take with you.  And the writing, while generally sort of shallow, is also akin to those old, musty books.

This isn't a game about doing what you want in the midst of space.  It's about experiencing everything we think of as mundane in games.

If that's not for you, if you want “real” flight controls, a hard-line story that rewards your effort, deep, meaningful alien interaction, quests, or even the ability to play with friends, this is not the game for you.  This game is part harvesting game, part walking simulator, and part point and click adventure game, wrapped around a universe that is expansive as it is small.

It may not be your kind of game, but it's mine, and I heartily recommend it.

It's October 18th, 2020, and I'm updating this review because a lot has happened to this game since release.  This now IS a game about doing what you want in the midst of space.  Of making bases and establishing yourself, of a more coherent storyline and lore throughout the too-big world of No Man's Sky. Aliens might not give meaningful interaction, but there's a chance that they'll give you a quest, or provide options to learn their language or practice it with them, there's specific quest NPCs on every space station, as well as several mostly unseen guilds that put out these random commissions that give more or less specific types of quests; mercenaries are about taking out pirates or depots or some other attack action, Explorer quests are usually about interacting with flora and fauna, and trader quests commonly ask you to buy/make/find some item and deliver it. There are even multiplayer features.  Giant worms on various planets (I've seen multiple planets with them thus far), freighters in mid-space with their own procedurally generated "dungeon" and story inside them, various other encounters of the random kind, both in space and on planets, sometimes crashed ships still have NPCs by them and helping fix the ship gives a reward, the tech is given out through tech trees now, there's a LOT more to this game.

If "part walking sim, part harvesting survival game" wasn't your thing, well, by god are there more options than you can shake a Vy'keen Dagger at now.

This game was a very interesting experience for me. Having watched a few hours of gameplay from the PS4 version and looking up more game footage and talks with developers, I bought it just before it released in my time zone, thinking it would be a fun Minecraft-type experience with some sweet space combat that came up as I circled over completely different worlds and places with new races or species or discoveries to be made, and my friends could jump in and out. At this time of writing, I have jumped to 6 different star systems, spending anywhere from 1-5 hours on any of the 10 planets I've seen.

There are no Minecraft elements. From all the descriptions I had heard, there was supposed to be some element of creating, whether it was a base, or yourself, or your ship. But thusfar, you can't build a base, and even if you could, how are you supposed to get back to it without being able to look at a map or set a waypoint? Sure, you could change a few names to make it easier, but that doesn't really make you able to track it at will (as far as I've seen). You don't really get to build a ship, you're just kind of tossed a tin can and there's no way to alter how it looks or how it flies in or out of the atmosphere, and if you want more room, it seems like you just have to buy a new ship. It doesn't really support zero-g combat, because it doesn't conserve your momentum. The species you encounter could hardly be called new or random, because it looks like they peeked at the Spore creature creator, took ten animals, and occasionally swap around pieces. A lot of times, the plants from one planet to the next are entirely the same, and even from system to system. I really wish by aligning myself with one faction it would impact how the other factions perceived me, but it seems like all you do is learn new words that might come in handy in the future, and there's really no problem with siding with all of the races. It lacks a conflict that makes my choice feel worthwhile, and leaves me dissatisfied. 

As it stands, this just feels like a wholly incomplete experience, and it burns me that I paid for it. It is still VERY much for a niche market, but seems to have been advertised as a game that everyone could enjoy together (like Minecraft).

Tried playing multiplayer from scratch with a friend.
Both the repair your starship and the build a base mission glitched out, luckily was still able to fly my ship however.
For the build your base mission i had to build my own base in a different area just for the missions.
Why can't a party-based quest progress exist, as an option, or have the game recognize/share some specific progress? Base building research is also not shared, effectively multiplying the costs by the number of players if everyone wants to be able to build everything.

NAVIGATION!
The worst mechanic in the game is navigation, which is ironic, because it's one of the core mechanics. Here's the shortcomings in my opinion:

- Only one personal marker. Want to add a new marker, or accidentally pressed E in scanner mode? your old marker is now gone, great.
- No planetary map. Want to see accurately where on the planet you are, be able to navigate a route, use compass directions? Nope. all you get is a very tiny marker in the discovery menu, and a rough coordinate system in your starship.
- Visited locations you know when you visit a building of interest, like a huge trading tower with lots of NPCs you want to interact with time and time again? Or when you used a beacon and you really just liked the view from that area? Welp, good luck finding them again, because there's no marker or coordinate info on places you've been to. You can only see a tiny screenshot from a beacon in the discovery menu. and you can only see the most recent six! 
- Claimed starships. Did you find a crashed starship that you might want to salvage or repair for yourself? Did you claim it, but not put down a custom marker, because you had an important marker elsewhere and didn't want to lose that one due to my first point? Welp, you're probably never gonna find that ship again. Once you have accessed a distress beacon, it will never show up again, and your claimed ship will have no indicator when you are on the planet, unless it's basically in direct sight. There goes your 6 million credits ship you were gonna sell, just because you needed some more materials to repair it.
- Marker tracking: The button to track a marker is the same as placing a custom marker, meaning that accidentally removing your important marker when trying to track something in scanner mode is pretty common. Most markers disappear properly when collected, because they are one-time use. Not so much for resource nodes though. you cannot know if an ore patch has already been mined by you or a friend of yours.
- Menu navigation: The build menu, inventory, quick access menu, and escape menu are all completely different menus with different buttons, and navigating them can be quite annoying. The interaction between menus with certain buttons is also inconsistent. Right click might do one thing in one menu, but something else in another. Want to exit out of the build menu? hope you didn't expect escape to work, because that will just open the escape menu! Want to leave a shop? only right click will work! Quick access menu navigates similarly to the build menu, but options are hidden behind far too many subcategories or confusing names. Most of the quick access options aren't even that useful. You can bind hotkeys 0-9 for some quick access actions but a pretty obvious action missing from that is selecting your multi-tool primary weapon. The only way to swap from e.g. beam to gun is to cycle through your options. 

Controls:
Although it isn't as bad as it was at launch, a lot of the mouse and keyboard controls are still hold mouse or button and hold click to pick up, move cursor, click to place down. It's not a huge problem but it can get a bit annoying. Flight controls with mouse and keyboard are very strange, the tethered control sensitivity and delay makes it impossible to do quick manouvres, and the locked control lags behind and sometimes just has a mind of its own. You really aren't in control, you're more suggesting a movement.


While the game has received massive amounts of content it still severely lacks improvements to:
- New player experience (also for multiplayer)
- NAVIGATION (including menus)
- UI
- Controls (especially flight)
- Economy

"I don't believe I've written many reviews for games here on Steam but I feel compelled to for No Man's Sky.

Somewhere out there in No Man's Sky's procedurally generated universe is a group of players who this magic never faded for. Given time, effort, and a series of content and patches by the developers I believe NMS could really be a great game. Reviews.195585:
[H1]Where do I even start now with this game. It's sure not what it was at launch...[/H1]

Fast recap time. No Man's Sky when it launched was a -mess- , it was an interesting mess to be sure, but it was a mess. One which showed both the potential and pitfalls of procedurally generated content. There was a game in there, somewhere, but it was buried under masses of bugs, and a lack of content beyond the concept that sure, there was a million planets, but much like Elite:Dangerous, it's not exactly saying much when many of those planets look and feel kinda the same. Ditto for the ships, and the wildlife, and the rocks, and the trees. It became a sortof homogeneous mush that didn't quite -work-.

Hello Games could have taken the money and run. Given the sheer backlash, it would have been easily the most sensible thing to do, shut down the studio, collect their fees from the game individually, and wait out the storm before reforming under a new name. Instead they did what Frontier has conclusively failed to do with Elite Dangerous and what CGI are threatening to fail to do with Star Citizen.

They've turned around a hot mess and created out of the raw materials a masterchef special.

Right now all it's missing is a knob of butter and a dash of salt (and you can throw those into your dish which you can cook for Space Gordon Ramsay who will then berate you for your substandard cooking efforts).

[H1]So wait, this is legit good now?[/H1]

It's better than good. It's *excellent*. It's doing all the things that Elite Dangerous promised to do and it's doing them without charging you for them. Cosmetics? Free. You just need to do missions in game, scoop up some quicksilver for your efforts and visit the -in game- cosmetic shop and buy up whatever your greedy heart desires. In ship bobbleheads? You *pay* for those in other games. Here - Free. Same deal. 

Freighters (a.k.a. Fleet Carriers), okay sure you can't run commodity shops out of them, but you can run fleet expeditions out of these, and you're not being hammered for weekly rental for your freighter, in fact, the reverse, you get REWARDED for visiting your frigates on a semi-regular basis. You get REWARDED for sending your fleets out to the distant bits of the galaxy. 

Ships visit your hangar and you can trade with them or even buy them if you want to add them to your collection (and with the ability now to scrap and salvage ships you no longer need, you can keep your personal fleet very manageable, it's -fantastic-). You can find all sorts of freighters, from small junkers right the way through to massive capital ships bristling with defences (which will terrify you when they leap to you in VR).

[H1]And the hits just keep coming.[/H1]

Hello games have, incrementally and over time, got steadily closer to the original vision they presented in that hype trailer. They're not *quite* there yet, but they've gone from being miles and miles away to the point that if you squint, you can just about see it now. I always asserted if they got -to- the hype trailer levels of capability that it would be the game to "end them all" because it would be so far ahead of everything else that it would essentially redefine what a lot of games have to reach for to be worth playing. Naturally it never lived up to the hype so we never got to experience the whole genre-redefining fever-dream Sean Murray had, yet... here we are.

[H1]So what does it need now to get to that point where the game hits the final high notes?[/h1]

It needs actual threat. Not from other players, but from the universe itself. The aliens bursting from eggs if you have the temerity to mess with them is a good start, so is the underwater stuff, but now hello games needs to have more than just the sentinels to tie it together. There needs to be those massive capital ship fights that -you- can get involved with both either as an independent pilot or as a freighter pilot. There needs to be big, nasty creatures that are massive threats on extreme planets that can ruin your day. The aliens from the eggs need to coalesce into something that's more than just "WTF IS THAT" on the first encounter but then just a nuisance after that. It needs alien warriors, alien ranged mobs, and alien bosses.

It needs a world that introduces both danger and opportunity. That's the last remaining step. Everything else is there, all the building blocks have been assembled, you now have pretty much all the tools to engage with the universe, now all that's left is for the universe to say to you "Fite me, if you think you can".

With that, this game will have a universe that is going to last you into the thousands, possibly even tens of thousands of hours.

All for forty quid.

Give that some thought. Warframe requires significant grind to get into some of the really interesting stuff. Elite Dangerous is more a second job (and the endgame stuff even moreso), Star Citizen - who *knows* where that's going.

[H1]Closing thoughts[/H1]

This game is literally one significant development step off of being able to convincingly be ahead of *the lot*.

The launch should be remembered, but perhaps now it should be time to forgive it. The game we have on our hands now is not the game that was dropped on us at launch. What we have now is -worth- getting into.

Verdict: [b]Highly Recommended. But good god Hello Games, you had to really turn this boat around...[/b]

This game has been a massive disappointment. 

It's been gutted. Which is a shame because it has so much potential. Most of the content that was shown even up until the past few months has not made it into the release version. It's either land with ponds, oceans with very small islands. There are no continents (as far as I can see).

I've been playing this game since it's release and back then, I've already been enjoying it (despite the underwhelming lack of.... Pretty much everything shown in it's trailer). Something about it just vibed with me. Walking around on a planet, looking at alien creatures, looking up and thinking "Huh there's a planet up there, let's go there" AND JUST GOING THERE within a minute is just amazing. That's my dream. And that's been in the game from the start.
The updates kept on streaming in in what feels like 4 month intervals, and while some updates brought in questionable stuff literally no one asked for (like the synthesis update - players were enabled to compose music IN THE GAME ???????), Hello Games are pushing this game further and further in the right direction. At this point, it's fair to say the game has actually exceeded what was shown in that first trailer. 

The gameplay in No Man's Sky is.... what you make of it, really. It's a bit like Minecraft in many ways, as there are storylines you can follow by completing missions, but if you don't feel like doing that then fine, you can still enjoy the game your own way and even unlock items that would unlock by completing missions in other ways. 
Personally, for the past 200 hours of gameplay i mostly spent my time warping from system to system, just exploring what literally no one has ever seen (if someone else has been in a system before you, the game tells you) and just vaguely following the story lines. I've aquired a freighter that i store my ships and items in, and from which i'm coordinating missions that my fleet of specialist vessels complete. 
There are a handful of ship types to choose from, depending on your individual playstyle. For example, there are haulers, which, as their name would suggest have a large cargo space but are big, clunky and don't maneuver very well. In contrast, there are also fighters which are my personal favorite kinds of ships. They usually look badass and handle extremely well, plus as their name would suggest - they are made for combat. They have a higher base damage output that can be enhanced by upgrading it's weapons systems in numerous ways, depending on the playstyle. Their big drawback however is poor cargo capacity. BUT WAIT! You can actually expand said cargo capacity and actually make your tiny fighter a jack of all trades! If you spend enough time aquiring upgrades for storage space and hyperdrive, you are looking at a perfect ship that is worth way more than it initially was when you first bought it. 
All this goes to show that the amount of customizability in this game is pretty good. What i said about ships is about the same for the player's suit, multitools, freighters, and even the ground vehicles. Everything is pretty customizable. Preddygood.

I love this game, but there are still issues. The multiplayer is now [i]there[/i] but it's by no means good. People have reported lots of problems with synchronization and just... glitches that make the Multiplayer less fun than it could be. You can meet in-game yes, but cooperative missions are often clunky and unfun due to numerous issues.
Another issue in No Man's Sky is combat. It's not good. On ground, it's boring and also kinda glitchy (e.g. sentinel drones going through walls of factory buildings but not attacking you) and in space, it's pretty fun at the start when you don't have good weapons and shields but as soon as you are rocking that A class fighter with upgrades, you just annihilate any space enemy within seconds. At that point in the game, a pirate interception is more of a waste of time than an actual thread. Why are there no harder pirates (and better rewards than some chromatic metal and/or herox)? 
The Halloween 2020 update introduced a new currency to the game: Tainted metal. It can be used to buy black market upgrades among other things. Tainted metal can only be gained by completing the, in my opinion super tedious derelict freighter missions. I'd love to have another way of getting tainted metal.
As stated earlier, you can customize pretty much everything in this game. Everything but the look of your ship! I would love to give my favorite ship some new parts that make it look better. Heck, even just being able to give it another colour would make me happy! Please make this happen, Hello Games :)

As stated earlier, the dev team keeps updating NMS and I have good faith in them continuing until every citizen on earth can ride crab aliens. And you know what, a player that has bought the game at launch received all the previous updates (including being able to play NMS in VR)  FOR FREE.
This is no GTAV BS that requires you to spend 200 IRL bucks on top of the game's price to just get started in multiplayer. This is an all-inclusive space holiday.

Would i recommend this game? Yes, absolutely. At this point it's got some enjoyable way to play it for a lot more people than it did at the start. It's great. Would I pay 60 buck for it? Yeah I would, but obviously if you see it on discount, you should have a better deal on your hands.

Thanks and have fun

Imagine you appear at an unknown place that you've never been there before and what are around you are nothing alike what you've seen before. This should be your first impression when you enter the game at this moment of the game. 

It took me times,... a lot but to me it was worth it. But, yes, "BUT", this game is repetitive and empty. It supposed to be an exploration game but what the devs trying to do is set you in one place with base building features. This is not necessary since you can build stuffs on the freighter, a mobile-base. But I hate how devs trying to add more stuffs for it. Meanwhile exploration are plain and empty. 

Yeah, I'm really not getting why bytebeat is a thing.

I'll preface this whole rant with, I love NMS, because it probably wont seem like it from here to the end. It comes from the frustration that endless fluff gets added in while the core of the game is still just kind of...meh.

Remember the first trailers for the game? I remember seeing dense forests, big freaking animals, huge ruins that looked like they would be able to house a decent sized dungeon, planets that looked like you'd want to explore them forever. Mysterious portals that took you to some unknown location. When Murray said he found himself in an ocean that was so deep he couldnt get to the bottom with his gear, I was amazed.

They made an entire universe that is in dire need of life. They need to work on how planets work. you can fly for five seconds above ANY planet and you've seen literally all you need to see. To me it's not even that the planets aren't unique. They are. They're just all uniquely bland. How are there no waterfalls but there's a music editor? All mountains look like some kid just made a mound of sand on the beach. Not a single river but, hey, you can ride that space cow.

Speaking of space cows, they're on what, 95% of planets. Every other animal just looks similar to one you saw the other day. Scorpion spiders with crab claws, space cows with scales, squirrel birds and a small trex! This ones nosferatu hands are bent upwards though! Not down!

Who knows, maybe they'll get back on track and cut the fluff. I want to scan a planet, get a hit on some old ruins, and when I get there, not see the same assortment of useless bridges, golden balls and three story towers. or the one medium sized platform with a building and a stair case.

Sean Murray is terrible. Some fanboy of this game says the devs can do whatever they do with the game and I don't have a right to complain or quit the game if I don't like it but,... I paid for the game and it's my game, I didn't rent it. I will quit complaining about it if, they refund me.

Unfortunately, I will have to echo the thoughts of the majority of other negative reviews for No Man's Sky. To keep it simple I will do some pros and cons of the two hours I put into the game.

Pros:
[list]
[*] The game looks fantastic overall. The visuals are on par with other AAA titles.
[*] Exploration is fun, and I thoroughly enjoyed every planet I came across.
[*] Entering and exiting moons/planets from your ship is awesome, and something I have looked forward to.
[*] Procedural generation of plants/animals/planets is a plus for me even if it can get a bit repetitive at times.
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*] FPS is entirely too low even on top notch systems. AKA poor optimization (likely to change I hope).
[*] Combat on the ground was slow and not very fun at all.
[*] Sentinels get alerted too often/easy.
[*] Field of view is off. It feels as if I am both 2 foot tall, and I have my face pushed against the screen.
[*] I never felt like I truly discovered anything. Each planet already has NPC outposts and ships flying over which makes me feel like I am just second-hand discovering everything.
[*] Interaction with Alien races is very limited, and not enough variants in these.
[*] Repetitive crafting, resource gathering with no real deviation or goal.
[*] Micro-managing multiple systems feels more like a job than anything fun.
[*] Lack of intuitive space combat.
[*] Lack of systems to make NPC interactions and discovery feel more meaningful.
[/list]

I have refunded the game at this time, and as others before me have said I would only recommend it with a $20 or lower price tag. I truly hope the game improves, but for now the lack of any depth will make me stay distant for the near future.

Zen Everest Simulator 2016 - "I climb mountains because they are there".

This is a B list game with A list beauty at an AA price.  Some games enter Alpha with this much to do, but never as polished as this is.  Some few technical glitches are experienced by many, but then this is a company the size of other company's accounting departments, they have done very welll to get such perfection in deterministic equations.  And they have taken their time making this, with some of the files left in the background pointing to PS3 and XBox360 as targets.

Grav has vehicles and multiplayer, but not the variety of creatures or terrain.  Ark has better creatures, but not the variety.  Starbound has the terrain, the creatures, but the worlds are smaller and 2D like ant-farms.  Privateer and older Elite based games had the ship combat refined better than this, but very few games allowed space-atmosphere re-entry, and none of those allowed you to cruise at high altitude like this.  Very few games have ever tried to be this ambitious in reach, and at times this game does over-reach.

Full price is a laugh, wait till Hello Games finish putting the gears into the engine or get it on sale.  All the same, I rarely feel this calm and relaxed while playing a walking simulator.  I have seen some ugly rocks, but I have seen some beautiful vistas too.

----- Above review is from 16 Aug, 2016, below 18 Sep, 2019 -----
What's changed?  Nearly everything.  It's now almost wonderful enough for it's stated price, with ground vehicles, a submarine and the addition of lots of items in underwater biomes.  Building in multiple standards, with the same building possible in freighters.  Oh, and freighters are mobile hangars and bases.  Teleports between player made bases and most NPC stations.  Quests, we actually have them now.  Not much more than fetch and "find this place", but the story can take a few twists and is enjoyable to read, harsh in it's philosophy.

But then, each update has been a wonderful time of exploration, again.
Yeah, I still love the game, and I still recommend this.  I have spent days playing it, so can it be all that bad?

Reviews.211402:
Overall, I would say that Hello Games has greatly improved the disappointing game they released years ago. It is now one of the better survival games available on the market and is  worth playing if you like survival games.

Exploration: The universe is procedurally generated so you have essentially unlimited worlds. This was one of the key selling points at launch but the variation in the procedurally generated worlds was quite limited hence the "wide as an ocean, deep as a puddle" remarks it had received. Now it has been updated drastically to improve this generation as well as lots of additional content to fill the hole. There is a story to the game which serves as the baseline for "What do I do?" for those that aren't keen on doing their own thing. The game offers a social hub where you can interact with other players, invite them to your crew, and take on bounties/contracts across the galaxy.

Combat: Combat is generally simple, you have ground combat with your space laser that you can add to that changes it to fire grenades, automatic rifle, etc. You generally fight the fauna on dangerous planets or the *Sentinels* which are basically Space Police.

Survival: The game is relatively easy to play once you get off the starting planet (Do be prepared for a harsh start to the game; it tries to teach you how to play on a toxic planet but it's pretty tough). Base building is pretty fleshed out with decent prefab structures and also fully custom bases to build.

Vehicles: You have a simple spaceship to begin with. You can upgrade your own spaceship, find new destroyed ships to repair around the worlds, trade or buy ships from NPCs found across the galaxy. On the planets, you will be able to build different structures that allow for small cars, exo suits, trucks and such. You can have freighter class ships which serve as your "space base" as well as sending your own AI off to complete various missions for you; your freighter is essentially your mobile command centre.

[h1]2020[/h1]
Reposting, since editing doesn't refresh reviews.

This game has fully redeemed itself, numerous updates have been added since I last played, including:
[list]
[*]Coop, with seamless interaction with players you may encounter (and a universe hub).
[*]Ownership of frigates and other capital-sized ships that you can land on and manage a fleet to send on missions.
[*]Base building, both on planet and in a frigate, with teleporters that can link to bases belonging to you, your friends, your group, and NPC space stations. Underwater bases are an option.
[*]Real differences in ships, and on-planet exocraft (cars, submarines, etc) including fuckin' [i]mechs[/i].
[*]A shitload of satisfying incremental upgrades and customization, though customization of the cosmetic nature is not quite as fleshed out.
[*]Better inventory management by default, with the "classic" rules delegated to "survival" mode.
[*]A huge expansion on weapons in the game, both on foot and in ship (not to mention the new options in the addition of exocraft).
[*]Produce farming, taming/riding/farming creatures, and even more.[/list]

It's not perfect, and it won't appeal to everyone. It can be a little floaty at times, but overall it is profoundly improved. 

I'm no stranger to failure. A situation like [i]No Man's Sky[/i] would prompt most to walk away, start over. Criticism was deserved, but how often do we see developers try to fix things to states that were originally promised? To work to include features that were fished out of the excitement of developing something?

Yeah, I took a dump on this game; "No, Don't Buy" and "My mind is blown!" memes were some of my favorite at the time. However, keeping that opinion in the face of these changes is fucking stupid, and I'm glad I took the time to check it out again. In development of a game, if good results are the goal, if mistakes were acknowledged and fixed, if efforts were both earnest and effective... continuing to be mad about how the game released 4 years ago is an aspect of someone who can't objectively assess the [i]current[/i] situation of something. There are so many games that, over time, actually become worse, muddled, or lose the interest of the community that supported the game in the first place. Additionally, this has been done with [i][b]NO DLC[/b][/i]. 

[i]No Man's Sky[/i] is, [i][b]currently[/b][/i] a great game. I have hopes it will become even better with time.

I originally bought this game day 1, and like everyone else was sorely disappointed to find an empty tech-demo of a game. 4 years later, everything has changed.

With this now being a live-service game, I feel it deserves another shot at the spotlight. Several updates since the first major update have turned this game around with Hello Games being, in my opinion, one of the best developers to continually update their game well past the initial year. It took me less than 10 hours to "complete" the game on launch, but I now have over 80 hours (as of posting this) of playing with the new updates. I still haven't gotten to the "end game" yet, as there is so much to do.

Exploration no longer feels like a boring walking sim with a constant nagging of resource depletion, the story is no longer hiding behind a vague, veiled mystery where nothing leads to nothing, and there are far more interesting things in this game that it has kept me interested for four days straight since giving it another go.

I cannot go through every single thing I like about it, like base building, ships, upgrade, and so on; but I will say that if you're looking for a space sim, this is the one to try out. Do not let the procedural generation thing deter you, as I believe Hello Games has nailed how to make procedural generation actually interesting to play rather than solely relying on loose computerized randomness to have appeal - they have fine tuned the generation in this game to actually MEAN something now.

I will say, the only difference between this game and say, Star Citizen, is this one is actually playable and ongoing.
